snappy: A federal program that forces drugmakers to sell heavily discounted medicines to hospitals and clinics serving low-income patients — controversial because of how the savings get used.
detail: Created in 1992, 340B requires manufacturers to give qualifying safety-net providers steep discounts (often 25-50% off list price) on outpatient drugs. The program has ballooned in size and become a flashpoint: pharma argues hospitals pocket the savings instead of passing them to patients, while hospitals say it funds critical care. You'll see 340B fights surface in earnings calls, congressional testimony, and lawsuits between manufacturers and HRSA.
plain: A US rule that forces drug makers to sell medicines cheaply to hospitals and clinics that treat lots of low-income patients.

snappy: A blood test that captures average blood-sugar control over the past three months — the single most important number in diabetes care, and a near-universal trial measurement.
detail: A1C measures the percentage of hemoglobin that has glucose stuck to it — the higher your blood sugar, the higher the number. Diabetes is diagnosed at 6.5% and most patients aim for under 7%. Almost every diabetes drug trial uses A1C reduction as the primary measure of efficacy. You'll see A1C cited in every Phase 3 readout for diabetes drugs, in formulary justifications for newer agents, and in HEDIS quality metrics that drive insurer behavior toward better diabetes management.
plain: A blood test that shows your average sugar level over the last few months — the headline number doctors use to check diabetes.
A major cancer-research society whose meetings showcase the early laboratory science behind future treatments.
snappy: The major society for laboratory cancer research, where early science and translational data debut.
detail: AACR is more bench-science focused than ASCO; its annual meeting often hosts first-in-human and mechanistic data that mature into later clinical readouts. You'll hear AACR in any discussion of early-stage oncology pipelines.

plain: The drug company behind Humira, now built around its successor immunology drugs Skyrizi and Rinvoq.
snappy: The maker of Humira — and a case study in building a post-blockbuster franchise around Skyrizi and Rinvoq.
detail: AbbVie was spun out of Abbott around Humira, the best-selling drug ever, and engineered a soft landing past its patent cliff with immunology successors Skyrizi and Rinvoq plus the Imbruvica oncology franchise. You'll hear AbbVie in any patent-cliff or immunology discussion.

plain: The simple difference in how often something happens between two groups — if 10% drops to 6%, that's a 4-point reduction.
snappy: The *plain-arithmetic* drop in risk — one group's event rate minus the other's — the honest counterweight to a flashy relative risk.
detail: Subtracts the treated group's event rate from the control's, giving the real-world benefit in percentage points rather than a ratio. Its inverse is the number needed to treat. A therapy can boast a large relative risk reduction while its absolute risk reduction stays tiny when the disease is rare. You'll hear absolute risk reduction demanded by skeptical clinicians and HEOR reviewers weighing whether a benefit justifies the price.

snappy: An FDA fast-track that lets a drug reach patients based on early evidence — but requires the company to confirm benefit in follow-up trials, or risk getting yanked.
detail: Accelerated approval relies on a surrogate measure — like tumor shrinkage instead of survival — to grant approval years earlier than full evidence would allow. The pathway has been controversial: Aduhelm (aducanumab) for Alzheimer's was accelerated, then commercially failed. Companies must run confirmatory trials post-approval, and the FDA can withdraw the drug if benefit doesn't hold. You'll hear "accel approval" on every oncology earnings call and at ASCO when companies discuss launch timing.
plain: A faster green light from the FDA based on early hints a drug works, with a catch — the company must later prove it really does.

snappy: A class of blood-pressure drugs that blocks an enzyme the body uses to constrict blood vessels — first-line for hypertension, heart failure, and protecting the kidneys.
detail: ACE inhibitors — lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril — and the closely related angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs, like Diovan/valsartan) are workhorse cardiovascular drugs, all generic and prescribed by the millions. The 2018 valsartan recalls over nitrosamine contamination became one of pharma's biggest manufacturing crises. You'll hear ACE/ARB on cardio earnings calls as the durable generic baseline newer mechanisms have to compete with, and in FDA Form 483 discussions when API supply-chain quality surfaces.
plain: A common blood-pressure pill that stops the body from squeezing its blood vessels tight.

snappy: A chemical that releases hydrogen ions in water — sour-tasting, often corrosive, and central to many physiological processes.
detail: Stomach acid (hydrochloric acid, pH ~1.5-3.5) is one of the most concentrated acids in nature, and managing it is a multi-billion-dollar pharma category — H2 blockers (famotidine), proton-pump inhibitors (omeprazole, esomeprazole). 'Acidosis' (blood too acidic) is a medical emergency. Drug formulators care about acidity because the protonation state of a molecule changes its solubility and how it gets absorbed.
plain: A sour, often corrosive chemical — your stomach makes a strong one to break down food, and drugs exist to dial it back.
A group of doctors and hospitals that together take responsibility for the cost and quality of a group of patients' care.
snappy: A group of providers who share responsibility — and the savings or losses — for the total cost and quality of a patient population's care.
detail: An ACO is a network of doctors and hospitals jointly accountable for a defined population; if they keep spending below a benchmark while hitting quality targets, they share the savings. A flagship Medicare value-based-care model. You'll hear ACO in any payment-reform or population-health discussion.

plain: Short, active treatment for a sudden health problem, as opposed to the ongoing care of a long-term condition.
snappy: *Short-term, active treatment* for a sudden illness, injury, or flare — the opposite of the slow management of a chronic condition.
detail: Acute care is medicine in the urgent register: the emergency department visit, the intensive care unit admission, the surgery for appendicitis. It aims to stabilize and resolve, then hand the patient back to primary care or chronic care management for the long haul. The line matters for payment and planning, since acute episodes are unpredictable and expensive. You'll hear acute care set against chronic and post-acute care whenever hospitals and payers map where patients should be treated.

snappy: A clinical trial that lets researchers change course mid-study — adjusting dose, dropping a treatment arm, or expanding enrollment — based on what early data shows.
detail: Adaptive designs use pre-specified rules so changes don't compromise statistical integrity. Common adaptations include sample-size re-estimation, response-adaptive randomization, and seamless Phase 2/3 transitions. The FDA published guidance encouraging the approach, and COVID-era trials like RECOVERY popularized it. You'll hear adaptive design pitched at every R&D day as a way to cut development time and cost, and at ASCO when trials use early-stage signals to decide which combinations to push forward.
plain: A clinical trial built to change its own rules partway through — dropping doses or arms as early results come in.

snappy: Think of it as a guided missile for cancer: an antibody that hunts down tumor cells, fused to a chemo drug that destroys them on contact.
detail: ADCs deliver toxic chemotherapy directly to cancer cells while sparing healthy ones, which means stronger results with fewer side effects than traditional chemo. They're a fast-growing class across breast, bladder, and lung cancers — well-known examples include Kadcyla (trastuzumab emtansine) and Enhertu.
plain: A guided missile for cancer — a homing molecule that finds tumor cells and delivers a toxic payload straight to them.

snappy: Cancer that starts in cells lining your organs and making mucus or fluids — the most common form of lung, colon, prostate, and pancreatic cancer.
detail: Most cancers diagnosed in the lung, colon, prostate, and pancreas are adenocarcinomas — meaning they originate in glandular tissue rather than skin-like or supporting cells. The distinction matters because different cancer types respond to different treatments. You'll see the term in pathology reports, oncology trial enrollment criteria, and any commercial discussion of which patient population a new drug is targeting.
plain: A cancer that starts in the cells lining organs like lungs, colon, and prostate — by far the most common type in those places.

snappy: A condition marked by trouble focusing, controlling impulses, and sitting still — most often diagnosed in childhood, but increasingly recognized and treated in adults too.
detail: ADHD treatment leans heavily on stimulants like Adderall (mixed amphetamine salts) and Ritalin (methylphenidate), supplemented by non-stimulants like Strattera (atomoxetine). Adult diagnosis has surged, driving multi-year US shortages of generic Adderall that became front-page news in 2023. You'll hear ADHD pipelines pitched at investor days as a high-growth segment, and DEA quotas on stimulant manufacturing surface regularly in earnings calls and supply commentary.
plain: A condition where focusing, sitting still, and controlling impulses are unusually hard — often spotted in kids but common in adults too.

snappy: The follow-up treatment after surgery or radiation, designed to mop up cancer cells you can't see and stop the disease coming back.
detail: Adjuvant therapy — usually chemo, hormone therapy, or immunotherapy — is what oncologists use to lower the chance of recurrence after the visible tumor has been removed. You'll hear it constantly in breast, colon, and lung cancer trial readouts, often framed around the question "did adjuvant treatment improve survival?"
plain: Extra treatment given after surgery to mop up any leftover cancer cells too small to see and stop the disease coming back.

snappy: The four-step journey every drug takes through your body — getting in, getting around, getting broken down, and getting out.
detail: ADME is the framework drug developers use to predict how a drug behaves once it enters the body. Each step affects how much drug reaches the target, how long it lasts, and what side effects emerge. You'll hear ADME on biotech earnings calls when companies discuss whether a candidate has good "drug-like properties," and in early-stage trial design where these properties first get measured.
plain: The four-stage journey a drug takes through you — getting in, moving around, broken down, and out the other end.
An Alzheimer's drug whose disputed approval — against the FDA's own advisers — became a major controversy before it was pulled.
snappy: The anti-amyloid Alzheimer's antibody whose contested 2021 approval became a landmark FDA controversy.
detail: Aduhelm targets amyloid plaques in Alzheimer's; the FDA's accelerated approval over its own advisers' objections triggered investigations and near-total payer refusal, and it was withdrawn. You'll hear Aduhelm as the cautionary tale behind later anti-amyloid drugs like Leqembi.

snappy: Any unwanted or harmful effect a patient experiences during a clinical trial — whether or not the drug actually caused it.
detail: Adverse events are tracked exhaustively in trials because regulators need to know what users might experience. The term covers everything from a mild headache to a serious hospitalization — the more severe ones get reclassified as Serious Adverse Events (SAEs). You'll hear AEs come up in trial readouts ("the safety profile was consistent with…") and in FDA review letters that decide whether a drug gets approved.
plain: Any unpleasant thing a patient experiences during a trial, whether or not the drug was actually to blame.

snappy: A drug that flips a switch to activate a receptor in your body — telling cells to do something, like a thermostat dialing up the heat.
detail: Agonists mimic natural signaling molecules — when one binds to a receptor, the receptor activates as if its natural partner had arrived. Many medications work this way: opioids agonize pain receptors; asthma inhalers like albuterol agonize beta-2 receptors to relax airways. You'll hear the term in pharmacology basics and any discussion of how a new drug actually does its job in the body.
plain: A drug that switches on a tiny dock on cells, telling them to do something — like flipping a light switch on.
The main US heart-health organization, whose meetings and guidelines shape how heart disease is treated.
snappy: The leading cardiovascular organization, whose scientific sessions are a key venue for heart-drug data.
detail: The American Heart Association sets influential guidelines and hosts a major annual scientific meeting where cardiovascular outcome trials — for SGLT2 inhibitors, PCSK9 drugs, and more — are presented. You'll hear AHA in any cardiometabolic readout discussion.

snappy: A key signaling protein that pushes cells to grow and survive — and is often hijacked by cancer to fuel its own growth.
detail: AKT (also called Protein Kinase B) sits at the center of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, one of the most commonly disrupted signaling networks in cancer. When AKT is overactive, cells refuse to die and keep multiplying — so drugs that block it have been a long-running area of cancer research. You'll hear AKT in oncology trial designs, pipeline discussions, and commercial pitches involving "pathway inhibitors."
plain: A protein inside cells that pushes them to grow and stay alive — often hijacked by cancers to fuel themselves.

snappy: One of the 20 standard amino acids — small, simple, and the second-most-common in the average protein.
detail: Alanine is non-essential (your body makes it from pyruvate) and used by muscle to shuttle nitrogen to the liver via the alanine cycle. In drug design, swapping a residue to alanine ('alanine scanning') is a classic technique for figuring out which amino acid in a protein matters most for binding to a target.
plain: One of the 20 small building blocks that proteins are made from — a simple, abundant one your body makes itself.

snappy: A gene mutation that drives about 5% of lung cancers — and the target of some of oncology's biggest precision-medicine wins.
detail: ALK gene fusions cause uncontrolled cell growth in a subset of non-small-cell lung cancer patients. The story is a precision-medicine showcase: identify the mutation, prescribe a targeted drug like Xalkori (crizotinib) or Alecensa (alectinib), and patients live dramatically longer than they would on chemo. You'll hear ALK in lung cancer trial readouts and at ASCO whenever new generations of inhibitors are presented.
plain: A faulty gene found in about one in twenty lung cancers — and the bullseye for some of oncology's biggest success stories.

snappy: A fast-growing blood cancer that starts in immature lymphocytes — the most common cancer in children, though it also affects adults.
detail: ALL develops when lymphoid cells in the bone marrow turn cancerous and crowd out healthy blood cells. Treatment is intensive — combination chemo, sometimes a bone marrow transplant, increasingly CAR-T cell therapy in relapsed cases. You'll hear ALL discussed in pediatric oncology contexts and in any commercial story around CAR-T (Kymriah was approved for pediatric and young-adult ALL in 2017).
plain: A fast-growing blood cancer that mostly hits children — starts in young immune cells inside the bone marrow.

snappy: One of the alternative versions of a gene — for instance, the gene for eye color comes in blue, brown, green, and other alleles.
detail: Most humans inherit two alleles per gene, one from each parent. Some alleles are dominant (one copy is enough to show the trait), some recessive (you need both copies). Pharmacogenomics — tailoring drugs to a patient's specific alleles — is becoming routine: certain CYP2D6 alleles, for example, change how fast people metabolize codeine, antidepressants, and beta-blockers.
plain: One version of a gene — like the gene for eye color comes in blue, brown, or green flavors, each one is an allele.

snappy: A progressive brain disease — the most common form of dementia — where abnormal protein clumps build up and slowly destroy memory, thinking, and the ability to live independently.
detail: Alzheimer's affects roughly 6 million Americans. Symptomatic drugs like donepezil and memantine offer modest benefit; the new disease-modifying anti-amyloid antibodies — Leqembi (lecanemab) and Kisunla (donanemab) — slow decline by 25-35% but require infusions, MRI monitoring for brain swelling, and have driven uneven Medicare coverage. You'll hear Alzheimer's at every Eli Lilly and Biogen-Eisai earnings call, and at CTAD when readouts on next-generation drugs targeting tau and earlier intervention shape investor expectations.
plain: A brain disease where clumps of bad protein slowly destroy memory and thinking — the most common cause of dementia.
Medical care given in clinics and day-surgery centers, where patients walk in and leave the same day without a hospital bed.
snappy: Outpatient care delivered *on your own two feet* — clinics, day surgery, imaging, and infusion centers, no hospital bed required.
detail: Ambulatory care is the umbrella for services provided outside the inpatient ward: physician offices, ambulatory surgery centers, urgent care, and dialysis units. Shifting procedures into ambulatory settings cuts cost and infection risk, a trend payers and value-based care arrangements actively reward. It leans on primary care and specialty care clinics as its backbone. You'll hear ambulatory care in any conversation about site-of-care shift and outpatient capacity.

plain: One of the first biotech companies, a pioneer of protein-based 'biologic' medicines.
snappy: One of the original biotechs, a pioneer of protein-based biologic drugs.
detail: Amgen built biotech on biologics like Enbrel and the anemia drugs Epogen and Neupogen, and now markets the cholesterol antibody Repatha and the KRAS drug Lumakras, plus a growing biosimilars line. You'll hear Amgen in biologics and biosimilar discussion.

snappy: The 20 chemical building blocks that proteins are made of — string them together in different orders and you get every protein in nature.
detail: Nine of the 20 amino acids are 'essential' — your body can't make them, so you have to get them from food. Genetic code dictates the order amino acids are linked together for each protein, and that order determines how the protein folds and what it does. Single amino-acid changes from a mutation can be devastating: sickle cell, cystic fibrosis, and many cancers all trace to a swap of one amino acid in one critical protein.
plain: The 20 chemical Lego bricks that proteins are made from — stack them in different orders and you get every protein in nature.

snappy: A fast-moving blood cancer that starts in the bone marrow and demands urgent treatment — primarily affects older adults but can hit at any age.
detail: AML develops when myeloid cells — the precursors to red cells, platelets, and most white cells — become cancerous and overrun the bone marrow. Treatment is aggressive (high-dose chemo, often bone marrow transplant) and increasingly genotype-driven, with FLT3 and IDH inhibitors targeting specific mutations. You'll hear AML in oncology pipeline discussions, ASCO/ASH conference coverage, and around companies developing targeted leukemia therapies.
plain: A fast-moving blood cancer that takes over the bone marrow — mostly affects older adults and needs urgent treatment.
A therapy that harvests a patient's own tumor-fighting immune cells, multiplies them in the lab, and gives billions back.
snappy: The first tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) therapy — it grows a patient's own tumor-fighting T-cells and gives them back.
detail: Amtagvi expands T-cells harvested from a patient's own melanoma and reinfuses billions, a different cell-therapy approach from CAR-T, for advanced melanoma after other treatments fail. You'll hear Amtagvi as the first TIL therapy in cell-therapy discussion.

plain: A group of rare diseases where misfolded proteins build up in organs like the heart and nerves, gumming up how they work.
snappy: Rare diseases of misfolded-protein deposits damaging heart or nerves; a hot area since RNA drugs like Onpattro arrived.
detail: In amyloidosis, misfolded proteins (often transthyretin, ATTR) deposit in tissue. ATTR therapies — Onpattro, an siRNA, plus Vyndaqel — energized rare-disease pipelines. You'll hear amyloidosis in cardiology and rare-disease readouts and any RNA-therapeutics discussion.

snappy: The shortcut a generic drug company files instead of a full new-drug application — proving its copy is bioequivalent to the original branded drug.
detail: ANDAs let generic manufacturers skip duplicating safety and efficacy trials, since the original drug already proved them — they only need to show their version delivers the same active ingredient at the same rate. After the brand's patents expire, multiple generics typically file ANDAs to compete on price. You'll see ANDA filings drive earnings volatility for any company with a major drug nearing patent cliff, and "first-to-file" generics earn 180-day exclusivity.
plain: The shorter paperwork a generic drug maker files to copy an existing branded medicine — they just have to prove their version is the same.

snappy: The process where the body builds new blood vessels — which tumors hijack to feed their own growth.
detail: Tumors trick surrounding tissue into growing new blood vessels that supply oxygen and nutrients, letting them expand beyond what local blood supply can sustain. Drugs that block this process — including Avastin (bevacizumab) — are a major class in oncology. You'll hear angiogenesis come up in solid-tumor trial designs and in commercial discussions of how "anti-angiogenics" fit alongside immunotherapy and chemo.
plain: The body's process of building new blood vessels — which tumors trick into supplying them with food and oxygen.

snappy: A drug that blocks a receptor — like sliding tape over a light switch so it can't be turned on.
detail: Antagonists work by occupying a receptor site without activating it, preventing the body's natural signaling molecule from binding. Beta blockers like propranolol are antagonists at beta-adrenergic receptors, slowing the heart. Antihistamines block histamine receptors. You'll hear the term in pharmacology basics, in any drug-development discussion of mechanism, and on earnings calls when companies position their drug against a competitor's.
plain: A drug that plugs a tiny dock on cells so nothing else can switch it on — like sticking tape over a light switch.

snappy: A drug that kills or stops the growth of bacteria — the foundation of modern medicine since penicillin, and increasingly under threat as bacteria evolve resistance.
detail: Antibiotic classes range from penicillins and cephalosporins to fluoroquinolones, macrolides, and last-resort drugs like vancomycin and carbapenems. Despite enormous public-health value, antibiotics earn poor commercial returns — most are short-course generics — and the pipeline has thinned. You'll hear antibiotics framed on policy panels and at JPMorgan as a market-failure problem, and in PASTEUR Act discussions about subscription-style government payment models to revive the pipeline.
plain: A drug that kills bacteria or stops them growing — the backbone of modern medicine, increasingly outsmarted by evolving bugs.

snappy: A Y-shaped protein the immune system makes to recognize and neutralize a specific foreign target — a virus, a toxin, a cancer marker.
detail: Each antibody binds one specific target (the antigen) with extraordinary precision. Pharma has industrialized antibody production: monoclonal antibodies — Humira, Keytruda, Dupixent, Opdivo — are some of the best-selling drugs in history, generating tens of billions in annual revenue. They're manufactured in large bioreactors using engineered mammalian cells, and the high cost of making them is a perennial theme in drug-pricing debates.
plain: A Y-shaped protein your immune system makes to grab onto one specific intruder — a virus, a toxin, or a cancer marker.

snappy: A blood thinner — a drug that slows the clotting cascade so dangerous clots don't form in your veins, lungs, or brain.
detail: The class spans heparin and warfarin (cheap, requires monitoring) and the newer direct oral anticoagulants — Eliquis (apixaban), Xarelto (rivaroxaban), Pradaxa (dabigatran) — that don't require blood-test monitoring. DOACs have largely displaced warfarin in atrial fibrillation and venous thromboembolism. You'll hear anticoagulants in every BMS-Pfizer commentary on Eliquis franchise revenue, in IRA negotiation news (Eliquis is on the first Medicare list), and in stroke-prevention policy discussions.
plain: A blood thinner — a drug that slows clotting so dangerous clumps don't form in your veins, lungs, or brain.

snappy: Anything the immune system recognizes as foreign and mounts a response against — most commonly a protein on a virus, bacterium, or tumor cell.
detail: Vaccines work by exposing the immune system to an antigen (or instructions to make one, in mRNA vaccines) so it learns to recognize the real pathogen later. In oncology, 'tumor antigens' are the cancer-specific markers that immunotherapies and cell therapies (CAR-T) train the immune system to attack — CD19 on B-cell leukemias, BCMA on multiple myeloma, HER2 on certain breast cancers.
plain: Anything the immune system spots as foreign and attacks — usually a protein on a germ or a tumor cell.

snappy: What happens when bacteria, viruses, or fungi evolve to survive the drugs designed to kill them — turning routine infections into life-threatening ones.
detail: AMR is responsible for roughly 1.3 million deaths globally each year and rising, driven by overuse of antibiotics in human medicine and livestock. The CDC tracks priority pathogens like MRSA, drug-resistant gonorrhea, and CRE; the WHO calls AMR one of the top global health threats. You'll hear AMR at WHO assemblies, in CDC press releases, and at pharma policy panels arguing for new economic models — including the proposed PASTEUR Act — to fund antibiotic R&D that markets won't.
plain: What happens when germs evolve to shrug off the drugs designed to kill them — turning routine infections deadly again.

snappy: A drug that calms hallucinations, delusions, and severe mood disturbances by adjusting brain chemistry — used in schizophrenia, bipolar mania, and severe depression.
detail: Antipsychotics split into older ("typical" — haloperidol, chlorpromazine) and newer ("atypical" — Abilify/aripiprazole, Latuda/lurasidone, Vraylar/cariprazine) classes. The 2024 approval of Cobenfy (xanomeline-trospium), the first non-dopamine antipsychotic, opened a new chapter after decades of mechanism stagnation. Long-acting injectable forms address adherence. You'll hear antipsychotics on BMS, J&J, and Otsuka earnings calls, and at psychiatric conferences when novel-mechanism programs (TAAR1, muscarinic, glutamatergic) reset expectations for what's possible.
plain: A drug that calms hallucinations and severe mood swings by tweaking brain chemistry — used in schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.

snappy: A drug that targets viruses — typically by blocking the proteins they need to enter cells, copy themselves, or assemble new particles — without harming healthy human cells.
detail: Antiviral classes span HIV (integrase inhibitors, NRTIs), hepatitis C (cures like Harvoni/ledipasvir-sofosbuvir), influenza (Tamiflu/oseltamivir), herpes (acyclovir), and COVID (Paxlovid/nirmatrelvir-ritonavir). Unlike antibiotics, several blockbuster antiviral franchises remain — Gilead's HIV portfolio funded its rise. You'll hear antivirals at every Gilead, Pfizer, and Merck earnings call when COVID seasonality and HIV pipelines come up, and in WHO press communications about influenza pandemic readiness.
plain: A drug that goes after viruses by blocking the bits they need to break into cells or copy themselves.

snappy: Excessive, persistent worry that interferes with daily life — covering generalized anxiety, panic, social phobia, and PTSD as a related family of conditions.
detail: Anxiety disorders are the most common mental health condition in the US, affecting roughly 19% of adults. Treatment combines therapy with SSRIs, SNRIs, or short-term benzodiazepines like Xanax (alprazolam), though benzo dependence is a known risk. Newer entrants target GABA pathways without sedation. You'll hear anxiety markets framed at JPMorgan as massive but commoditized, and on investor days when companies pitch novel mechanisms designed to avoid the dependence problem of older sedatives.
plain: When worry gets so persistent and overwhelming that it gets in the way of everyday life — the most common mental-health condition.

snappy: A tumor-suppressor gene whose job is to keep cells from dividing out of control — and its breakdown is the first step toward most colorectal cancers.
detail: APC mutations are among the earliest genetic changes in colorectal cancer development — they're found in roughly 80% of sporadic cases and in nearly all patients with familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), an inherited cancer syndrome. You'll hear APC in colorectal cancer screening discussions, hereditary-cancer-syndrome contexts, and in any pipeline conversation involving Wnt-pathway-targeted therapies.
plain: A gene whose job is to put the brakes on cell growth — when it breaks, it kicks off most colon cancers.

snappy: The actual chemical inside a pill or injection that does the work — everything else (fillers, coatings, capsule) is just delivery.
detail: An API is what's pharmacologically active in a finished drug; the inactive components — called excipients — give it shape, stability, and a delivery mechanism. APIs are typically manufactured at specialized facilities, often in India or China, before being formulated into the final product. You'll hear API in supply-chain discussions (especially around shortages), at drug-pricing debates, and on earnings calls when companies discuss vertical integration.
plain: The actual working chemical inside a pill — everything else (the coating, the filler) is just there to deliver it.

snappy: Programmed cell death — the body's built-in self-destruct mechanism for damaged or unwanted cells. Cancer cells routinely figure out how to switch it off.
detail: Apoptosis is how the body removes cells that are no longer needed or are too damaged to function — about a million cells per second, in normal physiology. Cancer cells acquire mutations that disable apoptosis, allowing them to keep dividing instead of self-destructing. You'll hear apoptosis come up in cancer-mechanism discussions and in any drug-development pitch around restoring cell death (e.g., BH3 mimetics, BCL-2 inhibitors).
plain: A cell's built-in self-destruct button — the body uses it to clear out damaged cells, and cancer often disables it.
The main professional society for cancer doctors; its yearly meeting is where big new cancer-treatment results are revealed.
snappy: The largest cancer-doctor society; its annual meeting is where practice-changing oncology data lands.
detail: ASCO's annual meeting each spring is the field's biggest stage — major trial readouts there can move stock prices and rewrite guidelines overnight. You'll hear 'at ASCO' as shorthand for where new cancer data is unveiled and debated.

plain: The big professional society for blood diseases; its yearly meeting is where major leukemia and lymphoma results are shown.
snappy: The blood-disease equivalent of ASCO — its annual meeting is the marquee event for leukemia, lymphoma, and myeloma data.
detail: ASH's December meeting is where blood-cancer and blood-disorder trials are presented, driving sentiment on franchises like BTK inhibitors and CAR-T. You'll hear 'at ASH' wherever leukemia, lymphoma, or multiple myeloma results are discussed.

snappy: A laboratory test that measures something — usually whether a drug works, how much of it is present, or what it does to cells.
detail: Assays are the workhorses of drug development: high-throughput screens to find compounds that hit a target, ELISAs to detect proteins in blood, cell-based assays to measure tumor killing. Diagnostic companies sell assays as products in their own right. You'll hear the term across early-stage research papers, biotech investor decks describing platforms, and any FDA discussion of analytical validation.
plain: A lab test that measures something — like whether a drug works, how much of it is there, or what it does to cells.

snappy: A chronic condition where the airways tighten, swell, and fill with mucus — causing wheezing, coughing, and shortness of breath that ranges from mild to life-threatening.
detail: Asthma treatment escalates from rescue inhalers (albuterol) to maintenance inhaled corticosteroids and combination LABA/ICS inhalers like Advair, then to biologics for severe disease — Dupixent (dupilumab), Xolair (omalizumab), Nucala (mepolizumab), Tezspire (tezepelumab). The biologic shift has split the market between cheap generic inhalers and high-priced injectables. You'll hear asthma on every GSK, Sanofi-Regeneron, and AstraZeneca earnings call, and at ATS when biomarker-defined patient subsets reshape which biologic wins for whom.
plain: A long-term lung condition where the airways tighten and swell up, making it hard to breathe — ranges from mild to life-threatening.
An Anglo-Swedish pharmaceutical giant with an especially deep cancer-drug pipeline.
snappy: The Anglo-Swedish pharma giant with a deep oncology pipeline — Tagrisso, Imfinzi, Lynparza, Enhertu.
detail: AstraZeneca rebuilt around oncology (Tagrisso, Imfinzi, Calquence, Lynparza, Enhertu) and cardiometabolic drugs like Farxiga, after fending off a 2014 Pfizer takeover. You'll hear AstraZeneca across lung cancer and cardiometabolic readouts and biopharma M&A.

snappy: A brain tumor that arises from star-shaped support cells called astrocytes — the family includes glioblastoma, the most aggressive.
detail: Astrocytomas range from slow-growing low-grade tumors to glioblastoma multiforme — one of the deadliest cancers, with median survival measured in months despite surgery, radiation, and chemo. The category is graded I to IV by aggressiveness. You'll hear astrocytoma in neuro-oncology contexts, brain-cancer trial readouts, and around clinical-trial sponsors developing therapies for the underserved glioblastoma population.
plain: A brain tumor that grows from star-shaped support cells in the brain — the family includes the dreaded glioblastoma.

snappy: A gene that helps cells fix damaged DNA — when it's broken, cells accumulate mutations and cancer risk goes up.
detail: ATM is a key DNA-damage response gene; people who inherit mutations in both copies develop ataxia telangiectasia, a rare disorder with sharply elevated cancer risk. ATM mutations also turn up in breast, prostate, and pancreatic cancers, where they may flag tumors that respond to PARP inhibitors. You'll hear ATM in precision-oncology trial designs and any commercial discussion of biomarker-driven drug selection.
plain: A gene that helps cells patch up damaged DNA — when it stops working, mistakes pile up and cancer risk climbs.

snappy: The smallest unit of an element — protons, neutrons, and electrons arranged in a tiny solar-system-like structure.
detail: Everything in pharma is ultimately atoms: a small-molecule drug typically has 20-50 atoms, a protein biologic has tens of thousands. The arrangement of atoms determines what a drug binds to and what it does. Modern computational chemistry simulates drug-protein interactions one atom at a time, and AI-driven drug discovery (Insilico, Recursion, Iambic) leans on this atom-level simulation.
plain: The smallest building block of any chemical element — tiny clusters of protons, neutrons, and electrons that everything is made of.
The most common form of eczema — itchy, inflamed skin — now treatable with targeted biologic injections, not just creams.
snappy: Chronic itchy, inflamed skin (eczema); the arrival of Dupixent turned it into a major biologics market.
detail: Atopic dermatitis is driven by IL-4 and IL-13 immune signaling. Dupixent was the breakthrough biologic; JAK inhibitors like Rinvoq followed. You'll hear atopic dermatitis (often 'AD') in dermatology and immunology pipeline talk at JPMorgan.

snappy: The energy currency of every cell — your body makes and uses your body weight in ATP every day.
detail: ATP powers muscle contraction, nerve firing, biosynthesis, and active transport across membranes. Nearly all of it comes from breaking down glucose and fat in mitochondria. Many cancer cells reorganize their metabolism around ATP supply, and drugs that disrupt these reprogrammed pathways are a growing oncology focus. ATP-competitive kinase inhibitors — drugs that block enzymes by occupying their ATP-binding pocket — are an entire major class of cancer therapy.
plain: The tiny energy packet every cell runs on — your body makes and burns through your own body weight in it every single day.

snappy: An irregular, often fast heartbeat caused by chaotic electrical signals in the upper chambers — the most common heart-rhythm problem and a leading cause of stroke.
detail: Afib treatment has two arms: rhythm/rate control (drugs like amiodarone or procedures like ablation) and stroke prevention with anticoagulants. The shift from warfarin to direct oral anticoagulants — Eliquis (apixaban), Xarelto (rivaroxaban) — is one of the biggest commercial stories of the last decade. You'll hear afib on every BMS and Pfizer earnings call given Eliquis's status as one of pharma's largest drugs, and at HRS when ablation device makers report procedure volumes.
plain: An irregular, often racing heartbeat caused by chaotic electrical signals up top — the most common rhythm problem and a big stroke risk.

snappy: The total drug exposure your body experiences over time — calculated as the area under the blood-concentration-versus-time graph, and a fundamental measure of how much medicine actually reached you.
detail: AUC is the headline number regulators and clinicians use to compare drug exposures: between formulations, between patients, between dosing regimens. Bioequivalence studies — the foundation of generic-drug approval — are essentially comparisons of generic AUC and Cmax against the brand. You'll see AUC quoted in Phase 1 readouts, in any drug-drug interaction discussion, and in ANDA filings where generic manufacturers prove their version delivers within the FDA's 80-125% bioequivalence band.
plain: The total amount of drug your body sees over time — basically, how much medicine actually got in and stuck around.

snappy: When the body's immune system mistakes its own healthy cells for invaders and attacks them — sometimes triggered by cancer immunotherapy.
detail: Autoimmune diseases — rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, type 1 diabetes, multiple sclerosis — affect roughly 5% of the population and are a major commercial market for biologic drugs like Humira (adalimumab) and Stelara (ustekinumab). Cancer immunotherapy can also trigger autoimmune-like side effects called immune-related adverse events. You'll hear autoimmune in immunology pipeline discussions, biologic earnings calls, and immunotherapy trial readouts.
plain: When the immune system gets confused and starts attacking the body's own healthy cells instead of real invaders.
The first drug to starve tumors by cutting off their blood supply, blocking the signal cancers use to grow new vessels.
snappy: The first anti-angiogenesis drug — it starves tumors by blocking VEGF, the signal they use to grow new blood vessels.
detail: Avastin blocks VEGF to choke off a tumor's blood supply, used across colorectal, lung, kidney, and ovarian cancer, often with chemo. Now facing biosimilars. You'll hear Avastin as the founding angiogenesis story in oncology.

snappy: The antibody-producing white blood cell — central to the adaptive immune system and the target of much of immunology and oncology drug development.
detail: B-cells make the antibodies that recognize and neutralize pathogens, and they're the cell of origin for many lymphomas and leukemias. Drugs that deplete B-cells (rituximab, ocrelizumab) treat conditions ranging from lymphoma to multiple sclerosis to rheumatoid arthritis. CAR-T therapies targeting CD19 (a B-cell marker) revolutionized treatment of B-cell leukemias and lymphomas. BTK inhibitors (Imbruvica, Calquence, Brukinsa) block a key B-cell signaling enzyme.
plain: The white blood cell that makes antibodies — a key player in the immune system and the source of many blood cancers.
A bladder cancer drug for tumors with a specific gene fault, chosen by testing the tumor's DNA first.
snappy: An FGFR inhibitor for bladder cancer driven by FGFR gene alterations.
detail: Balversa targets FGFR mutations and fusions in advanced bladder cancer, selected by genetic testing — another precision approach in a historically chemo-driven cancer. You'll hear Balversa in FGFR-altered bladder cancer discussion.

snappy: The most common skin cancer — slow-growing, rarely spreads to other organs, but can quietly cause real damage to the skin and underlying tissue if left alone.
detail: BCC arises from the deepest layer of the skin's outer surface, usually on sun-exposed areas like the face, ears, and neck. Treatment is typically surgical removal, with high cure rates. For advanced or rare metastatic cases, hedgehog-pathway inhibitors like Erivedge (vismodegib) are options. You'll hear BCC in dermatology drug development and in commercial discussions of skin-cancer immunotherapy and topical agents.
plain: The most common skin cancer — slow-growing, rarely spreads, but can quietly chew through skin if left alone.

snappy: The chemical opposite of an acid — accepts hydrogen ions, often slippery to the touch, and balances the body's pH.
detail: In biology, 'base' has two unrelated meanings: chemistry bases (like sodium bicarbonate, antacids) and DNA bases (the four letters A, T, G, C). Pharma cares about both. Many drugs are weak bases or weak acids, and their behavior in the body — absorption, distribution, excretion — depends heavily on the local pH at each step.
plain: The chemical opposite of an acid — soaks up acidity, often feels slippery, and helps the body balance its pH.

snappy: Two DNA letters paired across the helix — A always with T, G always with C — like a rung on a twisted ladder.
detail: The human genome is about 3 billion base pairs long. The strict pairing rules (A-T, G-C) mean each strand of DNA carries the full information needed to copy the other, which is how cells faithfully replicate their DNA before dividing. Sequencing technology reads off the base pairs one at a time, and editing tools like CRISPR can swap one base pair for another with single-letter precision (base editing).
plain: Two DNA letters locked together across the twisted ladder — A always with T, G always with C, like puzzle pieces.
How many people, on average, one sick person infects when no one is immune. Above one means it spreads; below one means it dies out.
snappy: *R₀* — the average number of people one infected person passes a disease to in a fully susceptible population. Above 1 it spreads; below 1 it fades.
detail: Written R₀ and said 'R-nought,' it is contagion's headline statistic: measles sits near 15, seasonal flu near 1.3. It sets the herd immunity threshold — the share who must be immune to halt spread — and predicts whether an outbreak grows into an epidemic. Teams also track a real-time cousin, the effective reproduction number, to judge whether control measures are working.

snappy: The QC checkpoint where a batch of manufactured drug is tested against specs and formally cleared for shipment — or held back if anything is off.
detail: Each batch goes through a battery of tests — potency, sterility, endotoxin, particulate, identity — before a Qualified Person signs off on release. Failed batches can wipe out hundreds of millions in revenue and trigger supply shortages. You'll see batch-release issues surface in FDA Form 483 reports, in earnings calls when revenue misses get blamed on "manufacturing variability," and in commercial discussions of how supply-chain reliability shapes formulary positioning.
plain: The quality check where a freshly made batch of drug gets tested and signed off — or held back if anything's off.

snappy: A protein that helps cells avoid death — when it's overactive, cancer cells refuse to die, which is how many blood cancers stay alive.
detail: BCL-2 was the first cancer gene discovered to work by blocking apoptosis (programmed cell death) rather than by driving growth. It's overexpressed in CLL, follicular lymphoma, and AML, and Venclexta (venetoclax) is a BCL-2 inhibitor that has reshaped treatment in those settings. You'll hear BCL-2 at hematology conferences (ASH especially) and in any pipeline discussion involving "apoptosis-targeted" oncology.
plain: A protein that helps cells dodge death — when it's stuck on, cancer cells refuse to die, which is how many blood cancers stay alive.

snappy: A fused gene that drives chronic myeloid leukemia — and the target of one of the first and most successful precision-medicine drugs ever made.
detail: When parts of chromosomes 9 and 22 swap places, they form the abnormal BCR-ABL gene that produces a constantly active growth signal in white blood cells, causing CML. The story is legendary in oncology: Gleevec (imatinib), launched in 2001, transformed CML from a fatal disease into a manageable chronic condition. You'll hear BCR-ABL in any drug-development pitch invoking targeted therapy as a paradigm.
plain: A garbled gene formed when two chromosomes swap parts — it drives one specific blood cancer and was the target of a famous pill.

snappy: A class of cardiovascular drugs that blunts the effect of adrenaline on the heart — slowing it down and easing blood-pressure spikes — used since the 1960s.
detail: Beta blockers — metoprolol, carvedilol, atenolol, propranolol — are workhorses across hypertension, atrial fibrillation, heart failure, and post-heart-attack care. Non-cardiac uses include migraine prevention, performance anxiety, and essential tremor. Almost all are generic. You'll hear beta blockers framed in cardiology commentary as the durable foundation newer mechanisms have to beat, and in formulary discussions where their pennies-a-pill cost makes them the default first step in stepped-therapy protocols.
plain: A heart drug that blunts adrenaline's effect on the heart, slowing it down and easing blood pressure.

snappy: How much of a drug actually makes it into your bloodstream after you take it — the rest is broken down or never absorbed.
detail: When you swallow a pill, only a fraction reaches the circulation; the rest is destroyed by stomach acid, liver enzymes, or never absorbed by the gut. IV drugs are 100% bioavailable by definition; pills can range from 5% to 95% depending on chemistry. You'll hear the term in early drug development, formulation discussions, and at FDA reviews of generic-drug equivalence.
plain: How much of a swallowed drug actually makes it into your bloodstream — the rest gets destroyed or never absorbed at all.
Proof that a generic drug behaves the same in the body as the brand — the basis for approving generics without new trials.
snappy: The proof that a generic drug behaves the same in the body as the brand — the core of how generics get approved without new trials.
detail: Bioequivalence studies compare a generic's Cmax and AUC against the brand; if they fall within a tight statistical window, the FDA deems them interchangeable. It's why a generic can skip efficacy trials. You'll hear bioequivalence in any generic drug or ANDA discussion.

plain: A biotech focused on brain diseases — long a leader in multiple sclerosis and central to the Alzheimer's drug debate.
snappy: A neuroscience-focused biotech, long a leader in multiple sclerosis and a central figure in the Alzheimer's amyloid saga.
detail: Biogen built its business in multiple sclerosis and co-developed the contested Alzheimer's drug Aduhelm and its successor Leqembi (with Eisai). You'll hear Biogen in any neurology or anti-amyloid discussion.

snappy: A drug grown from living cells rather than synthesized in a chemistry lab — antibodies, proteins, vaccines, and gene therapies all fall under the biologic umbrella.
detail: Biologics are larger and more complex than small-molecule pills, must be injected or infused, and cost far more to manufacture — driving high prices and the rise of biosimilars after patents expire. Examples span Humira (adalimumab) for autoimmune disease, Keytruda (pembrolizumab) for cancer, and the COVID mRNA vaccines. You'll hear biologic versus small-molecule debates everywhere in pharma — at JPMorgan when companies pitch their pipeline mix, and on earnings calls when biosimilar erosion forecasts hit.
plain: A drug grown inside living cells rather than mixed in a chemistry lab — bigger, pricier, and usually injected instead of swallowed.

snappy: A measurable biological signal — like a fingerprint your body leaves behind — that tells doctors what's happening inside you.
detail: Biomarkers can be molecules in your blood (such as PSA for prostate cancer), genetic mutations (such as HER2 in breast cancer), or imaging signals. Pharma uses them to diagnose disease, predict which patients will respond to a drug, and track whether a treatment is working — they're the foundation of "precision medicine."
plain: A measurable biological clue — like a fingerprint your body leaves behind — that tells doctors what's happening inside you.
A German biotech that co-created the Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine and is now applying mRNA to cancer.
snappy: The German mRNA pioneer that co-developed the Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine and is pivoting to cancer.
detail: BioNTech's mRNA technology powered the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine and now drives a pipeline of mRNA cancer vaccines and immunotherapies. You'll hear BioNTech alongside Moderna in any mRNA-platform discussion.

snappy: Taking a small piece of tissue from your body to examine under a microscope — usually to confirm whether something is cancer.
detail: Biopsies range from a needle aspirate (a few cells from a lymph node) to a surgical excision (a whole lump removed). The sample is processed by a pathologist who diagnoses the disease and increasingly identifies genetic mutations that guide treatment selection. You'll hear biopsy in cancer trial design ("tumor biopsy required"), liquid-biopsy startup discussions, and any commercial conversation about companion diagnostics.
plain: Taking a tiny sample of tissue from your body to look at under a microscope, usually to check whether something is cancer.

snappy: A near-identical copy of an existing biologic drug — like a generic, but more complicated to make because biologics are produced by living cells.
detail: Unlike small-molecule generics, biosimilars can't be exactly identical to their reference biologic — biology doesn't allow it — so the FDA approves them based on showing no clinically meaningful differences. They drive down prices when biologics like Remicade (infliximab) and Humira (adalimumab) lose patent protection. You'll hear biosimilar in payer discussions about cost savings and at investor briefings on biologic patent cliffs.
plain: A near-copy of a biologic drug — like a generic, but trickier because the originals are grown by living cells, not just mixed in a beaker.

snappy: A mental illness marked by dramatic swings between depressive lows and manic or hypomanic highs — sometimes lasting weeks, sometimes hours, and often diagnosed in early adulthood.
detail: Treatment combines mood stabilizers like lithium and Depakote (valproate), atypical antipsychotics like Latuda (lurasidone) and Vraylar (cariprazine), and SSRIs paired with mood stabilizers for depressive phases. Roughly 1-3% of US adults live with bipolar I or II. You'll hear bipolar disorder framed at investor days as a stable specialty market with clear unmet need, and on earnings calls discussing the long-acting injectable antipsychotic franchise expanding from schizophrenia into bipolar maintenance.
plain: A mental illness where moods swing between deep lows and racing highs that can last days or weeks at a time.

snappy: An engineered antibody with two grabbers instead of one — designed to grab a cancer cell with one hand and an immune cell with the other, forcing them together.
detail: Bispecifics — also called BiTEs (Bispecific T-cell Engagers) — physically yoke a tumor cell to a T-cell so the immune system kills it on contact. Approved examples include Blincyto (blinatumomab) for leukemia and Tecvayli (teclistamab) for multiple myeloma. The class has expanded fast across blood and solid cancers, and is one of the most-watched modalities at ASCO and in oncology investor decks.
plain: A lab-made antibody with two hands — one grabs a cancer cell, the other grabs an immune cell, dragging them together so the cancer gets killed.

snappy: The paperwork a company files with the FDA to win approval to sell a biologic drug — anything from a vaccine to an antibody to a cell therapy.
detail: BLAs go to the FDA's biologics center (CBER) or drug center (CDER) depending on the product, and run on the PDUFA review clock just like small-molecule applications. Recent high-profile BLA approvals include bluebird's gene therapies for sickle cell and several GLP-1 biologics. You'll hear "BLA filing" celebrated in press releases and earnings calls — it marks the moment a company has handed its full dossier to regulators and is awaiting the verdict.
plain: The official paperwork a company hands the FDA to get permission to sell a biologic drug, like a vaccine or antibody.

snappy: The FDA's strongest safety alert — a warning printed in a literal black-bordered box on a drug's label when the risks are serious enough to demand prescriber attention.
detail: Black Box Warnings are added when post-market surveillance or clinical trials reveal a risk of serious harm — well-known examples include certain antidepressants flagged for suicide risk in young patients, and some immunotherapies for severe autoimmune side effects. The warning doesn't pull a drug from the market; it requires prescribers to weigh the risk explicitly. You'll see the term in FDA press releases, legal proceedings, and any commercial discussion of a drug's market trajectory after the warning lands.
plain: The FDA's loudest safety alert — printed inside a literal black box on the label when a drug carries serious risks doctors must weigh.

snappy: Cancer that starts in the lining of the bladder — most often in long-time smokers — and frequently recurs even after early-stage treatment.
detail: Bladder cancer is overwhelmingly urothelial carcinoma, with FGFR3 and TP53 mutations driving subsets. Treatment ranges from intravesical BCG for early-stage disease to systemic therapy for advanced cases — Keytruda (pembrolizumab), Padcev (enfortumab vedotin), and the FGFR inhibitor Balversa (erdafitinib) are recent additions. You'll hear bladder cancer at ASCO in commercial discussions of immunotherapy and ADC market expansion.
plain: Cancer that starts in the lining of the bladder, most often in long-time smokers, and tends to keep coming back even after treatment.

snappy: Hiding from patients, doctors, or both whether a person is getting the real drug or a placebo — so expectations don't bias the results.
detail: Trials can be single-blind (only patients don't know) or double-blind (neither patients nor doctors know); placebo bias is real and measurable, so blinding is essential to clean results. The unblinded readout is what triggers stock-moving headlines. You'll hear blinding in trial-design discussions, FDA review documents, and at investor conferences when companies preview Phase 3 data they expect to release.
plain: Keeping patients or doctors in the dark about who's getting the real drug versus a fake pill, so wishful thinking can't sway the results.

snappy: The body's bouncer for the brain — a tight wall of cells that keeps most chemicals (including most drugs) from crossing from the blood to the brain.
detail: The BBB protects the brain from toxins but also keeps out most therapeutic drugs, making CNS conditions especially hard to treat. Crossing the BBB is a central engineering problem in neurology drug development — solved with small-molecule design, antibody shuttles, or ultrasound. You'll hear BBB in pipeline discussions for Alzheimer's, brain cancer, and any neuro-immunotherapy conversation, often as the reason something failed.
plain: The brain's bouncer — a tight wall of cells that blocks most chemicals, including most drugs, from passing into the brain.
The FDA's strongest safety alert — a warning boxed at the top of a drug's label to flag a serious or life-threatening risk.
snappy: The FDA's strongest safety alert, boxed at the top of a drug's label to flag a serious or life-threatening risk.
detail: A boxed warning (the old 'black box') signals risks like clotting, suicidality, or organ damage and can sharply curb a drug's use — the JAK inhibitor class carries one. You'll hear boxed warning in any pharmacovigilance, label-negotiation, or commercial-risk discussion.

snappy: A gene that, when mutated, drives uncontrolled cell growth — found in about half of all melanomas, plus some lung and colon cancers.
detail: The BRAF V600E mutation makes the protein constantly "on," pushing cells to proliferate. Tafinlar (dabrafenib) plus Mekinist (trametinib) is the standard combo for BRAF-mutant melanoma — together they shrink tumors dramatically, though resistance often develops. You'll hear BRAF in melanoma trial readouts, precision-oncology discussions, and in any company commentary on tumor-agnostic mutation testing.
plain: A gene that, when broken, jams the cell's growth signal stuck in the on position and drives about half of all melanoma skin cancers.

snappy: Cancer that has spread from somewhere else in the body — usually lung, breast, or melanoma — into the brain.
detail: Once cancer reaches the brain, treatment options narrow because most drugs can't cross the blood-brain barrier; whole-brain radiation, stereotactic radiosurgery, and a small group of brain-penetrant drugs (Tagrisso, Alecensa, Tukysa) become the toolkit. You'll hear brain metastases in oncology trial-enrollment criteria (often excluded) and in any drug pitch claiming "CNS activity" — a key commercial differentiator.
plain: Cancer that started elsewhere — often lung, breast, or skin — and spread into the brain, where most drugs can't easily reach it.
Two genes that normally repair DNA. Inherited faults sharply raise breast and ovarian cancer risk — the 'Angelina Jolie gene.'
snappy: The DNA-repair genes whose inherited mutations drive hereditary breast and ovarian cancer — and flag who benefits from PARP inhibitors.
detail: BRCA1 and BRCA2 normally repair DNA. Inherited mutations sharply raise breast and ovarian cancer risk and leave a tumor unable to repair DNA well — making it vulnerable to PARP inhibitors like Lynparza. You'll hear BRCA in genetic-testing, HRD, and hereditary-cancer discussion at ASCO.

snappy: Two genes that normally help cells repair damaged DNA — when inherited as broken copies, they sharply raise the lifetime risk of breast and ovarian cancer.
detail: BRCA mutations affect roughly 1 in 400 people; carriers face up to 70% lifetime breast cancer risk and elevated risk for ovarian, prostate, and pancreatic cancers. The genes are also a treatment target — PARP inhibitors like Lynparza (olaparib) work especially well on BRCA-mutated tumors. You'll hear BRCA in genetic-testing conversations, oncology trial enrollment criteria, and at any company developing PARP-class therapies.
plain: Two genes that normally fix damaged DNA; when inherited broken, they sharply raise the lifetime odds of breast and ovarian cancer.

snappy: An FDA designation that fast-tracks development of a drug that shows substantial improvement over existing treatments for a serious condition.
detail: Breakthrough Therapy designation gets a drug intensified FDA support, more frequent meetings, and rolling review of submitted data — meaningfully accelerating time to market when it works. Designation isn't a guarantee of approval but is a strong positive signal. About 30-40% of recent novel approvals have had Breakthrough Therapy at some point. Companies announce designation as a milestone because investors recognize it as derisking.
plain: An FDA fast-pass for a drug that looks much better than anything currently available for a serious illness.

snappy: An FDA badge granted to drugs targeting serious conditions when early evidence suggests they're substantially better than existing options — bringing intensive agency support along the way.
detail: Created in 2012, Breakthrough Therapy is one of four FDA expedited programs and includes more frequent FDA meetings, intensive guidance on trial design, and eligibility for rolling review. Roughly half of recent oncology approvals carried the designation. You'll see "Breakthrough" stamped on press releases the day it's granted — pharma stocks often pop on the news, and analysts track the running tally of breakthrough drugs at every JPMorgan.
plain: An FDA badge for promising drugs against serious illness — speeds development with extra agency meetings and earlier reviews of incoming data.

snappy: The most common cancer in women — classified by which receptors are present (estrogen, progesterone, HER2), because the receptors decide treatment.
detail: Breast cancer subtypes — ER+, PR+, HER2+, triple-negative — drive entirely different treatment paths: hormone therapies for ER+, HER2-targeted drugs like Herceptin (trastuzumab) and ADCs like Enhertu for HER2+, and immunotherapy plus chemo for triple-negative. You'll hear breast cancer almost everywhere in oncology — at every major conference, in every pharma pipeline, and in any commercial discussion of women's-health markets.
plain: The most common cancer in women, sorted by which receptors sit on the tumor cells because those receptors decide which drugs will work.
A 'living drug' of re-engineered immune cells for lymphoma, one of several rival CAR-T treatments.
snappy: Bristol Myers Squibb's CD19-directed CAR-T therapy for large B-cell lymphoma and CLL.
detail: Breyanzi is a CD19 CAR-T competing with Yescarta and Kymriah, with a profile that pushed CAR-T into earlier lines of lymphoma therapy. You'll hear Breyanzi in CAR-T competitive and manufacturing-capacity discussion at ASH.

plain: A pharmaceutical company best known for the cancer immunotherapy Opdivo and the blood thinner Eliquis.
snappy: The pharma company behind the checkpoint inhibitor Opdivo and the blood thinner Eliquis.
detail: Bristol Myers Squibb (BMS) built its immuno-oncology franchise on Opdivo and Yervoy, co-markets Eliquis with Pfizer, and added Celgene's blood-cancer portfolio. Recent launches include Krazati, Breyanzi, and Cobenfy. You'll hear BMS in immuno-oncology and patent-cliff discussion.

plain: A blood cancer pill that blocks the same target as Imbruvica — notable as a major cancer drug developed largely in China.
snappy: BeiGene's BTK inhibitor for CLL and lymphomas, notable as a major drug developed largely in China.
detail: Brukinsa is a selective BTK inhibitor competing in CLL and several lymphomas, and a landmark for Chinese-originated oncology drugs reaching global markets. You'll hear Brukinsa in BTK-class share debates at ASH.

snappy: A signaling protein that helps cancerous B-cells survive and multiply — and the target of a major class of leukemia and lymphoma drugs.
detail: BTK is essential for B-cell development; in CLL and certain lymphomas, blocking it stops the cancer's growth signals. Imbruvica (ibrutinib) and Calquence (acalabrutinib) are the leading BTK inhibitors and major commercial products. You'll hear BTK at ASH, in CLL trial readouts, and in pipeline discussion of next-generation "covalent" or "non-covalent" inhibitors and their resistance profiles.
plain: A signaling protein cancerous immune cells lean on to survive — block it with a drug and certain blood cancers stop growing.

snappy: A chemical mixture that resists changes in pH — what keeps your blood at a precise 7.4 even when you eat, exercise, or hold your breath.
detail: Blood's main buffer system is bicarbonate, regulated by the lungs (CO2) and kidneys. Pharmaceutical formulations almost always include buffers to keep the drug stable at a specific pH during storage and infusion. Choice of buffer can affect injection-site comfort and drug stability — Humira's reformulation to a citrate-free buffer in 2018 was a big deal for patients who'd previously found injections painful.
plain: A chemical mixture that resists changes in acidity — what keeps your blood at a steady balance no matter what you eat or do.
One payment that covers everything for a single treatment episode — like a knee replacement — instead of paying each provider on its own.
snappy: A single payment covering everything involved in one episode of care — say a hip replacement — instead of paying each provider separately.
detail: A bundled payment pays one lump sum for an entire care episode (surgery plus hospital stay plus rehab), making providers split a fixed budget and coordinate. It's a core value-based-care model alongside ACOs. You'll hear bundled payment in surgical and CMS payment-reform discussion.

snappy: A very fast-growing blood cancer of B-cells — one of the most aggressive cancers known, but often curable with intensive chemo when caught early.
detail: Burkitt lymphoma is driven by a translocation that activates the MYC gene — the cancer cells double in less than a day, making it one of the fastest-growing tumors. Treatment is intensive, hospital-based combination chemotherapy, with cure rates exceeding 80% in younger patients. You'll hear Burkitt in hematology pipeline discussions and at ASH, often referenced as a benchmark for aggressive lymphoma biology.
plain: A blood cancer so fast-growing the cells can double in under a day, but often curable with intense chemo when caught early.
A more refined version of the first BTK-blocking blood cancer pill, designed to hit its target more cleanly.
snappy: AstraZeneca's more selective second-generation BTK inhibitor for CLL and mantle cell lymphoma.
detail: Calquence blocks BTK like Imbruvica but more selectively, aiming for fewer off-target side effects. A key AstraZeneca hematology product. You'll hear Calquence alongside Brukinsa in any next-generation BTK discussion at ASH.

plain: Paying a doctor a fixed monthly amount per patient to cover all their care — so the incentive shifts from volume to efficiency.
snappy: Paying a provider a fixed amount per patient per month to cover all their care — flipping the incentive from volume to efficiency.
detail: Under capitation a provider receives a set per-member-per-month payment regardless of services used, bearing the financial risk if care costs more. It underpins many HMOs and value-based-care arrangements. You'll hear capitation in managed-care and risk-sharing discussion.

snappy: A treatment where doctors take your own immune cells, reprogram them in a lab to recognize cancer, and infuse them back to attack the disease.
detail: CAR-T therapies engineer T-cells with a synthetic receptor that targets a specific cancer marker (typically CD19 on B-cell cancers). Approved CAR-Ts include Kymriah (tisagenlecleucel) and Yescarta (axicabtagene ciloleucel), with cure-level responses in some leukemias and lymphomas. The therapies are expensive ($400-500k) and require specialty centers. You'll hear CAR-T at ASH, in commercial discussions of cell-therapy market access, and around new solid-tumor expansion attempts.
plain: A treatment where doctors take your own immune cells, rewire them in a lab to spot cancer, and put them back to attack it.

snappy: Sugars and starches — your body's preferred quick-burn fuel and the main thing your blood glucose levels respond to.
detail: Carbohydrate metabolism is the central drama of diabetes: type 2 diabetes is fundamentally a problem of how the body handles glucose. SGLT2 inhibitors (Jardiance, Farxiga) cause the kidneys to dump excess glucose into urine. Carbohydrate counting is a daily practice for anyone on insulin. Drugs that slow carbohydrate absorption (acarbose, miglitol) were once a class of their own but have been largely supplanted by GLP-1s and SGLT2s.
plain: Sugars and starches — your body's go-to quick fuel, and the main thing that pushes your blood sugar up after a meal.

snappy: Cancer that starts in the cells lining your skin, organs, and tissues — covers most of the cancers you've heard of.
detail: Carcinomas — including adenocarcinomas, squamous cell carcinomas, and basal cell carcinomas — account for around 80-90% of all cancer diagnoses. The category is broad: lung, breast, prostate, colon, skin, head-and-neck cancers all fall here. You'll see carcinoma in almost every pathology report and oncology trial-enrollment criterion, distinguishing solid epithelial tumors from blood cancers and sarcomas.
plain: Cancer that begins in the cells lining your skin and organs — the bucket that covers most cancers you've ever heard of.
Out of everyone diagnosed with a disease, the percentage who die from it. A measure of how deadly it is once you catch it.
snappy: The share of *diagnosed cases* who die of a disease — how lethal it is once caught, distinct from population mortality.
detail: Deaths divided by confirmed cases — Ebola's can top 50%, seasonal flu's stays well under 1%. It gauges severity but is slippery early in an outbreak, when uncounted mild cases make it look scarier than it is. Don't confuse it with the infection fatality rate, which counts everyone infected including the undiagnosed, or with overall mortality. Reported constantly during any epidemic.

plain: A study that starts with people who already have a disease and looks back to find what might have caused it, versus people who don't.
snappy: An observational study that starts *with the sick*, then looks backward for their exposures — fast and cheap for rare diseases.
detail: Compares people who have a disease (cases) with similar people who don't (controls), looking back for differences in exposure. It's efficient for rare conditions where a cohort study would take decades, but prone to recall bias and confounding, and it gives odds ratios rather than direct risk. It helped tie smoking to lung cancer, and is a staple of epidemiology and pharmacovigilance signal work.

snappy: The most-ordered blood test in medicine — measuring red cells, white cells, and platelets to check for anemia, infection, clotting problems, and a hundred other conditions.
detail: CBC values are the bread-and-butter labs every chemo, immunotherapy, or autoimmune drug requires monitoring — neutrophil counts dictate whether the next dose of chemotherapy can go ahead, platelet counts gate decisions about anticoagulants. The components (hemoglobin, WBC, platelets, hematocrit) are referenced in nearly every clinical trial protocol. You'll see CBC monitoring requirements in FDA approval letters and REMS programs, and in commercial discussions of drugs that demand frequent lab visits — a known barrier to patient adherence.
plain: The most-ordered blood test in medicine — counts red cells, white cells, and platelets to check for anemia, infection, and much more.
A flag found on B-cells. Because it marks them so reliably, it's the bullseye for CAR-T therapies that treat blood cancers.
snappy: A protein on the surface of B-cells; because it marks them so reliably, it's the target of CAR-T cell therapies for blood cancers.
detail: CD19 sits on nearly all B-cells, normal and cancerous. CAR-T therapies — Kymriah, Yescarta, Breyanzi — re-engineer a patient's T-cells to hunt CD19, curing some otherwise-fatal leukemias and lymphomas. You'll hear CD19 in any cell-therapy or B-cell-malignancy discussion at ASH.

full: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
plain: The US public-health agency that tracks diseases and sets guidance on prevention and vaccines.
snappy: The US public-health agency that tracks disease, runs surveillance, and sets prevention and vaccine guidance.
detail: The CDC monitors outbreaks, runs disease surveillance, and issues immunization and prevention recommendations that shape clinical practice and reimbursement. You'll hear the CDC in any public-health, epidemiology, or vaccine-policy discussion.

snappy: Two proteins that act as the cell's accelerator pedal — when overactive in cancer, drugs that block them slam the brakes on tumor growth.
detail: CDK4/6 inhibitors — Ibrance (palbociclib), Kisqali (ribociclib), and Verzenio (abemaciclib) — have transformed treatment for ER-positive, HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer, doubling progression-free survival when combined with hormone therapy. The class is one of the biggest oncology launches of the past decade. You'll hear CDK4/6 in breast-cancer trial readouts, ASCO commercial discussions, and any pipeline conversation about expansion into adjuvant breast or other tumor types.
plain: Two proteins that act like a cell's gas pedal; drugs that block them slam the brakes on certain breast cancers.

snappy: A diagnostic test paired with a specific drug — used to find the patients whose biology makes the drug likely to actually work for them.
detail: The FDA approves many targeted therapies — especially in oncology — only alongside an approved diagnostic test that confirms the patient has the specific mutation or protein the drug targets. Herceptin (trastuzumab) for HER2-positive breast cancer is the textbook example. You'll hear CDx in approval announcements and commercial discussions, where access to testing often matters as much as access to the drug itself.
plain: A lab test paired with a specific drug — used to find the patients whose biology means the drug is actually likely to work.

snappy: The smallest unit of life — the building block every tissue, organ, and organism is made of.
detail: Humans have roughly 30 trillion cells in about 200 distinct types: neurons, skin cells, immune cells, liver cells, and so on. Most drugs ultimately act inside or on the surface of cells. Cell therapy — engineering and infusing living cells as a drug — is one of pharma's hottest frontiers: CAR-T cancer therapies (Kymriah, Yescarta), stem-cell treatments, and TIL therapies (Amtagvi) all deliver living cells rather than molecules.
plain: The smallest unit of life — the tiny building block every tissue and organ in your body is made from.

snappy: The thin oily skin around every cell — controls what gets in and out and is studded with receptors and channels for sensing the outside world.
detail: Cell membranes are made of a phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins. The surface receptors on cell membranes — GPCRs, kinase receptors, ion channels — are the targets of about half of all approved drugs. Cell membranes are also a barrier: getting drugs across them (or designing drug-delivery systems like lipid nanoparticles for mRNA vaccines) is an entire field of pharmaceutical science.
plain: The thin oily skin wrapped around every cell, controlling what gets in and out and dotted with sensors for the outside world.

snappy: Treatment using living cells as the active ingredient — most commonly engineered immune cells trained to attack cancer.
detail: CAR-T therapies (Kymriah, Yescarta, Breyanzi, Tecartus, Carvykti, Abecma) are the leading examples — patient T-cells are genetically modified to recognize a tumor antigen, then infused back. TIL therapy (Amtagvi, approved 2024) uses tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes for melanoma. Stem-cell transplants are an older form. Cell therapies are logistically intense — manufacturing happens per-patient with multi-week vein-to-vein turnaround times — which is why allogeneic 'off-the-shelf' approaches are an active development frontier.
plain: Treatment that uses living cells as the actual medicine — most often immune cells trained in a lab to hunt down cancer.

snappy: A class of cancer drugs that releases the immune system's brakes — letting your own T-cells recognize and attack tumors that have been hiding.
detail: Checkpoint inhibitors block proteins like PD-1, PD-L1, and CTLA-4 that normally restrain the immune system. By taking the brakes off, drugs like Keytruda (pembrolizumab), Opdivo (nivolumab), and Yervoy (ipilimumab) have turned metastatic melanoma and lung cancer from often-fatal to often-manageable. You'll hear checkpoint inhibitor everywhere in oncology — at every conference, in every pharma pipeline, and in any commercial discussion of immuno-oncology combinations.
plain: A class of cancer drug that releases the immune system's brakes so your own defenses can finally see and attack hidden tumors.

snappy: A specific subfamily of cytokines whose job is to summon immune cells to a particular location — they're the 'come here' signals of inflammation.
detail: Chemokines and their receptors steer immune cells through tissues during infection, wound healing, and (problematically) tumor growth and metastasis. Maraviroc — an HIV drug — works by blocking the CCR5 chemokine receptor. Mogamulizumab targets the chemokine receptor CCR4 in T-cell lymphomas. Chemokine pathways are a perennial drug-discovery target in autoimmunity and oncology.
plain: A chemical 'come here' flare released to summon immune cells to the spot where they're needed.

snappy: Drug treatment that kills fast-growing cells — devastating for cancer cells, but also tough on hair, gut lining, and bone marrow.
detail: "Chemo" historically meant cytotoxic drugs that target rapidly dividing cells; the side effects (hair loss, nausea, immune suppression) come from the same mechanism damaging healthy cells that also divide quickly. Modern oncology blends chemo with targeted therapies and immunotherapies. You'll still hear chemotherapy at every cancer-treatment discussion, in trial readouts as a comparator arm, and in patient experience around tolerability.
plain: Drug treatment that kills fast-growing cells — punishing for cancer, but rough on hair, gut, and bone marrow too.

snappy: A rare cancer of the bile ducts — the small tubes that carry digestive juices from the liver to the small intestine.
detail: Cholangiocarcinoma is uncommon but increasingly the focus of precision oncology because subsets carry IDH1/2 mutations or FGFR2 fusions, both of which now have approved targeted therapies (Tibsovo, Truseltiq, Pemazyre). You'll hear cholangiocarcinoma in rare-cancer trial readouts and in commercial discussions of how precision medicine creates niche-but-defensible markets in difficult-to-treat tumors.
