plain: A rare cancer in the small tubes that carry digestive juices from the liver to the gut.

snappy: A waxy lipid your body needs in small amounts — for cell membranes and to make hormones — but trouble in large amounts in the wrong places.
detail: LDL ('bad') cholesterol is the lab number that drives statin prescribing — the higher it is, the higher cardiovascular risk, and lowering it pharmacologically reduces heart attacks and strokes. Statins were the bestselling drug class in pharma history. PCSK9 inhibitors and Inclisiran target the same lipid pathway via different mechanisms, and oral PCSK9 inhibitors are in late-stage development.
plain: A waxy fat your body needs a little of to build cells and hormones, but which causes trouble when there's too much in the blood.

snappy: A tightly packaged bundle of DNA — humans have 23 pairs, including the X and Y that determine biological sex.
detail: Each chromosome contains hundreds to thousands of genes wound around scaffold proteins called histones. Extra or missing chromosomes cause major syndromes: an extra chromosome 21 causes Down syndrome, and broken chromosomes drive many cancers — the Philadelphia chromosome behind chronic myeloid leukemia gave rise to Gleevec, one of pharma's iconic targeted therapies.
plain: A tightly packed bundle of DNA — humans get 23 pairs, including the X and Y that decide biological sex.
The ongoing work of keeping long-term illnesses like diabetes under control, so they don't flare into emergencies.
snappy: The *ongoing coordination* of care for people with long-term conditions — keeping diabetes and heart failure stable so they don't end up back in the hospital.
detail: Chronic care management is the structured, continuous work of keeping long-term conditions — hypertension, type 2 diabetes, COPD, heart failure — under control between acute episodes. It lives mostly in primary care: medication management, monitoring, and coaching, increasingly paid for directly under value-based care because preventing a crisis is cheaper than treating one. Patients with several comorbidities benefit most. You'll hear chronic care management championed as the antidote to fragmented, reactive, expensive care.

snappy: A slow-growing blood cancer of B-cells, usually in older adults — many patients live for years with monitoring before any treatment is needed.
detail: CLL is the most common leukemia in adults and often causes few symptoms early on, with a "watch and wait" approach for low-risk patients. When treatment becomes necessary, BTK inhibitors like Imbruvica (ibrutinib) and BCL-2 inhibitors like Venclexta (venetoclax) have largely replaced chemotherapy. You'll hear CLL constantly at ASH and in commercial pipelines, often as a stepping stone toward other B-cell-cancer indications.
plain: A slow-growing blood cancer mostly seen in older adults — many patients live with it for years before any treatment is needed.

snappy: A blood cancer driven by a single gene fusion — and the historic proof that targeted drugs can turn cancer into a manageable chronic disease.
detail: CML is caused by the BCR-ABL fusion gene (the "Philadelphia chromosome"), and Gleevec (imatinib) was the first drug to specifically inhibit it — turning a once-fatal cancer into a long-term survivable condition with a daily pill. Newer-generation TKIs like Tasigna (nilotinib), Sprycel (dasatinib), and Scemblix (asciminib) handle resistance. You'll hear CML referenced as the textbook precision-medicine success story.
plain: A blood cancer caused by one specific gene mishap, and the first one ever turned from deadly into a manageable daily pill.
The billing records insurers create for every paid service — a huge real-world dataset researchers use to study how medicine is really used.
snappy: The billing records insurers generate for every paid service — a vast real-world dataset researchers mine for how medicine is actually used.
detail: Because every reimbursed visit, test, and prescription creates a claim, claims data offers population-scale evidence on utilization, outcomes, and cost — a backbone of health economics and real-world evidence, despite gaps versus the clinical record. You'll hear claims data in HEOR and outcomes-research discussion.

plain: Software that gives doctors alerts and reminders — like flagging a dangerous drug combination — to help them make safer choices.
snappy: Software prompts — alerts, reminders, order sets — that *help clinicians decide*, usually built right into the electronic health record.
detail: It delivers knowledge to clinicians at the point of care: drug-interaction alerts, dosing guidance, screening reminders, diagnostic suggestions. Embedded in the electronic health record, it can cut errors — but poorly tuned alerts cause 'alert fatigue.' Increasingly powered by AI and real-world evidence. You'll hear CDS in patient-safety, health-IT, and software-as-a-medical-device discussion.

snappy: A research study that tests whether a new drug, device, or treatment is safe and works — done in carefully controlled groups of volunteer patients.
detail: Clinical trials run in phases: Phase 1 tests safety in a small group, Phase 2 tests effectiveness, Phase 3 confirms benefit in large populations to support approval, and Phase 4 monitors after approval. The whole drug-development industry runs on these readouts — they drive stock prices, deal-making, and regulatory decisions. You'll hear "clinical trial" everywhere in pharma; understanding the phase usually tells you the stakes.
plain: A research study that tests whether a new drug or treatment is safe and actually works, run on volunteer patients in careful stages.
The most common adult leukemia — often slow-growing — now treated with targeted pills instead of chemo.
snappy: The most common adult leukemia; BTK inhibitors like Imbruvica and the BCL2 blocker Venclexta largely replaced chemo.
detail: CLL is a slow B-cell leukemia. Treatment shifted from chemo to targeted agents — BTK inhibitors Imbruvica, Calquence, and Brukinsa, plus BCL2 inhibitor Venclexta. You'll hear CLL dominate ASH hematology sessions and BTK-franchise earnings discussion.

plain: The peak level a drug reaches in your blood after a dose — the high-water mark.
snappy: The peak blood concentration a drug reaches after a dose; paired with Tmax (the time to reach it) in every PK profile.
detail: Cmax is the high-water mark of a drug in plasma; Tmax is when it occurs. With AUC and half-life they define pharmacokinetics and drive dosing. You'll hear Cmax in bioequivalence, formulation, and drug-interaction reviews at the FDA.

snappy: The two most-watched numbers when a drug is being measured in the blood — Cmax is the peak concentration it reaches, Tmax is how long it took to get there.
detail: Together with the AUC (total exposure), Cmax and Tmax are the basic shape parameters of any drug's blood-concentration curve. Drugmakers tune formulations — extended-release coatings, lipid carriers, dosing schedules — to control these numbers so peaks don't trigger side effects and troughs don't drop below therapeutic level. You'll see Cmax/Tmax in every Phase 1 readout press release and in formulation comparisons at investor R&D days when companies pitch a longer-acting or once-daily version of an existing drug.
plain: The two big numbers when tracking a drug in the blood — how high it peaks, and how long it took to get there.

snappy: The detailed package describing how a drug is actually made, tested, and kept consistent — required for FDA approval and ongoing oversight.
detail: CMC documents cover every step from raw materials to final product: synthesis routes, formulation, testing methods, stability data, manufacturing-facility audits. Weak CMC packages are a common reason FDA delays approval even when efficacy data is strong. You'll hear CMC in late-stage drug development discussions and at FDA Complete Response Letters that cite manufacturing issues rather than clinical concerns.
plain: The detailed file describing exactly how a drug is made, tested, and kept the same batch after batch — required for FDA approval.
A slow blood cancer driven by one gene glitch — the first cancer turned into a manageable condition by a targeted pill.
snappy: A blood cancer caused by the BCR-ABL fusion gene; Gleevec turned it from fatal into a near-normal lifespan — oncology's targeted-therapy poster child.
detail: CML is driven by the Philadelphia-chromosome BCR-ABL fusion. Gleevec and later tyrosine kinase inhibitors made near-normal life expectancy routine — the landmark proof that targeting a cancer's specific driver works. You'll hear CML at ASH and as the reference story in any targeted-therapy pitch.

plain: The US agency that runs Medicare and Medicaid — together the biggest payer for healthcare in the country.
snappy: The federal agency that runs Medicare and Medicaid — the single biggest payer for healthcare in the US.
detail: CMS administers Medicare and Medicaid, so its coverage and payment decisions — and now Medicare drug-price negotiation — move the entire market. You'll hear CMS in any reimbursement, formulary, or drug-pricing-policy discussion.

plain: The brain and spinal cord. Drugs struggle to reach it because of a protective barrier, which shapes how diseases there are treated.
snappy: The brain and spinal cord; the blood-brain barrier makes it a pharmacological fortress, so 'CNS penetration' is a prized drug property.
detail: Whether a drug crosses into the CNS determines its use against brain metastases and neurological disease. Newer kinase inhibitors like Tagrisso are valued for CNS penetration. You'll hear 'CNS activity' and 'CNS progression' in lung-cancer and neurology readouts and any blood-brain-barrier discussion.

plain: The first schizophrenia drug in decades to work in a brand-new way, aiming to avoid the side effects of older antipsychotics.
snappy: The first schizophrenia drug in decades to work a new way — through muscarinic receptors rather than blocking dopamine.
detail: Cobenfy targets muscarinic receptors, a mechanism shift from every prior antipsychotic and a chance to avoid their weight and movement side effects. A Bristol Myers Squibb product (via Karuna). You'll hear Cobenfy as the big mental-health launch and new mechanism story.

snappy: A three-letter 'word' of DNA or RNA that codes for one amino acid in a protein.
detail: There are 64 possible codons (4 letters × 4 × 4) and 20 amino acids, so the genetic code is redundant — multiple codons can specify the same amino acid. Three codons mean 'stop translating here.' A single-letter typo that changes a codon can cause disease: the mutation behind sickle cell anemia swaps one codon, changing one amino acid in hemoglobin.
plain: A three-letter 'word' written in DNA or RNA that tells the cell which building block to add next when making a protein.
A study that follows a group of people over time to see who gets sick, comparing those exposed to something with those who weren't.
snappy: An observational study that *follows a group forward in time*, comparing disease rates in the exposed and unexposed — epidemiology's workhorse.
detail: Tracks a defined group into the future, watching who develops disease based on exposures like smoking or a drug. Because it measures incidence directly, it can compute relative risk — but it's slow and costly for rare outcomes, and must adjust for confounding. Contrast the case-control study, which works backward from disease. Landmark cohorts like Framingham shaped what we know about cardiovascular risk; it ranks below the randomized controlled trial in evidence.

plain: Your share of a medical bill as a percentage — like 20% — that you pay after meeting your deductible.
snappy: Your share of a medical bill expressed as a percentage — say 20% — that you keep paying after meeting your deductible.
detail: Coinsurance is percentage-based cost-sharing (e.g., the plan pays 80%, you pay 20%) that kicks in after the deductible and continues until the out-of-pocket maximum. It differs from a flat copay. You'll hear coinsurance in benefit-design and specialty-drug affordability discussion.

snappy: An unbroken refrigeration network from factory to patient — required for biologics, vaccines, and cell therapies that lose potency the moment they warm up.
detail: Cold chain logistics range from standard 2-8°C refrigeration for most biologics to ultra-cold -70°C handling for the original Pfizer COVID vaccine and cell therapies like Kymriah (tisagenlecleucel). A single excursion outside spec can force a shipment to be discarded. You'll hear cold chain framed as a barrier in commercial discussions of biologic launches in emerging markets, and as a competitive moat for companies that have built reliable logistics partnerships.
plain: An unbroken chain of refrigeration from factory to patient, needed for vaccines and biologics that spoil the moment they warm up.

snappy: Cancer of the colon or rectum — the third most common cancer globally, and one of the most preventable through screening colonoscopies.
detail: CRC develops over years from precancerous polyps that screening can catch. Treatment depends on stage and molecular profile: surgery for early disease; chemo plus drugs like Erbitux (cetuximab) for KRAS-wild-type metastatic disease; immunotherapy for the small subset with high microsatellite instability. You'll hear CRC at GI-focused oncology meetings and in any commercial discussion of biomarker-guided treatment selection.
plain: Cancer of the colon or rectum — the third most common cancer worldwide, and one of the easiest to catch early with screening.
Having more than one health condition at the same time, which makes treatment more complicated.
snappy: *More than one condition at once* — the type 2 diabetes plus heart failure plus kidney disease that makes real patients so much harder to treat than trial subjects.
detail: A comorbidity is an additional disease a patient carries alongside the main one, and most people with a chronic illness have several. Comorbidities complicate everything: they raise the risk of a hospital admission, lengthen the length of stay, multiply drug interactions, and are exactly the messy patients a clean randomized controlled trial tends to exclude. Managing them is the daily work of primary care and chronic care management. You'll hear comorbidity invoked whenever trial results are questioned for how well they transfer to ordinary patients.

plain: A test that decides who should get a drug — pairing a targeted therapy with the marker it needs to work.
snappy: A test that decides who gets a drug — pairing a targeted therapy with the biomarker it requires, often approved alongside it.
detail: A companion diagnostic identifies patients whose tumor or genetics match a drug's target — PD-L1 staining for Keytruda, EGFR testing for Tagrisso. The FDA often approves drug and test together. You'll hear 'CDx' in any precision-medicine or diagnostics-partnership discussion.

snappy: A pathway letting seriously ill patients access an experimental drug before it's approved — when no other treatment works and the risk-benefit math leans toward trying it.
detail: Also called "expanded access," compassionate use is run by the FDA in coordination with manufacturers, who must agree to provide the drug. The 2018 federal Right to Try law added a parallel route bypassing the FDA, though uptake has been limited. You'll see compassionate-use stories surface in FDA press releases, in patient-advocacy campaigns, and in commercial discussions of the careful balance between humanitarian access and protecting trial enrollment for the formal approval pathway.
plain: A pathway letting very sick patients try an unapproved drug when nothing else works and the gamble seems worth taking.
A range showing how sure we are of a result — narrow means a precise estimate, wide means we're guessing more.
snappy: The *range of plausible values* around a result — wide signals uncertainty, narrow signals precision, and crossing 'no effect' means non-significant.
detail: Usually a 95% interval: the band that would capture the true value 95% of the time across repeated studies. For a hazard ratio or odds ratio, an interval crossing 1 — or for a risk difference, crossing 0 — isn't statistically significant, echoing the p-value. Its width shrinks with sample size and statistical power. You'll hear confidence interval scrutinized in every trial readout and forest plot.

plain: When a hidden factor fools you into thinking one thing causes another. Like blaming coffee for a disease that's really caused by smoking.
snappy: When a *hidden third factor* distorts an apparent link between cause and effect — the bane of every observational study.
detail: Happens when a variable tied to both the exposure and the outcome creates a misleading association — coffee seems to 'cause' cancer until you notice coffee drinkers smoked more. The intruder masquerades as a cause. A cohort study or case-control study fights it with matching and statistical adjustment; the randomized controlled trial defeats it by design, which is why it outranks them in evidence. Spotting it is core to reading any epidemiology paper.

plain: Tracking down everyone a sick person may have exposed, then warning them, so they can stay home before spreading the disease further.
snappy: Finding everyone an infected person *may have exposed*, then alerting or isolating them — shoe-leather epidemiology that breaks transmission chains.
detail: Identifies, notifies, and monitors the people a confirmed case has been near, so they can quarantine or get tested before infecting others. A frontline tool against any outbreak — central to controlling TB, STIs, Ebola, and COVID-19. Paired with disease surveillance and rapid testing, it can hold an epidemic's reproduction number below one. Effectiveness collapses once cases outpace the tracers, as happened during the pandemic.

snappy: The flat fee you pay at the pharmacy counter when you fill a prescription — separate from your premium and your deductible.
detail: Copays are set by your insurance plan and vary by formulary tier — generics might cost $5, preferred brands $30, specialty drugs hundreds or thousands. Pharma often offers "copay cards" to cover the patient's share for branded drugs, a practice insurers and PBMs argue inflates overall spend. You'll hear copay strategy debated on launch-readiness calls and in commercial discussions of how patients actually access a newly approved drug.
plain: The flat fee you hand over at the pharmacy counter when you fill a prescription, separate from your monthly insurance premium.

snappy: Long-term lung damage, mostly from smoking, that makes breathing progressively harder and can't be reversed — only slowed and managed with the right treatment.
detail: COPD covers chronic bronchitis and emphysema and affects roughly 16 million diagnosed Americans, with millions more undiagnosed. Treatment relies on inhaled bronchodilators (LABA, LAMA) and corticosteroids — Trelegy (fluticasone-umeclidinium-vilanterol) is the leading triple-therapy inhaler. The first IL-targeting biologic, Dupixent (dupilumab), was approved for COPD in 2024, opening a new chapter. You'll hear COPD on GSK, AstraZeneca, and Sanofi-Regeneron earnings calls as a market shifting from generic inhalers to biologics.
plain: Long-term lung damage, mostly from smoking, that makes breathing harder over time and can be slowed but not reversed.

snappy: A strong chemical bond where two atoms share electrons — the glue holding most biological molecules together.
detail: Most drugs bind their targets reversibly, but a growing class of 'covalent inhibitors' forms a permanent covalent bond with the target. Examples include aspirin (covalently modifies COX enzymes), the proton-pump inhibitors (Nexium, Prilosec), and several KRAS inhibitors in oncology (Lumakras, Krazati). Covalent drugs can be exquisitely selective and long-lasting but require careful safety design to avoid off-target reactivity.
plain: A strong chemical bond where two atoms share electrons — the glue holding most biological molecules together.

snappy: A precision gene-editing tool — molecular scissors that can cut, replace, or silence specific stretches of DNA — and the foundation of a new wave of therapies.
detail: CRISPR (originally a bacterial defense system) lets researchers rewrite the genome with unprecedented accuracy. Casgevy (exa-cel), the first CRISPR-based therapy approved by the FDA in 2023, treats sickle cell disease and beta-thalassemia. You'll hear CRISPR in genetic-disease pipeline discussions, in any biotech IPO involving Editas, Beam, Verve, or Intellia, and in ethical debates about germline editing.
plain: Molecular scissors that can cut, swap, or silence chosen stretches of DNA — and the foundation of a new wave of gene-based therapies.

snappy: A specialist company that runs clinical trials for drug companies — handling the operational complexity so the sponsor can focus on the science.
detail: CROs like IQVIA, ICON, and Labcorp design protocols, recruit patients, collect data, and submit to regulators on behalf of pharma sponsors — at scale, they're how trials actually happen. The industry is multi-billion-dollar and highly consolidated. You'll hear CRO in commercial discussions of trial timelines, in M&A activity, and in any drug-development pitch where the sponsor doesn't have in-house clinical operations.
plain: A specialist company hired by drugmakers to actually run their clinical trials — handling all the operational heavy lifting.

snappy: An inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any part of the digestive tract, causing pain, diarrhea, weight loss, and bowel-wall damage.
detail: Crohn's runs on the same drug pipeline as ulcerative colitis but the patient experience is more variable — disease can hit the small bowel, large bowel, or both. Major brands include Humira, Remicade, Stelara, Skyrizi, Entyvio, Rinvoq. The IL-23 class (Skyrizi, Tremfya) has been gaining share in recent years. Crohn's commentary is part of the broader 'IBD switching' narrative as patients cycle through mechanisms.
plain: An inflammatory gut disease that can hit anywhere from mouth to colon, causing pain, diarrhea, weight loss, and lasting damage.
A study where each person tries both the treatment and the comparison at different times, acting as their own basis for comparison.
snappy: A design where each patient *receives both treatments in sequence* — serving as their own control, which sharpens the comparison and shrinks the sample.
detail: Each participant takes one therapy, then switches to the other after a washout period, so within-person comparisons cancel out individual variability — powerful for stable, chronic conditions. It needs fewer patients than a parallel randomized controlled trial but breaks down when effects carry over or the disease shifts. Blinding still applies. You'll hear crossover trial in early-phase and rare-disease study design.

snappy: An immune checkpoint that holds T-cells back from attacking — and the first one ever drugged successfully, kicking off the modern immunotherapy era.
detail: CTLA-4 normally prevents the immune system from attacking the body's own tissues; tumors exploit this brake to evade immune attack. Yervoy (ipilimumab), approved in 2011, was the first checkpoint inhibitor and is now combined with PD-1 drugs in melanoma and other cancers. You'll hear CTLA-4 in any immuno-oncology pipeline discussion, often as the older sibling of PD-1.
plain: An immune brake that holds T-cells back from attacking — and the first such brake doctors ever learned how to release with a drug.

snappy: The family of liver enzymes that breaks down most of the drugs you take — and the reason one medication can change the safe dose of another.
detail: CYPs (especially CYP3A4, CYP2D6, CYP2C9) metabolize roughly 75% of marketed drugs. Some drugs inhibit or induce these enzymes, slowing or speeding the breakdown of others — the basis of most clinically important drug-drug interactions. Grapefruit juice's warning is CYP3A4 inhibition. You'll see CYP450 in every drug's package insert, in pharmacovigilance signal investigations, and in trial-design discussions where drug-drug interaction studies are required before approval.
plain: A family of liver enzymes that breaks down most drugs you swallow — and the reason one pill can change the safe dose of another.

snappy: A genetic disease that thickens mucus in the lungs and pancreas — devastating in earlier eras, transformed by recent CFTR-modulator drugs.
detail: Vertex Pharmaceuticals essentially owns the CF franchise: Trikafta (elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor) became standard of care for ~90% of patients and turned a brutal pediatric disease into something far more manageable. The Trikafta franchise generates ~$10B annually. Vertex's next-gen vanzacaftor combo and casgevy gene-edited approaches keep the pipeline rolling. CF is a textbook example of how targeted small-molecule chemistry can rewrite a disease.
plain: An inherited disease that thickens mucus in the lungs and pancreas — once devastating, now far more manageable thanks to recent drugs.

snappy: A small signaling protein released by immune cells to coordinate inflammation, infection response, and immune-cell communication.
detail: Cytokines are the targets of many of the biggest-selling biologics: TNF-alpha (blocked by Humira, Enbrel, Remicade in autoimmune disease), IL-6 (blocked by Actemra in rheumatoid arthritis and COVID), IL-17 (blocked by Cosentyx, Taltz in psoriasis), IL-23 (blocked by Skyrizi, Tremfya). 'Cytokine storm' — runaway cytokine release — is the dangerous overshoot that drives the worst outcomes in severe COVID and CAR-T side effects.
plain: A small signaling protein immune cells fire off to coordinate inflammation, infection response, and chatter with other immune cells.

snappy: The jelly-like fluid that fills the inside of a cell, holding all the organelles and where most of the cell's chemistry happens.
detail: Cytoplasm is where glycolysis happens, where most protein synthesis occurs, and where signaling cascades from cell-surface receptors get relayed inward. When pharma talks about whether a drug is 'cell-permeable,' they mean: can it cross the cell membrane and reach targets in the cytoplasm? Most small molecules can; most biologics (antibodies, peptides) cannot, which limits them to extracellular or surface targets.
plain: The jelly-like fluid filling the inside of a cell, where most of its everyday chemistry happens.

snappy: Cell-killing — the formal word for traditional chemotherapy drugs that destroy fast-dividing cells, including cancer (and unfortunately some healthy ones).
detail: Cytotoxic agents include classic chemo drugs like cisplatin, doxorubicin, and paclitaxel — they damage DNA or microtubules to kill dividing cells. The term distinguishes these from cytostatic drugs (which stop growth without killing), targeted therapies, and immunotherapies. You'll hear cytotoxic in trial-design discussions, ADC payload conversations (the "warhead" is usually cytotoxic), and in any conversation contrasting chemo with newer drug classes.
plain: Cell-killing — the formal word for old-school chemo drugs that wipe out fast-dividing cells, cancerous and otherwise.

snappy: A clinical trial that lets patients participate from home — using telehealth, wearables, and home-shipped meds — instead of traveling to a research center.
detail: DCTs grew during COVID and stuck around because they cut patient burden, broaden geographic recruiting, and reduce dropouts. Pure-DCT trials are rare; most are hybrid. You'll hear DCT in trial-design discussions, in pitches from companies like Medable and Science 37, and in commercial conversations about including underserved populations.
plain: A clinical trial that lets patients take part from home using video calls, wearables, and mailed medicine instead of traveling in.
A clinical trial run partly or fully at patients' homes — using telehealth, apps, and local labs — instead of only at trial sites.
snappy: A clinical trial brought *to the patient* — telehealth visits, home nursing, e-consent, wearables — rather than requiring travel to a site.
detail: These shift study activities to participants' homes via telehealth, remote patient monitoring, electronic consent, and local labs, widening access and retention. Wearable devices and digital biomarkers supply continuous endpoints. The FDA has issued guidance encouraging the model, accelerated by the pandemic. You'll hear decentralized trial in clinical-operations and digital health discussion.

plain: The amount you pay out of your own pocket each year before your insurance starts chipping in.
snappy: The amount you pay out of pocket each year before your insurance starts paying.
detail: A deductible is the annual threshold a patient must cover before the plan contributes; high-deductible plans trade lower premiums for more upfront cost. After it's met, coinsurance and copays apply up to the out-of-pocket maximum. You'll hear deductible in any benefit-design or patient-affordability discussion.

snappy: A new class of drugs that don't just block a harmful protein — they tag it for the cell's own waste-disposal system to destroy it entirely.
detail: Targeted protein degraders (PROTACs, molecular glues) recruit the cell's ubiquitin system to mark and destroy disease-driving proteins. The class extends drug development to previously "undruggable" proteins. You'll hear degrader at biotech conferences, in oncology and immunology pipelines from Arvinas, C4 Therapeutics, and Kymera, and in any commercial framing of next-generation small molecules.
plain: A new class of drug that doesn't just block a harmful protein — it tags the protein for the cell's own garbage disposal to destroy.
A health signal measured by a digital device — like gait from a phone or heart rhythm from a watch — used to track disease.
snappy: A *device-measured* physiological or behavioral signal — gait, sleep, heart rhythm — used like a lab biomarker to track disease or drug effect.
detail: Objective measures captured by sensors and apps — typing speed in Parkinson's, nocturnal cough, continuous glucose — that stand in for disease state or treatment response. Drawn from wearables and phones, they enable continuous endpoints in decentralized trials and remote patient monitoring. Validation against clinical outcomes is the hurdle. You'll hear digital biomarker in trial-innovation and digital health discussion.

snappy: A devastating childhood brain tumor that grows in a part of the brainstem too critical for surgery — historically nearly always fatal.
detail: DIPG affects 200-400 children a year in the US, with median survival under a year despite radiation. The location prevents biopsy or resection. Recent trials with ONC201 and CAR-T directed at the H3K27M mutation common in DIPG have shown the first signs of progress in decades. You'll hear DIPG in pediatric oncology fundraising, rare-disease biotech pitches, and patient-advocacy contexts.
plain: A devastating childhood brain tumor in a spot too critical for surgery, and historically almost always fatal.
Being formally released from the hospital, along with instructions and a plan for follow-up care.
snappy: The *formal release* from a hospital stay — paired with instructions, prescriptions, and a plan to keep you from coming back.
detail: Discharge ends an inpatient admission and is a surprisingly risky moment: medications change, follow-up gets arranged, and a shaky handoff is a leading cause of readmission. A good discharge loops in primary care, reconciles the medication list, and sets up any follow-on care. Payers and value-based care programs scrutinize it because avoidable readmissions are expensive and often preventable. You'll hear discharge planning discussed wherever hospitals try to shorten the length of stay without sending people home too soon.

plain: Constantly tracking who is getting sick across a population, so health officials can catch and stop outbreaks early.
snappy: The continuous *watch* for disease in a population — collecting case data so outbreaks are spotted and stopped before they spread.
detail: The ongoing collection and analysis of health data — lab reports, doctor visits, death records — to detect threats and guide response. Notifiable diseases must by law be reported into it. It's how the CDC and WHO spot an outbreak before it becomes an epidemic, follow incidence trends, and target immunization. Modern systems fold in wastewater, pharmacy sales, and search queries for faster signals.

plain: A creature like a mosquito or tick that carries a disease from one person or animal to another without usually getting sick itself.
snappy: A living carrier — usually a *mosquito, tick, or flea* — that ferries a pathogen between hosts, as mosquitoes do for malaria.
detail: An organism that transmits a pathogen between hosts without necessarily falling ill itself. Mosquitoes (malaria, dengue, Zika), ticks (Lyme), and fleas (plague) are the classics. Many vector-borne diseases are a kind of zoonosis, jumping from animals to people, and climate change is widening their range — a growing worry for outbreak preparedness and disease surveillance.

snappy: The most common aggressive lymphoma — fast-growing but often curable with combination chemotherapy and antibody drugs.
detail: DLBCL accounts for around 30% of non-Hodgkin lymphomas, traditionally treated with R-CHOP (rituximab plus chemo) with cure rates around 60%. For relapsed/refractory cases, CAR-T therapies (Yescarta, Breyanzi) and ADCs (Polivy) have changed the landscape. You'll hear DLBCL at ASH, in CAR-T pipeline expansions, and in commercial discussions of frontline lymphoma combinations.
plain: The most common fast-growing lymphoma — aggressive but often curable with a mix of chemotherapy and antibody drugs.

snappy: A drug that doesn't just calm symptoms but slows the underlying joint damage of rheumatoid arthritis — anchored for decades by methotrexate, now expanded by biologics and JAK inhibitors.
detail: Conventional DMARDs (methotrexate, sulfasalazine, leflunomide) remain first-line for RA and inflammatory arthritis, often kept alongside biologics (Humira/adalimumab, Enbrel/etanercept) and targeted-synthetic DMARDs like Rinvoq (upadacitinib). Methotrexate alone is one of the most-prescribed RA drugs globally — and cheap. You'll hear DMARD strategy on AbbVie and Lilly earnings calls when JAK inhibitor uptake versus biologic positioning surfaces, and at ACR when head-to-head readouts redefine the order in which DMARDs get tried.
plain: A drug that doesn't just ease arthritis pain but actually slows the joint damage underneath.

snappy: An independent group of experts that reviews trial data while a study is running — and can stop the trial if patients are being harmed or already clearly benefiting.
detail: DMCs (sometimes DSMBs) protect trial participants by watching for safety signals or overwhelming efficacy. Their interim analyses can halt trials early — sometimes for the right reason (drug works, give it to everyone), sometimes the wrong (futility). You'll hear DMC decisions move stocks when they recommend stopping a trial early for benefit, and in ethics-committee reviews of late-stage protocols.
plain: An outside panel that peeks at a running clinical trial's data and can call it off if patients are getting hurt or already clearly helped.

snappy: The double-helix molecule that stores the genetic instructions for building and running every living thing.
detail: DNA is a long chain of four chemical letters — A, T, G, C — twisted into the famous double helix discovered by Watson and Crick in 1953. Stretches of DNA called genes encode the proteins that do the work of the cell. Modern medicine reads, writes, and edits DNA: gene therapy delivers corrected DNA, CRISPR rewrites it, and sequencing reads it cheaply enough to be a routine clinical test.
plain: The twisted ladder of chemicals inside every cell that stores the instructions for building and running a living thing.

snappy: The body's spell-checker for DNA — when it breaks, mutations pile up uncorrected and cancer risk rises sharply.
detail: MMR deficiency creates microsatellite instability (MSI-H), a state of hypermutation that produces tumors visible to the immune system — which is why MSI-H/dMMR cancers respond unusually well to immunotherapy like Keytruda. Inherited MMR mutations cause Lynch syndrome. You'll hear MMR/dMMR in colorectal and endometrial cancer trial designs and in any precision-immunotherapy pipeline discussion.
plain: The body's spell-checker for DNA — when it breaks, errors pile up and cancer risk climbs.

snappy: The careful step-by-step approach in early trials of giving small groups of patients increasing doses of a new drug until side effects become unacceptable.
detail: Dose escalation is the heart of Phase 1 trials. Standard designs (3+3, BOIN, mTPI) treat tiny cohorts at each dose level, watching for dose-limiting toxicities, before deciding whether to escalate further. The maximum tolerated dose (MTD) is the headline output, though modern oncology has shifted toward optimal biological dose. You'll hear dose escalation in Phase 1 readouts and at ASCO/AACR poster sessions.
plain: The careful early-trial process of slowly increasing how much of a new drug patients get until side effects become too much.
The system that pays a hospital a flat amount for an admission based on the diagnosis, rather than per day or per service.
snappy: The classification that pays a hospital a fixed amount per admission based on the diagnosis — not on how many days or services it racks up.
detail: Medicare pays inpatient stays by DRG: each admission is grouped by diagnosis and procedure into a category with a set payment, so hospitals profit by being efficient. It reshaped hospital economics when introduced in the 1980s. You'll hear DRG in any hospital-reimbursement discussion.

snappy: When one drug changes how another drug works in your body — sometimes making it weaker, sometimes dangerously stronger.
detail: DDIs typically occur through liver enzymes (CYP450) or transporter proteins. Some interactions are mild; others are serious enough to require dose adjustments or to ban combinations entirely. You'll see DDI sections in every drug label, hear them at FDA reviews of polypharmacy populations, and in any commercial discussion of competitor drugs that share metabolic pathways.
plain: When one drug changes how another works in your body — sometimes weakening it, sometimes dangerously amplifying it.

snappy: The TV, web, and print ads that pitch prescription drugs straight to patients — a uniquely American practice that the rest of the developed world has largely banned.
detail: Pharma spends roughly $7 billion a year on DTC ads in the US, telling viewers to "ask your doctor about" everything from Humira (adalimumab) to GLP-1s. The FDA requires balanced risk disclosure (the famous "side effects may include") but otherwise lets the ads run. You'll see DTC framed in policy debates as a driver of branded-drug demand, on earnings calls when launch teams talk about awareness campaigns, and at hearings on pharmaceutical pricing.
plain: The TV and web ads that pitch prescription drugs straight to patients — a uniquely American practice most other countries ban.

snappy: A software-based treatment — usually an app — designed to prevent or manage a medical condition, sometimes prescribed by a doctor like a pill.
detail: Digital therapeutics deliver evidence-based interventions through software, ranging from cognitive behavioral therapy apps for insomnia to attention-training games for ADHD. Some are FDA-cleared and prescription-only — known as "PDTs" (Prescription Digital Therapeutics) — while others are over-the-counter. You'll hear DTx in pharma earnings calls when companies pitch software as the next growth frontier, and at health-tech conferences where pilots are being run with insurers.
plain: A software treatment — usually a phone app — that a doctor can prescribe to prevent or manage a medical condition.

snappy: A devastating X-linked genetic disease that destroys muscle tissue progressively — boys typically lose the ability to walk by their early teens.
detail: DMD is caused by mutations in the dystrophin gene, the largest gene in the human genome. The space has been one of the most contentious in biotech: Sarepta's exon-skipping drugs (Exondys 51, Vyondys 53, Amondys 45) got approved despite controversial efficacy data, and their gene therapy Elevidys won full FDA approval in 2024 after a complicated review. DMD investment commentary is dominated by FDA flexibility, parent advocacy pressure, and the unmet need vs trial-design tension.
plain: A devastating inherited disease that slowly destroys muscle — boys typically lose the ability to walk by their early teens.
A breakthrough injection for severe eczema and asthma that calms the specific kind of inflammation driving allergic disease.
snappy: An IL-4/IL-13 blocker that opened the biologics era in atopic dermatitis, then asthma and beyond — a Sanofi/Regeneron megabrand.
detail: Dupixent calms type-2 inflammation, transforming moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis and asthma and expanding into COPD and other allergic diseases. You'll hear Dupixent as the breakout immunology drug on every Sanofi and Regeneron call.

snappy: How long a drug keeps working in patients who initially respond to it — a measure of staying power, not just whether tumors shrink at first.
detail: DoR is a key efficacy metric especially in oncology — a drug that produces brief responses isn't as valuable as one delivering durable ones. The metric is reported alongside overall response rate (ORR) in trial readouts. You'll hear DoR in any drug pitch claiming durable benefit, in regulatory discussions of accelerated-approval confirmations, and in commercial differentiation between drugs with similar response rates.
plain: How long a drug keeps working in patients who responded at first — a measure of staying power, not just initial effect.

snappy: Abnormally growing cells that aren't cancer yet but are well on their way — a warning sign that gets caught and treated early when possible.
detail: Dysplasia describes disorganized cell growth — graded as low or high — that often precedes invasive cancer. It's commonly found in cervical, esophageal, and colon screening, where treatment of high-grade dysplasia prevents progression to cancer. You'll hear dysplasia in pathology reports, in screening-program discussions, and in any commercial conversation about cancer prevention vs. treatment.
plain: Cells that are growing oddly but aren't cancer yet — a warning sign caught and treated early when possible.

snappy: A simple, painless test that records the heart's electrical activity through stickers on the chest — used to spot rhythm problems, heart attacks, and drug-induced effects.
detail: ECGs (called EKG in the US) are everywhere in pharma trials, especially the QTc interval — a measurement of heart-rhythm stability that the FDA requires for almost every new drug since several blockbusters were withdrawn for QTc-related arrhythmias. Wearable ECG patches and Apple Watch ECG features have moved monitoring from clinic to home. You'll see ECG flagged in FDA safety communications, in cardiovascular trial readouts, and in digital-health pitches at JPMorgan.
plain: A quick, painless test that records the heart's electrical activity through stickers on the chest.

snappy: A cell-surface receptor that, when mutated, drives uncontrolled growth — found in about 15% of lung cancers, plus head-and-neck and colon cancer.
detail: EGFR mutations are the foundation of lung-cancer precision medicine. Drugs like Tagrisso (osimertinib) target EGFR-mutant non-small-cell lung cancer with dramatic response rates; the T790M mutation is a famous resistance pathway that drove second-generation drug development. You'll hear EGFR everywhere in lung-cancer trial readouts, ASCO commercial discussions, and pipeline conversations about overcoming resistance.
plain: A switch on the outside of cells that, when broken, drives uncontrolled growth — found in many lung cancers.
The digital version of a patient's chart — diagnoses, medications, test results — shared across the clinicians who treat them.
snappy: A patient's *digital chart* — meds, labs, diagnoses, notes — built to follow them across every clinician and setting, unlike a single practice's records.
detail: The longitudinal digital record of a patient's health, built to be shared across providers — the backbone of modern care and a prerequisite for interoperability. Vendors like Epic and Cerner dominate US hospitals. These systems feed clinical decision support, patient portals, and real-world evidence, though clinician burnout from clunky interfaces is a chronic complaint. Distinguish it from the narrower electronic medical record, confined to one practice.

plain: A digital chart within a single doctor's office or hospital — like a paper record gone electronic, but not easily shared elsewhere.
snappy: A *single practice's* digital chart — the narrower, older cousin of the electronic health record, which is built to travel between providers.
detail: An EMR digitizes the records of one practice or hospital — diagnoses, treatments, history — but isn't designed to move between organizations. The terms are often used interchangeably, though strictly the electronic health record is the broader, shareable version enabling interoperability and health information exchange. The distinction matters in health-IT policy and procurement.

plain: A US pharmaceutical company that, with Novo Nordisk, leads the GLP-1 weight-loss and diabetes boom.
snappy: The US pharma company that, with Novo Nordisk, leads the GLP-1 boom via Mounjaro and Zepbound.
detail: Eli Lilly's tirzepatide (Mounjaro for diabetes, Zepbound for obesity) and the SGLT2 drug Jardiance made it a cardiometabolic powerhouse, alongside a growing Alzheimer's and oncology pipeline. You'll hear Lilly in every GLP-1 and obesity-market discussion.

plain: A widely used blood thinner that prevents strokes and clots, simpler to take than the older warfarin it replaced.
snappy: A factor Xa blood thinner — one of the world's top-selling drugs — used to prevent strokes and clots.
detail: Eliquis is a direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) that largely replaced warfarin for atrial fibrillation and clot prevention, with no routine monitoring. A BMS/Pfizer franchise facing looming generics. You'll hear Eliquis in any anticoagulant or Medicare drug-pricing discussion.

snappy: The FDA's European counterpart — the body that approves drugs and biologics for use across the EU.
detail: EMA reviews go through committees (CHMP for human medicines), with national-level reimbursement decisions following separately in each member state. EMA approval often lags FDA by 6-12 months, which matters commercially. You'll hear EMA in any global drug-launch sequencing discussion, at investor calls breaking out US vs. EU revenue projections, and in regulatory affairs strategy.
plain: Europe's drug regulator — the body that decides which medicines can be sold across the EU.
The part of a hospital that treats sudden, serious problems at any hour, seeing the most urgent cases first.
snappy: The hospital's *always-open front line* for sudden, serious illness and injury — where triage decides who is seen first.
detail: The emergency department treats anyone who walks or is wheeled in, around the clock, sorting them by urgency through triage rather than appointment. It's the classic acute care setting and the main gateway to an inpatient admission for the seriously ill, while also absorbing primary care that patients couldn't get elsewhere — a costly mismatch payers track closely. Crowding and boarding are chronic operational headaches. You'll hear emergency department crowding cited in every debate about access and the safety-net role of hospitals.

plain: An early drug that calms the inflammation behind arthritis and psoriasis by soaking up an inflammatory signal.
snappy: One of the first anti-TNF biologics, long a mainstay for rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis.
detail: Enbrel is a decoy receptor that mops up TNF, easing rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, and psoriatic arthritis. An early biologic blockbuster for Amgen and Pfizer. You'll hear Enbrel alongside Humira and Remicade as the founding anti-TNF trio.

plain: A disease that is always around at a steady, low level in a place — never gone, but not exploding either.
snappy: A disease *constantly present* at a baseline level in an area — always smoldering, like malaria in the tropics, rather than surging or vanishing.
detail: Describes a disease that circulates steadily without dying out or exploding. Malaria is endemic to much of the tropics; chickenpox was before vaccines. A disease can shift between states — an epidemic or pandemic may settle into this kind of steady equilibrium once enough herd immunity builds. Public-health teams work to push these baseline levels down through immunization and disease surveillance.

snappy: Cancer of the lining of the uterus — the most common gynecologic cancer in developed countries, often linked to obesity and hormonal factors.
detail: Endometrial cancer is increasingly classified by molecular subtype (POLE-mutant, MSI-H/dMMR, p53-mutant, no-specific-profile), each with different prognoses and treatment paths. Keytruda is approved for MSI-H endometrial cancer; Lenvima (lenvatinib) plus Keytruda is another important combination. You'll hear it at gynecologic oncology meetings and in immunotherapy expansion narratives.
plain: Cancer of the lining of the womb — the most common female reproductive cancer in wealthy countries.

snappy: A maze of membranes inside the cell where proteins destined for the cell surface or for export get folded, modified, and quality-checked.
detail: When the ER gets overwhelmed with misfolded proteins, it triggers the 'unfolded protein response' — a stress signal implicated in diabetes, neurodegeneration, and cancer. ER stress is a hot drug target. Cystic fibrosis 'modulator' drugs like Trikafta work in part by helping the misfolded CFTR protein get past ER quality control and reach the cell surface.
plain: A maze of folded membranes inside the cell where new proteins get shaped, checked, and prepared for the journey out.

snappy: What a clinical trial actually measures to decide if a drug works — survival, tumor shrinkage, time to progression, or quality of life.
detail: Endpoints are picked carefully because they determine what the trial proves. Overall survival (OS) is the gold standard but takes years; progression-free survival (PFS) and overall response rate (ORR) are faster surrogates often used for accelerated approval. You'll hear endpoint everywhere in pharma — in trial design, in FDA discussions, and in any earnings call where management defends or explains a topline readout.
plain: What a clinical trial actually measures to decide if a drug works — survival, tumor shrinkage, or quality of life.
A 'guided missile' breast cancer drug so potent it helps even patients with very low levels of its target — a recent breakthrough.
snappy: A next-generation HER2 antibody-drug conjugate that redefined the field by working even in 'HER2-low' breast cancer.
detail: Enhertu is an ADC whose potent payload and 'bystander effect' expanded treatment to HER2-low tumors once thought HER2-negative. A major AstraZeneca/Daiichi Sankyo product, it's reshaped breast and lung cancer. You'll hear Enhertu as the standout ADC at every ASCO.

snappy: A protein that speeds up a specific chemical reaction in the body without being used up itself — biology's catalysts.
detail: Enzymes drive every metabolic process: digestion, DNA replication, signal transduction, drug metabolism. Many drugs are 'enzyme inhibitors' — statins block HMG-CoA reductase to lower cholesterol; ACE inhibitors block angiotensin-converting enzyme to lower blood pressure; protease inhibitors block HIV's protease enzyme. Enzyme replacement therapies (Cerezyme, Aldurazyme) treat rare metabolic diseases where patients lack a working copy of one critical enzyme.
plain: A protein that speeds up a specific chemical reaction in the body without itself being used up — biology's catalyst.

snappy: A relatively rare brain or spinal cord tumor that arises from cells lining the fluid-filled cavities of the central nervous system.
detail: Ependymomas are graded I to III by aggressiveness and treated primarily with surgery and radiation. Pediatric posterior-fossa ependymomas are the most studied subset. The disease has limited targeted-therapy options, which makes it an active area of pediatric oncology research. You'll hear ependymoma in pediatric brain-tumor trial readouts and rare-disease drug development contexts.
plain: A relatively rare tumor of the brain or spine that grows from the cells lining its fluid-filled cavities.
A disease spreading through a community much faster or wider than usual. Bigger than a local outbreak, but not yet worldwide.
snappy: A sudden surge of a disease *above* its normal level in a region — bigger than an outbreak, more contained than a pandemic.
detail: Cases climb well beyond what's expected for a place and time. It sits on a spectrum: a localized outbreak can grow into one, and when it crosses continents it becomes a pandemic. Whether it ignites depends partly on the Basic Reproduction Number and the population's herd immunity; a disease that never surges this way is instead called endemic. The CDC and WHO declare and track them.

snappy: A neurological disorder defined by recurring seizures — sudden bursts of disordered electrical activity in the brain — affecting people of every age and background.
detail: Epilepsy treatment leans on a long list of antiseizure drugs (older ones like phenytoin and valproate, newer ones like Vimpat/lacosamide and Briviact/brivaracetam), with surgery and devices for drug-resistant cases. Cannabidiol (Epidiolex) was the first FDA-approved cannabis-derived drug, indicated for rare pediatric epilepsies. You'll hear epilepsy on UCB, Jazz, and SK earnings calls as a steady specialty market, and at AES when readouts on novel mechanisms shift expectations.
plain: A brain condition where bursts of disordered electrical activity cause repeated seizures.

snappy: The exact patch on an antigen that an antibody actually grabs onto — usually just a few amino acids' worth of surface.
detail: A single antigen can have multiple epitopes, and different antibodies target different ones. 'Epitope mapping' is a routine step in antibody drug development to confirm where on a target protein an antibody binds. The fast-evolving spike-protein epitopes of SARS-CoV-2 are why successive COVID variants escaped earlier antibodies and required updated vaccines.
plain: The exact spot on a target that an antibody actually grabs onto — usually just a tiny patch of surface.
Patients reporting their own symptoms and quality of life through an app or device during a study or their care.
snappy: *Patient-reported* symptoms and outcomes captured electronically — on an app or device — rather than on paper at a clinic visit.
detail: It captures what patients say about their own symptoms, function, and quality of life directly through apps or handheld devices, replacing paper diaries. This improves data quality and timeliness in trials and routine care, and is a natural fit for decentralized trials, remote patient monitoring, and real-world data. You'll hear ePRO in trial-design and digital health discussion.

snappy: Hormone receptors found on most breast cancer cells — when present, they make tumors vulnerable to anti-hormone drugs that block or starve them.
detail: About 70% of breast cancers are ER-positive (and usually PR-positive too), meaning estrogen drives their growth. Treatment includes tamoxifen, aromatase inhibitors, and SERDs like Faslodex (fulvestrant), often combined with CDK4/6 inhibitors in metastatic disease. You'll hear ER/PR at every breast-cancer trial readout and in commercial discussions of the largest commercial segment in oncology.
plain: Hormone sensors on most breast cancer cells — when present, they make tumors vulnerable to drugs that block hormones.

snappy: Another name for the HER2 gene — and a key driver in about 20% of breast cancers, plus subsets of stomach, lung, and colon cancers.
detail: ERBB2 amplification or overexpression makes tumors vulnerable to HER2-targeted therapies — Herceptin (trastuzumab), Perjeta (pertuzumab), Kadcyla, and Enhertu. Even "HER2-low" tumors are now eligible for some of these drugs. You'll hear ERBB2 in pathology reports and in commercial discussions of the rapidly expanding HER2-targeted franchise.
plain: Another name for the HER2 gene — a major driver of about a fifth of breast cancers.

snappy: Cancer of the esophagus — the tube connecting throat to stomach — with two main types tied to very different risk factors.
detail: Adenocarcinoma is associated with chronic acid reflux and Barrett's esophagus, while squamous cell carcinoma is linked to smoking and alcohol. Treatment is multimodal — surgery, chemoradiation, and increasingly immunotherapy with Keytruda or Opdivo. You'll hear esophageal cancer at GI oncology meetings, in commercial discussions of immunotherapy expansion, and in screening-program advocacy.
plain: Cancer of the tube that carries food from throat to stomach, with two main types tied to very different risk factors.
A docking point for the hormone estrogen. Many breast cancers grow through it, so blocking it is a core treatment.
snappy: The protein estrogen binds to; most breast cancers are 'ER-positive' and grow on estrogen — the rationale for endocrine therapy.
detail: About 70% of breast cancers are ER-positive, meaning estrogen fuels them; endocrine therapies such as tamoxifen and aromatase inhibitors starve that signal. ER status, with the progesterone receptor and HER2, defines breast-cancer subtype and treatment. You'll hear 'ER-positive' in every breast cancer discussion at ASCO.

snappy: A rare bone and soft-tissue cancer that mostly affects teenagers and young adults — driven by a single, almost-defining gene fusion.
detail: Nearly all Ewing sarcomas carry the EWSR1-FLI1 (or related) gene fusion. Treatment is intense chemotherapy plus surgery and/or radiation, with cure rates around 70% in localized disease. The single fusion makes it a long-running target for novel therapies. You'll hear Ewing in pediatric and adolescent oncology contexts and in rare-disease biotech pipelines.
plain: A rare bone and soft-tissue cancer mostly hitting teenagers, driven by one almost-defining gene mix-up.

snappy: Everything in a pill that isn't the actual drug — the binders, fillers, coatings, and preservatives that turn a chemical into something you can swallow.
detail: Excipients give a drug its shape, stability, taste, and release profile. They're regulated alongside the API, since impurities or interactions can affect product safety. You'll hear excipient in formulation discussions, manufacturing-quality reviews, and in any drug-development pitch involving novel delivery (e.g., long-acting injectables, oral solutions for pediatric patients).
plain: Everything in a pill that isn't the actual drug — the binders, fillers, and coatings that turn a chemical into something swallowable.

snappy: An enzyme that controls which genes get turned on or off — when mutated, it scrambles cellular instructions and helps drive certain blood cancers.
detail: EZH2 mutations are common in follicular lymphoma and DLBCL, leading to inappropriate gene silencing. Tazverik (tazemetostat) is an FDA-approved EZH2 inhibitor for follicular lymphoma and epithelioid sarcoma. You'll hear EZH2 in epigenetic-therapy pipeline discussions and at hematology conferences as part of the broader interest in epigenetic-target oncology.
plain: An enzyme that controls which genes get switched on or off — when broken, it scrambles cell instructions and feeds certain blood cancers.

snappy: An inherited cancer syndrome where people develop hundreds to thousands of polyps in the colon — virtually all of which will turn into cancer if untreated.
detail: FAP is caused by mutations in the APC gene; affected people typically need preventive removal of the colon. The condition affects roughly 1 in 10,000 people. You'll hear FAP in hereditary-cancer genetic counseling discussions, in pediatric/young-adult oncology screening contexts, and as a model condition in colorectal cancer prevention research.
plain: An inherited condition where someone grows hundreds or thousands of bowel polyps — almost all of which will turn into cancer without surgery.
A diabetes pill, like Jardiance, that also protects the heart and kidneys — now used for far more than blood sugar.
snappy: AstraZeneca's SGLT2 inhibitor, like Jardiance a diabetes drug that became a heart-failure and kidney mainstay.
detail: Farxiga spills glucose into urine and proved cardiovascular and kidney benefit in major outcome trials, broadening far beyond diabetes. You'll hear Farxiga alongside Jardiance as the leading SGLT2 inhibitors at AHA and ACC.

snappy: An FDA designation that speeds up review of drugs targeting serious conditions with unmet needs — letting companies submit pieces of their application as they finish, rather than all at once.
detail: Fast Track allows for rolling reviews and more frequent FDA meetings; it doesn't change the criteria for approval, just the pace. About 30% of new approvals carry Fast Track designation. You'll hear Fast Track in biotech press releases (it's positive news), in regulatory affairs strategy, and on earnings calls when companies discuss expected approval timelines.
plain: A US regulator status that speeds up review of drugs for serious diseases with no good existing treatments.

snappy: The long carbon chains that make up most of the lipids in your body — saturated and unsaturated, depending on the chemical bonds.
detail: Omega-3 fatty acids (EPA, DHA from fish oil) are the basis of Vascepa (icosapent ethyl), shown in REDUCE-IT to lower cardiovascular events. Free fatty acids in blood are a marker of metabolic health. Drugs that change how the body burns fat (rather than how it stores it) are an active research area in obesity and NASH/MASH (where Madrigal's Rezdiffra became the first approved drug in 2024).
plain: The long carbon chains that make up most fats in your body — the building blocks of cell membranes and energy stores.

snappy: The US agency that decides whether new drugs, vaccines, devices, and food additives are safe and effective enough to be sold in America.
detail: FDA reviews most pharmaceutical applications through CDER (drugs) or CBER (biologics, vaccines, gene therapy), with action goals set by PDUFA. The agency's decisions move billions in market value and define which products doctors can prescribe. You'll hear FDA constantly in pharma — every approval announcement, every Complete Response Letter, every advisory committee meeting is news.
plain: The US agency that decides whether new drugs, vaccines, and medical devices are safe and effective enough to sell in America.
Paying a doctor or hospital for each separate test or procedure — the old model critics say rewards doing more, not doing better.
snappy: Paying providers for each test, visit, or procedure — the traditional model critics blame for rewarding volume over health.
detail: Under fee-for-service, every service generates a separate payment, which can incentivize more care rather than better outcomes. It's the baseline that value-based care models — ACOs, bundled payments, capitation — are designed to replace. You'll hear FFS as the foil in any payment-reform discussion.

snappy: A family of cell-surface receptors with mutations and gene fusions in several cancers — and the target of a small but growing class of precision drugs.
detail: FGFR2 fusions drive a subset of cholangiocarcinoma; FGFR3 mutations are common in bladder cancer and a rare bone disorder called achondroplasia. Approved FGFR inhibitors include Pemazyre (pemigatinib), Truseltiq (infigratinib), and Balversa (erdafitinib). You'll hear FGFR in rare-cancer trial readouts and in commercial discussions of how mutation-based eligibility creates niche markets.
plain: A family of cell switches whose mutations drive several rare cancers — and the target of a small but growing group of precision drugs.
A modern web-based standard that makes it much easier for health apps and systems to share specific pieces of data on demand.
snappy: The *modern, app-friendly* standard (said 'fire') for exchanging health data — HL7's web-era successor, now mandated for US patient-data access.
detail: Pronounced 'fire,' it is HL7's modern standard: it uses ordinary web APIs to share discrete data elements, making it far easier for apps to plug into an electronic health record. US regulations require FHIR-based patient-access APIs, accelerating interoperability. It's why a phone app can now pull your lab results — a staple of every health-IT integration discussion.

snappy: The final step of biologic drug manufacturing — taking the bulk drug substance and filling it into vials, syringes, or pens, sealed sterile and ready for patients.
detail: Fill-finish is one of pharma's biggest capacity bottlenecks: COVID vaccines exposed how few facilities could fill billions of doses to sterile standards. Specialist contract manufacturers like Catalent and Lonza have ridden the wave, and biologics-heavy companies have invested billions building dedicated fill-finish lines. You'll hear fill-finish in earnings calls when launch-supply commentary surfaces, and in FDA inspection news — Form 483 observations on fill-finish quality have led to multi-year supply disruptions for major drugs.
plain: The final step of making a biologic drug — taking the bulk liquid and putting it into vials or syringes, sterile and ready for patients.

snappy: The very first time a new drug is given to people — a high-stakes Phase 1 study where everything is unknown until it isn't.
detail: FIH studies typically dose tiny cohorts of healthy volunteers or patients with carefully escalating amounts, watching for safety signals. Famous failures (TGN1412, BIA 10-2474) have made FIH design more cautious. You'll hear FIH in early biotech pipeline discussions, in conference posters reporting first safety data, and in any pitch where a novel mechanism is reaching humans for the first time.
plain: The very first time a new drug is given to people — a high-stakes early study where everything is unknown until it isn't.

snappy: The treatment doctors try first when a patient is diagnosed — usually the regimen with the best track record for that disease and stage.
detail: If first-line fails, second- and third-line therapies follow. The first-line setting is commercially valuable because it captures the largest patient population; companies fight hard to win first-line indications and resist getting pushed into later lines. You'll hear first-line everywhere in oncology — in trial design, FDA labels, and earnings-call discussions of market positioning.
plain: The treatment doctors try first when a patient is diagnosed — usually the regimen with the best track record for that disease.

snappy: A signaling receptor mutated in about 30% of acute myeloid leukemia patients — a marker of more aggressive disease and a target of specific drugs.
detail: FLT3-ITD and FLT3-TKD mutations drive proliferation in AML and historically meant worse prognosis. Targeted FLT3 inhibitors — Rydapt (midostaurin), Xospata (gilteritinib), Vanflyta (quizartinib) — added to standard treatment have improved outcomes meaningfully. You'll hear FLT3 at ASH, in AML trial readouts, and in any commercial discussion of mutation-stratified leukemia therapy.
plain: A signal switch that's mutated in roughly a third of acute myeloid leukemia patients, marking more aggressive disease.

snappy: The second-most-common non-Hodgkin lymphoma — slow-growing, generally treatable but rarely curable, with patients living many years through repeated treatments.
detail: Follicular lymphoma usually carries the BCL2 translocation that prevents cancer cells from dying. Treatment options include rituximab plus chemo, EZH2 inhibitor Tazverik (tazemetostat), CAR-T (Yescarta), and bispecifics like Lunsumio (mosunetuzumab). You'll hear follicular lymphoma at ASH and in any pipeline pitch around B-cell malignancies.
plain: The second-most-common slow-growing lymphoma — generally treatable but rarely cured, with patients living many years through repeated rounds.

snappy: The list of drugs your insurance will pay for — and the rules that decide what it costs you when you fill a prescription.
detail: Insurers and pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) build formularies to control costs, negotiating rebates with drugmakers in exchange for preferred placement. A drug's tier on the formulary determines patient copays, prior-authorization requirements, and ultimately how easily it gets prescribed. Pharma launch teams obsess over formulary access — at JPMorgan and on earnings calls you'll hear it called "access" or "reimbursement," and it's often the difference between a drug's commercial success and failure.
plain: The list of drugs your insurance will pay for — and the rules deciding what each one costs you at the pharmacy counter.

snappy: The specific recipe and physical form of a drug product — pill, injection, patch, inhaler — and the choices that affect how (and whether) it works.
detail: Formulation determines bioavailability, dosing schedule, patient adherence, and shelf life. Reformulating a drug (e.g., from IV to subcutaneous, or from twice-daily to once-daily) can be a major commercial play and patent-extension strategy. You'll hear formulation in late-stage drug development, lifecycle-management discussions, and in any pitch involving long-acting injectables or improved patient experience.
plain: The recipe and physical form of a drug — pill, injection, patch, inhaler — and the choices that affect how well it works.

snappy: A hybrid gene formed when two normally separate genes accidentally join together — often producing an abnormal protein that drives cancer.
detail: Fusion genes — BCR-ABL in CML, EML4-ALK in lung cancer, EWSR1-FLI1 in Ewing sarcoma, NTRK fusions across many tumors — are powerful drug targets because they're cancer-specific. Targeted therapies like Gleevec, Xalkori, and Vitrakvi (larotrectinib) all hit fusion proteins. You'll hear fusion gene in precision-oncology trial readouts and in commercial pitches around tumor-agnostic biomarker-driven approvals.
plain: A hybrid gene formed when two normally separate genes accidentally join together, often making an abnormal protein that drives cancer.

snappy: A rare and usually late-diagnosed cancer of the small organ that stores bile — most often discovered incidentally during gallstone surgery.
detail: Gallbladder cancer is uncommon in the US but more frequent in parts of South America and South Asia. HER2 amplification occurs in a subset, opening targeted therapy options like Herceptin and ADCs. You'll hear gallbladder cancer in biliary-tract oncology contexts and in expanding HER2-tumor-agnostic discussions.
plain: A rare and usually late-diagnosed cancer of the small organ that stores bile, often found by accident during gallstone surgery.

snappy: Stomach cancer — a major killer worldwide, especially in East Asia, with subtypes that respond differently to modern targeted and immune drugs.
detail: Gastric cancer is classified into intestinal and diffuse (signet ring) types, with HER2-positive, MSI-H, and EBV-positive subsets carrying targeted-therapy implications. Keytruda, Opdivo, Herceptin, and Enhertu all have approved roles. You'll hear gastric cancer at GI oncology meetings, in immuno-oncology global expansion stories, and in HER2 lifecycle discussions.
plain: Stomach cancer — a major killer worldwide, especially in East Asia, with several subtypes that respond differently to modern drugs.

snappy: International quality standards that govern how clinical trials must be designed, conducted, and reported — to protect patients and produce trustworthy data.
detail: GCP guidelines (codified by ICH) cover everything from informed consent to data integrity to investigator qualifications. FDA inspectors audit trial sites for GCP compliance; violations can invalidate data and tank approvals. You'll hear GCP in any clinical operations role, in regulatory inspections, and in CRO selection discussions.
plain: International quality rules that govern how clinical trials must be designed, run, and reported — to protect patients and make data trustworthy.

snappy: A stretch of DNA that contains the recipe for one specific protein (or RNA molecule) that does a job in the body.
detail: Humans have roughly 20,000 protein-coding genes, far fewer than scientists once expected. A defective gene can cause disease — sickle cell, cystic fibrosis, hemophilia — and gene therapies like Luxturna and Zolgensma deliver working copies to fix the underlying cause. You'll hear 'gene' constantly in pharma: gene panels for diagnosis, gene targets for new drugs, gene editing for next-gen therapies.
plain: A stretch of DNA holding the recipe for one specific protein that does a job in the body.

snappy: Treatments that work by adding, replacing, or correcting genes inside cells — aiming to fix the root cause of a genetic disease rather than manage its symptoms.
detail: Approved gene therapies include Luxturna (RPE65 mutations causing blindness), Zolgensma (SMA), Hemgenix (hemophilia B), and the CRISPR-based Casgevy (sickle cell). One-time price tags often exceed $2 million, raising payer-access questions. You'll hear gene therapy in rare-disease biotech pipelines, at investor calls about durable-response economics, and in payer-access debates.
plain: A treatment that adds, replaces, or corrects genes inside cells to fix the root cause of a genetic disease, not just its symptoms.

snappy: A copy of a brand-name pill containing the same active ingredient — sold at much lower prices once the original patent expires.
detail: Generic drugs are approved through abbreviated NDAs (ANDAs) by demonstrating bioequivalence to the reference product. They make up about 90% of US prescriptions but only around 20% of drug spending. Generic competition can collapse a brand's revenue overnight. You'll hear generics in patent-cliff discussions, payer formulary contracts, and antitrust debates.
plain: A copy of a brand-name pill containing the same active ingredient — sold at much lower prices once the original patent expires.

snappy: The complete set of DNA in an organism — every gene plus all the non-coding stretches in between.
detail: The human genome was first fully sequenced in 2003 at a cost of about $3 billion; today it costs a few hundred dollars. Whole-genome sequencing is becoming standard in oncology to match patients to targeted therapies, and in rare disease to identify the single mutation causing an unexplained illness. Companies like Illumina, Pacific Biosciences, and Oxford Nanopore make the machines that read genomes at industrial scale.
plain: The complete set of DNA in a living thing — every gene plus all the non-coding stretches in between.

snappy: Cancer that arises from reproductive cells — most often in the testicles or ovaries, but occasionally elsewhere if those cells migrated during fetal development.
detail: Germ cell tumors are notable as the cancer most likely to be cured even at advanced stages, especially testicular cancer cured with cisplatin-based chemotherapy. Subtypes include seminomas/dysgerminomas and non-seminomatous tumors. You'll hear germ cell tumor in testicular and ovarian cancer contexts and in pediatric/young-adult oncology research.
plain: Cancer that grows from reproductive cells — most often in the testicles or ovaries, occasionally elsewhere if those cells wandered before birth.
A biotech company that made hepatitis C curable and leads in HIV treatment.
snappy: The biotech that cured hepatitis C with Sovaldi and Harvoni and built the modern HIV-treatment market.
detail: Gilead Sciences dominates HIV therapy and cured hepatitis C with Sovaldi and Harvoni — whose pricing sparked national debate — and entered cell therapy by buying Kite, maker of Yescarta. You'll hear Gilead in antiviral and drug-pricing discussion.

snappy: A rare sarcoma of the digestive tract — and one of oncology's biggest precision-medicine wins after Gleevec turned a deadly cancer into a manageable disease.
detail: Most GISTs carry KIT or PDGFRA mutations, making them dramatically responsive to imatinib (Gleevec) and successor drugs Sutent (sunitinib), Stivarga (regorafenib), and Qinlock (ripretinib). The cancer is the textbook proof that targeted therapy works in solid tumors. You'll hear GIST in sarcoma research and in any commercial discussion of KIT-driven oncology.
plain: A rare digestive-tract cancer — one of precision medicine's biggest wins after a targeted drug turned a deadly disease into a manageable one.
The pill that launched targeted cancer therapy — turning a once-fatal leukemia into a condition people live with for decades.
snappy: The drug that started targeted therapy — a daily pill that turned BCR-ABL-driven CML from fatal into a near-normal lifespan.
detail: Gleevec blocks the BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase that causes chronic myeloid leukemia, and also treats GIST. Its 2001 success proved a cancer's specific driver could be drugged. You'll hear Gleevec as the reference story in any targeted-therapy or TKI discussion.

snappy: The most aggressive brain cancer — fast-growing, deeply infiltrating, and despite intensive treatment, currently incurable in nearly all cases.
detail: GBM has median survival of about 15 months despite surgery, radiation, and temozolomide chemotherapy. Tumor Treating Fields (Optune) is one of the few additions in decades. The disease is a perennial focus of biotech-and-academic effort, but most trials have failed. You'll hear GBM in neuro-oncology research, in patient-advocacy fundraising, and in commercial pitches highlighting an underserved indication.
plain: The most aggressive brain cancer — fast-growing, deeply spreading, and despite intense treatment, currently incurable in almost all cases.

snappy: The umbrella name for brain tumors arising from glial cells — the supporting cells of the nervous system — graded by aggressiveness from 1 to 4.
detail: Gliomas include astrocytomas, oligodendrogliomas, and ependymomas, each with distinct genetics. The 2021 WHO classification reorganized them around mutations like IDH and 1p/19q codeletion rather than just appearance. Targeted therapies like Voranigo (vorasidenib) for IDH-mutant glioma are reshaping treatment. You'll hear glioma in neuro-oncology discussions and in the steady flow of brain-cancer biotech pitches.
plain: The umbrella name for brain tumors growing from the supporting cells of the nervous system, graded by aggressiveness from 1 to 4.

snappy: A drug that mimics a natural gut hormone to lower blood sugar and curb appetite — the engine behind the Ozempic and Wegovy phenomenon.
