detail: GLP-1 receptor agonists — Ozempic (semaglutide), Mounjaro (tirzepatide, dual GLP-1/GIP), Trulicity (dulaglutide), Wegovy — were originally approved for type 2 diabetes, then revolutionized obesity treatment with weight loss of 15-20%. New trials show benefit in heart failure, kidney disease, and possibly Alzheimer's. You'll hear GLP-1 dominate every Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly earnings call, and at JPMorgan it's the single most-discussed therapeutic class — supply, oral formulations, and label expansions are the running storylines.
plain: A drug that copies a natural gut hormone to lower blood sugar and curb appetite — the engine behind Ozempic and Wegovy.

snappy: The simple sugar your cells run on — when blood glucose is too high (diabetes) or too low (hypoglycemia), things go badly.
detail: Glucose metering — fingersticks and now continuous glucose monitors (Dexcom, Abbott's Libre) — is the daily reality of type 1 and increasingly type 2 diabetes. Insulin lowers glucose; GLP-1 agonists, SGLT2 inhibitors, metformin, and sulfonylureas all reduce blood glucose by different mechanisms. Glucose is also the raw material that gets metabolized through glycolysis to make ATP.
plain: The simple sugar your cells run on — when blood levels are too high (diabetes) or too low, things go badly.

snappy: The smallest amino acid — just a hydrogen atom for its side chain — and a major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the spinal cord.
detail: Because glycine is so small, it lets protein chains bend and pivot in ways no other amino acid permits; it's overrepresented at hinges in protein structures. Glycine receptors are the target of strychnine poisoning and a focus of research into chronic pain. Glycine is also a building block of glutathione, the body's main antioxidant.
plain: The smallest building block of proteins, and a signaling chemical that helps quiet down activity in the spinal cord.

snappy: The storage form of glucose — long branching chains kept in liver and muscle for quick-access fuel.
detail: Liver glycogen is what keeps your blood sugar steady between meals; muscle glycogen powers exertion. 'Glycogen storage diseases' are rare inherited conditions where one of the enzymes for handling glycogen is missing — Pompe disease (treated with Sanofi's Lumizyme/Nexviazyme and now newer enzyme replacements) is the best-known example.
plain: The storage form of sugar — long branching chains kept in liver and muscle, ready to release energy when the body needs it.

snappy: The series of chemical steps that breaks one glucose molecule into two pyruvates, with a small ATP payoff and no oxygen needed.
detail: Glycolysis is biology's fastest way to get energy from glucose, which is why it's revved up in cancer cells (the 'Warburg effect'). PET imaging exploits this: tumors greedily take up the radiolabeled glucose analog FDG, making them light up on scans. Drugs that target glycolytic enzymes specifically in cancer cells are an active research area but have struggled to deliver clinical wins.
plain: The cell's quickest way to squeeze energy out of sugar — and one of the tricks cancer cells crank up to fuel their growth.

snappy: The quality standards drug manufacturers must follow to make sure every batch is safe, pure, and consistent — enforced by FDA inspections.
detail: GMP covers facility design, equipment, processes, documentation, and personnel training. Failing a GMP inspection can result in Warning Letters, import bans, or recalls. You'll hear GMP in supply-chain discussions, manufacturing-deviation reviews, and at the FDA's annual list of Form 483 observations and Warning Letters.
plain: The rulebook drugmakers must follow so every pill or vial is clean, pure, and the same from batch to batch.

snappy: The cell's shipping department — a stack of flattened sacs that processes, packages, and sorts proteins before sending them to their final destinations.
detail: Many secreted proteins get their sugar coatings (glycosylation) added in the Golgi, and getting glycosylation right is one of the hardest parts of manufacturing biologics — a key reason why biosimilars are not exactly identical to the originator drugs and need their own clinical trials. Disorders of Golgi function cause a growing list of rare 'congenital disorders of glycosylation.'
plain: The cell's mailroom — a stack of pouches that wraps and labels proteins before shipping them off to where they're needed.

snappy: A pathologist's measure of how abnormal cancer cells look under a microscope — higher grades mean more aggressive disease.
detail: Grade is distinct from stage (which describes how far the cancer has spread). Most cancers use a 1-3 or 1-4 grade scale; high-grade tumors generally grow faster and require more intensive treatment. You'll see grade in pathology reports, oncology trial enrollment criteria, and in any treatment-decision discussion at tumor boards.
plain: How wild and abnormal cancer cells look under a microscope — uglier cells usually mean a faster, nastier disease.

snappy: The gap between a drug's list price and what the manufacturer actually keeps after rebates, discounts, fees, and chargebacks — often half of revenue or more.
detail: Gross-to-net adjustments are the deductions pharma takes off list price before booking real revenue: PBM rebates, 340B discounts, Medicaid mandatory rebates, distributor fees, and patient assistance. For drugs like Humira (adalimumab) or Eliquis (apixaban) the GTN bubble can exceed 50%. You'll hear analysts grill CFOs on "net pricing" at every earnings call, and it's the single biggest line item between a drug's headline price and what reaches the bottom line.
plain: The gap between a drug's sticker price and what the maker actually pockets after all the rebates and discounts come off.

snappy: How long it takes for half of a drug to be eliminated from your body — a critical number that determines how often you need to take it.
detail: Drugs with short half-lives (a few hours) need frequent dosing; drugs with long half-lives (days or weeks) can be dosed once a week, monthly, or even less often. Half-life shapes patient adherence and competitive positioning. You'll hear half-life in formulation discussions, in long-acting injectable pitches, and in any commercial framing of dosing convenience.
plain: How long it takes your body to clear out half of a drug — the clock that decides how often you need to take it.
A one-pill-a-day cure for hepatitis C that made treatment simpler than the breakthrough drug before it.
snappy: A single-pill hepatitis C cure that built on Sovaldi, simplifying treatment to one tablet a day.
detail: Harvoni combined sofosbuvir with a second antiviral so most patients needed no interferon or ribavirin, achieving cure rates above 95%. A Gilead follow-up to Sovaldi. You'll hear Harvoni in any hepatitis C or drug-pricing retrospective.

snappy: A statistical number comparing the risk of an event happening between a treatment group and a control group — under 1.0 means the treatment helps.
detail: An HR of 0.7 means a 30% reduction in the rate of the event (e.g., death or progression). Hazard ratios are the standard way oncology trials report time-to-event endpoints; they're paired with confidence intervals and p-values. You'll see HR in every trial readout, on Kaplan-Meier curves, and in any FDA review summary.
plain: A number that says how much a treatment cuts the risk of something bad happening — under 1.0 means the drug is helping.

snappy: The most common type of liver cancer — strongly tied to chronic hepatitis B/C infection or cirrhosis from alcohol or fatty-liver disease.
detail: HCC treatment depends on stage and liver function. Early-stage disease is treated with surgery, ablation, or transplant; advanced disease relies on combinations like Tecentriq (atezolizumab) plus Avastin, or Imjudo (tremelimumab) plus Imfinzi. You'll hear HCC in liver-cancer trial readouts and in commercial discussions of immunotherapy expansion in solid tumors.
plain: The most common type of liver cancer — usually linked to long-running hepatitis infection or heavy drinking.

snappy: Cancers of the mouth, throat, larynx, and related regions — historically tied to smoking and alcohol, increasingly driven by HPV.
detail: HPV-positive head and neck cancers respond better to treatment than HPV-negative ones, prompting de-escalation trials. Treatment combines surgery, radiation, chemo, and immunotherapy with Keytruda or Opdivo. You'll hear HNSCC at oncology meetings, in HPV-vaccination policy debates, and in commercial discussions of immunotherapy expansion.
plain: Cancers of the mouth, throat, and voice box — once mostly caused by smoking, now increasingly linked to a common virus.
Sharing patient records electronically between different hospitals and clinics, so providers can see care you received elsewhere.
snappy: The *electronic sharing* of patient records across organizations — both the act and the regional networks that broker it.
detail: It lets unaffiliated providers share records, so an emergency room can pull your history from another system. It depends on interoperability and standards like FHIR, and runs through regional or state networks. Done well, it cuts duplicate testing and medication errors. You'll hear HIE in health-IT policy and care-coordination talk, alongside the electronic health record systems it connects.

snappy: A condition where the heart can't pump enough blood to meet the body's needs — not the same as a heart attack, and increasingly manageable as a chronic disease.
detail: Heart failure is split into reduced (HFrEF) and preserved (HFpEF) ejection fraction — for years only HFrEF had effective drugs, but SGLT2 inhibitors like Jardiance (empagliflozin) changed that. The four-pillar regimen (ARNI, beta blocker, MRA, SGLT2) is now guideline-standard. You'll hear heart failure framed on Boehringer, AstraZeneca, and Novartis earnings calls as a multi-billion-dollar growth story driven by HFpEF expansion, and at AHA and ESC when trial readouts redefine standard of care.
plain: When the heart gets too weak or stiff to pump enough blood for the body — different from a heart attack, and now manageable for years.

snappy: The umbrella term for cancers of the blood, bone marrow, and lymphatic system — leukemias, lymphomas, and myelomas.
detail: Hematologic malignancies behave very differently from solid tumors and have driven much of the past decade's innovation: BTK inhibitors, BCL-2 inhibitors, CAR-T, bispecifics. ASH (December) is the field's defining conference. You'll hear hematologic malignancy in any trial-design discussion that distinguishes from solid tumors, and in commercial pipeline framing.
plain: The umbrella name for cancers that start in the blood or bone marrow rather than forming a solid lump.

snappy: An inherited bleeding disorder caused by missing or defective Factor VIII — almost exclusively affects males via X-linked inheritance.
detail: Hemophilia A is the more common form (about 80% of hemophilia cases). Standard care is recombinant Factor VIII infusions; Hemlibra (emicizumab) revolutionized treatment with subcutaneous prophylaxis. Gene therapy arrived in 2023 with BioMarin's Roctavian, the first one-time gene therapy for the condition. The hemophilia franchise is one of the highest-revenue rare-disease categories in pharma.
plain: An inherited bleeding disorder where the blood can't clot properly because one key clotting protein is missing or broken.

snappy: The Factor IX-deficient form of hemophilia — about 20% of hemophilia cases, also X-linked, also predominantly male.
detail: Treatment paralleled hemophilia A historically (Factor IX replacement instead of VIII), then leapt ahead in 2022 when CSL/uniQure's Hemgenix became the first FDA-approved gene therapy for any form of hemophilia, with a $3.5M price tag making it one of the most expensive drugs ever launched. Pfizer's Beqvez followed in 2024. Hemophilia B is a smaller market than A but a key proof-point for the AAV gene-therapy platform.
plain: A rarer cousin of hemophilia A — same bleeding problem, but caused by a different missing clotting protein.

snappy: The discipline that translates a drug's clinical benefit into dollars and quality-of-life numbers — building the case payers actually want to see before they'll cover it.
detail: HEOR teams produce the evidence pharma uses in formulary submissions, ICER reviews, and payer negotiations: cost-effectiveness models, budget-impact analyses, and real-world outcomes data. Quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) are a common currency, especially in markets like the UK's NICE. You'll hear HEOR cited at every launch readiness review and ISPOR conference, and in commercial discussions of how to position a drug against existing treatments on value, not just clinical results.
plain: The work of turning a drug's medical benefit into dollar-and-cents arguments — the case insurers need before they'll pay.

snappy: A chronic viral infection of the liver that can lead to cirrhosis and liver cancer — managed with antivirals but not yet routinely curable.
detail: Hep B treatment is dominated by Gilead's tenofovir-based antivirals (Vemlidy, Viread) — they suppress the virus indefinitely but rarely clear it. Functional cure is the holy grail and a busy biotech research area: GSK, Arrowhead, Vir Biotechnology, and Aligos all have late-stage candidates using siRNA, capsid inhibitors, or therapeutic vaccines. Vaccine prevention (recombinant Engerix-B/Heplisav-B) is highly effective and routine in pediatric immunization.
plain: A long-lasting liver infection caused by a virus — kept in check with daily pills, but rarely fully cured.

snappy: A bloodborne viral liver infection that became routinely curable after 2014's Sovaldi/Harvoni revolution — one of pharma's all-time blockbuster stories.
detail: Gilead's sofosbuvir-based regimens (Sovaldi, Harvoni, Epclusa) and AbbVie's Mavyret cure 95%+ of hep C in 8-12 weeks of pills. Pricing for these drugs sparked the modern drug-pricing debate (Sovaldi launched at $1,000/pill). The market collapsed under its own success — fewer patients to treat each year as the prevalent pool gets cured. Gilead's hep C revenue went from $19B in 2015 to under $2B by 2020.
plain: A liver-attacking virus carried in blood — once a slow killer, now curable in most people with a few months of pills.

snappy: A protein on the surface of cells that tells them to grow — when overexpressed in breast or stomach cancer, it makes the disease aggressive but also targetable.
detail: HER2 amplification occurs in about 20% of breast cancers and around 15% of gastric cancers. Herceptin (trastuzumab) was the first targeted therapy here, followed by Perjeta, Kadcyla, and the ADC Enhertu (trastuzumab deruxtecan), which has expanded into HER2-low tumors. You'll hear HER2 at every breast-cancer trial readout and in any commercial discussion of the HER2 franchise.
plain: A growth signal on the surface of some breast and stomach cancer cells that makes them aggressive but also easier to target with drugs.
The first targeted drug for an aggressive breast cancer subtype, turning a once-grim diagnosis into a treatable one.
snappy: The original anti-HER2 antibody — it turned HER2-positive breast cancer from a death sentence into a treatable disease.
detail: Herceptin targets the HER2 protein overexpressed in ~20% of breast cancers and some stomach cancers. A landmark of targeted therapy, it now faces biosimilar competition. You'll hear Herceptin as the founding HER2 story in any breast cancer or biosimilars discussion.

plain: When so many people are immune to a disease that it can't spread easily, which protects even the few who aren't immune.
snappy: The point where *enough* of a population is immune that a disease can't find new hosts — shielding even those who aren't immune themselves.
detail: Also called community immunity, it kicks in once immune people — through vaccines or past infection — are dense enough to break chains of transmission. The threshold rises with the Basic Reproduction Number: highly contagious measles needs ~95% coverage. Immunization programs target it explicitly, which is why vaccine hesitancy can let an endemic disease flare into an outbreak. It guards infants and the immunocompromised who can't be vaccinated.

snappy: Inherited gene mutations that pass cancer risk down through families — the reason some people develop multiple cancers, or get them young.
detail: Common hereditary syndromes include Lynch syndrome (colon, endometrial), BRCA1/BRCA2 (breast, ovarian, prostate, pancreatic), Li-Fraumeni (TP53, many cancers), and FAP (colon polyposis). Genetic testing influences screening intensity and treatment selection — including PARP-inhibitor eligibility. You'll hear hereditary cancer syndromes in genetic counseling and in any precision-oncology pipeline discussion.
plain: Faulty genes passed down through families that make certain cancers far more likely — and often strike at younger ages.

full: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act
plain: The US law that protects the privacy of your health information and limits who can see or share it.
snappy: The 1996 US law that *protects health-data privacy* — its Privacy and Security Rules govern who may use protected health information.
detail: It sets national rules for safeguarding patients' protected health information, governing how providers, insurers, and their vendors may use and disclose it. The Privacy and Security Rules carry real penalties for breaches. It shapes everything from electronic health record access to what a telehealth app may store. You'll hear HIPAA invoked in any health-data, privacy, or digital health discussion.

snappy: The virus that attacks immune cells and, untreated, leads to AIDS — but with modern antiretroviral therapy is now a chronic, manageable condition for life.
detail: HIV treatment has progressed from the toxic AZT cocktails of the 1990s to today's single-tablet, once-daily regimens — Biktarvy (bictegravir-emtricitabine-tenofovir), Dovato (dolutegravir-lamivudine) — that bring viral load below detection. Long-acting injectables like Cabenuva given monthly are next. You'll hear HIV on every Gilead and ViiV earnings call as one of pharma's most durable franchises, and in policy debates about the End the HIV Epidemic initiative and 340B-funded programs.
plain: The virus that attacks the body's immune defences — once a death sentence, now a manageable lifelong condition with daily pills.
A long-standing set of standards for how health computer systems format and swap messages, so they can understand each other.
snappy: The *messaging-standards* body whose formats let health IT systems talk — the older foundation beneath the newer FHIR.
detail: Health Level Seven sets the messaging standards that move data between health IT systems — lab results, admissions, orders. Its older 'v2' messages are still everywhere in hospitals, while its modern, web-friendly successor FHIR is taking over new work. Both serve interoperability. You'll hear HL7 whenever integration engineers and electronic health record vendors discuss connecting systems.

plain: A cheaper but stricter insurance plan: you pick a main doctor, need referrals for specialists, and must stay in its network.
snappy: A managed-care plan that's cheaper but stricter — you pick a primary care doctor and need referrals to see specialists, all within a set network.
detail: An HMO keeps premiums low by requiring care within its network and routing access through a primary care gatekeeper, with little out-of-network coverage. You'll hear HMO contrasted with the looser PPO whenever plan design or managed care comes up.

snappy: A cancer of B-cells with a distinct microscope appearance — historically among the most curable cancers, even at advanced stages.
detail: Hodgkin lymphoma is defined by Reed-Sternberg cells. Treatment with combination chemo (ABVD, BV-AVD) and the ADC Adcetris (brentuximab vedotin), often with checkpoint inhibitors for relapsed disease, achieves cure rates above 80%. You'll hear Hodgkin in lymphoma research, in long-term-survivorship discussions about late effects, and as a benchmark cancer for combination-therapy strategies.
plain: A cancer of immune cells with a distinct look under the microscope — and one of the most curable cancers known, even when advanced.

snappy: A chemical messenger released by one tissue that travels through the bloodstream to give instructions to distant tissues.
detail: Insulin, thyroid hormone, cortisol, estrogen, testosterone, growth hormone — these and dozens of others coordinate metabolism, growth, reproduction, and stress responses. Hormone replacement and hormone-blocking drugs are entire pharma franchises: insulin and GLP-1s in diabetes, levothyroxine for thyroid, anti-estrogens (tamoxifen, fulvestrant) and anti-androgens (enzalutamide) in cancer, GnRH analogs in fertility and prostate cancer.
plain: A chemical messenger one part of the body sends through the blood to tell another part what to do.

snappy: Proteins on certain cancer cells that bind to hormones (mostly estrogen or progesterone) — when present, they make the tumor sensitive to anti-hormone treatments.
detail: In breast cancer, hormone-receptor status (ER+, PR+, or both) defines a major subtype that's treated with tamoxifen, aromatase inhibitors, or SERDs alongside CDK4/6 inhibitors. Prostate cancer is similarly hormone-driven, treated with androgen-deprivation therapy. You'll hear HR/HR+ at every breast-cancer discussion and in any commercial discussion of endocrine-therapy lifecycle management.
plain: A docking spot on certain cancer cells that catches body hormones — when present, blocking those hormones can starve the tumor.
Comfort-focused care for people near the end of life, easing symptoms rather than trying to cure the illness.
snappy: Comfort-focused care for the *end of life* — when the goal shifts from fighting a terminal illness to living the remaining time as well as possible.
detail: Hospice is the care model for people expected to have months, not years: it sets aside curative treatment in favor of relieving pain and symptoms, usually at home, with a team that works alongside the patient's primary care doctor and supports the family too. It overlaps with palliative care but differs in timing and intent — palliative care runs alongside active treatment at any stage, while hospice begins when that treatment stops, often as the humane alternative to another intensive care unit admission. Medicare's hospice benefit makes it widely available in the US. You'll hear hospice discussed wherever goals-of-care and the cost and quality of dying are weighed.

plain: A doctor who only treats patients while they are admitted to the hospital, instead of in a regular clinic.
snappy: A physician who works *only inside the hospital* — managing inpatients from admission to discharge while their regular doctor stays outside.
detail: The hospitalist is a relatively new specialty built around the inpatient setting: rather than a primary care doctor rounding before clinic, a dedicated physician coordinates the whole stay, orders, and discharge. The model speeds decisions and can shorten the length of stay, but adds a handoff back to primary care that has to be managed carefully. Hospitalists now staff most US hospitals. You'll hear hospitalist whenever inpatient care models and care continuity are discussed.

snappy: A common virus that causes cervical cancer and a growing share of head-and-neck cancers — and is largely preventable with vaccination.
detail: HPV is responsible for nearly all cervical cancers and a rising fraction of oropharyngeal cancers. The Gardasil 9 vaccine prevents the highest-risk strains and is recommended for adolescents. The result has been a measurable drop in cervical cancer rates wherever vaccination is widespread. You'll hear HPV in oncology prevention discussions and in vaccination-policy debates.
plain: A very common virus that causes nearly all cervical cancers and many throat cancers — and is now largely preventable with a vaccine.

snappy: A defect in the cell's ability to fix a specific kind of DNA damage — and a marker that predicts which tumors will respond well to PARP inhibitors.
detail: HRD is most often caused by BRCA mutations but extends to other DNA-repair genes (ATM, PALB2, RAD51). HRD-positive ovarian cancers and a subset of breast and prostate cancers respond particularly well to Lynparza (olaparib), Zejula (niraparib), and similar drugs. You'll hear HRD in precision-oncology trial readouts and in commercial discussions of biomarker-driven drug selection.
plain: A flaw in a cell's DNA-repair toolkit — and a clue that certain targeted cancer drugs are likely to work well.
The US agency that improves healthcare access for underserved communities and runs the 340B drug-discount program.
snappy: The federal agency for healthcare access in underserved communities — and the administrator of the 340B drug-discount program.
detail: HRSA funds community health centers and the safety net, and runs 340B, which requires drugmakers to discount outpatient drugs for qualifying hospitals and clinics — a growing flashpoint between pharma and providers. You'll hear HRSA mostly in 340B disputes.

plain: A drug that calms inflammation in arthritis and gut disease — and, for years, the single best-selling medicine in the world.
snappy: The anti-TNF biologic that became the best-selling drug in history before biosimilars finally arrived.
detail: Humira blocks TNF to calm rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, and inflammatory bowel disease. AbbVie's franchise peaked above $20B a year, and its long-delayed loss of exclusivity is a case study in patent strategy. You'll hear Humira whenever biosimilars or the patent cliff come up.

snappy: A weak chemical attraction between a hydrogen atom and certain neighboring atoms — individually small, but biology stacks them by the millions to hold things together.
detail: Hydrogen bonds are what zip the two strands of the DNA double helix together, what makes water behave like water, and what drives the precise folding of every protein. In drug design, getting the right pattern of hydrogen bonds between drug and target is often the difference between a tight-binding clinical candidate and an inactive molecule. AI-driven structure-based design is essentially an industrial-scale optimization of hydrogen-bond patterns.
plain: A weak tug between atoms that, stacked by the millions, holds together DNA, proteins, and water itself.

snappy: Chronically high blood pressure — the silent driver of heart attacks, strokes, and kidney failure that affects nearly half of US adults.
detail: Hypertension is treated with a stepwise stack: ACE inhibitors or ARBs first, often layered with diuretics, calcium-channel blockers, and beta blockers. Most drugs are generic and cheap, making it a low-margin commercial space. You'll hear hypertension less on earnings calls than in policy commentary — uncontrolled blood pressure is the biggest preventable driver of US cardiovascular disease, and population-health programs at insurers and integrated systems live or die on their hypertension numbers.
plain: Long-term high blood pressure — the quiet driver behind heart attacks, strokes, and kidney damage in roughly half of US adults.

snappy: Low oxygen levels — a condition tumors create as they outgrow their blood supply, paradoxically making them harder to kill with radiation and chemo.
detail: Hypoxic tumor regions resist treatment because radiation needs oxygen to damage DNA effectively, and many drugs reach hypoxic areas poorly. Tumor hypoxia also drives angiogenesis and metastasis through HIF-1α signaling. You'll hear hypoxia in radiation-oncology discussions, in advanced-tumor biology research, and in any drug-development pitch around hypoxia-activated prodrugs.
plain: When tissue runs short on oxygen — something tumors often create, which paradoxically makes them tougher to kill.
Short for inflammatory bowel disease — long-term gut inflammation, mainly Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis.
snappy: The common abbreviation for inflammatory bowel disease — chronic gut inflammation, mainly Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis.
detail: IBD covers Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, both driven by an overactive gut immune response and treated with anti-TNF biologics, IL-23 blockers, and JAK inhibitors. You'll hear 'IBD' across gastroenterology and immunology pipeline talk.

full: Institute for Clinical and Economic Review
snappy: An independent US watchdog that crunches the numbers on whether a new drug is worth its price — and publishes verdicts that increasingly shape what insurers will pay.
detail: Founded in 2006, ICER models cost-effectiveness using QALYs (quality-adjusted life years) and benchmarks, then issues reports that influence formulary decisions and rebate negotiations. Pharma argues ICER underestimates value; payers cite ICER reports in coverage decisions. You'll see ICER reports drive earnings-call defenses and Q&A when expensive drugs get rated unfavorably, and at JPMorgan when access strategy comes up — they're the closest thing the US has to a NICE equivalent.
plain: An independent US group that crunches the math on whether a new drug is worth its price, and publishes verdicts insurers watch.
An enzyme that, when mutated, can drive certain leukemias and brain tumors — and a target for newer drugs.
snappy: A metabolic enzyme whose mutations drive some AML and gliomas; IDH inhibitors are a targeted option in those cancers.
detail: Mutated IDH1/IDH2 produce an 'oncometabolite' that blocks cells from maturing. Inhibitors such as Tibsovo treat IDH-mutant AML and glioma. You'll hear IDH in leukemia and brain-tumor readouts at ASH and ASCO and in precision-oncology pipeline talk.

snappy: Genes encoding metabolic enzymes — when mutated, they produce a cancer-causing molecule that scrambles cell development. Found in some leukemias, brain tumors, and bile-duct cancers.
detail: IDH-mutant cancers produce 2-hydroxyglutarate, an "oncometabolite" that disrupts normal gene regulation. Tibsovo (ivosidenib) and Idhifa (enasidenib) target IDH1 and IDH2 mutations in AML; Voranigo (vorasidenib) was approved for IDH-mutant glioma in 2024. You'll hear IDH at hematology and neuro-oncology meetings, and in any precision-oncology pipeline discussion.
plain: Genes that normally run cell metabolism — when broken, they pump out a chemical that fuels certain leukemias and brain tumors.
A family of messenger proteins immune cells use to talk. Blocking specific ones — like IL-23 — treats psoriasis and other diseases.
snappy: Signaling cytokines immune cells use to coordinate; pinning down specific ones (IL-23, IL-17, IL-4) created precise inflammation drugs.
detail: Interleukins are numbered cytokines. Targeting them spawned blockbusters: IL-23 blockers Skyrizi, Stelara, and Tremfya for psoriasis; IL-4/13 blocker Dupixent for atopic dermatitis. You'll hear specific IL numbers in every immunology pipeline pitch at JPMorgan.

snappy: The first true targeted cancer therapy — approved in 2001 for CML, and still the textbook proof that designing drugs against specific mutations works.
detail: Imatinib blocks BCR-ABL in CML, KIT in GIST, and PDGFRA in some sarcomas. It transformed CML from a fatal disease into a manageable chronic condition with a daily pill. The drug's commercial success and cultural impact made precision oncology mainstream. You'll hear Gleevec referenced as the historical benchmark in any targeted-therapy pitch.
plain: The first drug ever designed to hit a specific cancer mutation — and the proof that precision oncology could actually work.
The first pill to replace chemo for a common blood cancer, by blocking a switch the cancer cells depend on to survive.
snappy: The first BTK inhibitor — it transformed CLL and other B-cell cancers from chemo to a daily pill.
detail: Imbruvica blocks Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) that B-cell cancers depend on, reshaping treatment of CLL and mantle cell lymphoma. A major AbbVie/J&J franchise. You'll hear Imbruvica as the pioneer BTK inhibitor at every ASH.

plain: A cancer immunotherapy that blocks a tumor's immune off-switch, used especially in lung cancer after chemo and radiation.
snappy: AstraZeneca's anti-PD-L1 checkpoint inhibitor, established in lung, biliary, and liver cancer.
detail: Imfinzi blocks PD-L1 and is a mainstay after chemoradiation in stage III NSCLC, plus small-cell lung and biliary cancer. It's central to AstraZeneca's oncology growth. You'll hear Imfinzi in lung and GI readouts at ASCO.

snappy: The biological 'off-switches' that keep your immune system from attacking your own body — and that tumors hijack to hide from immune attack.
detail: Immune checkpoints — PD-1, PD-L1, CTLA-4, LAG-3, TIGIT, TIM-3 — are now major drug targets. Releasing the brakes with checkpoint inhibitors lets T-cells recognize and kill tumors. You'll hear immune checkpoint at every immuno-oncology discussion, at every major oncology conference, and in commercial competition between companies racing for next-generation targets.
plain: The brakes on your immune system that stop it attacking your own body — brakes that tumors sneakily push to hide from attack.
Making someone protected against a disease, usually with a vaccine. Also the programs that get shots to whole populations.
snappy: The process of making someone *immune* to a disease — usually via a vaccine — and the programs built to deliver them at scale.
detail: How a person becomes protected against an infection, most often by a vaccine that trains the immune system without causing illness. National schedules and campaigns aim to reach the herd immunity threshold that shields whole communities. Coverage gaps — from access barriers or vaccine hesitancy — let preventable diseases like measles resurge. The WHO and CDC set and monitor schedules; it's among the highest-return moves in public health.

snappy: The technical name for an antibody — comes in five flavors (IgG, IgA, IgM, IgD, IgE) that handle different jobs in the immune system.
detail: IgG is the most abundant in blood and the format used for nearly all therapeutic monoclonal antibodies. IgE drives allergic reactions and is the target of Xolair (omalizumab). IgA dominates at mucosal surfaces (gut, airways). 'IVIG' — pooled human immunoglobulin given by IV — is a treatment for many autoimmune and immunodeficiency conditions and is one of the most lucrative blood-derived products globally.
plain: The proper scientific name for an antibody — the Y-shaped protein the immune system uses to tag threats for destruction.

snappy: Treatments that harness the immune system to fight cancer — by removing brakes, training T-cells, or engineering immune cells from scratch.
detail: Immunotherapy includes checkpoint inhibitors, CAR-T, bispecific antibodies, cancer vaccines, cytokines, and adoptive cell therapies. It has transformed melanoma, lung cancer, and several blood cancers. The category is now the dominant theme in oncology drug development. You'll hear immunotherapy across all of oncology, especially around combination strategies trying to expand who responds.
plain: Treatments that turn the body's own immune system loose on cancer — by lifting its brakes or sharpening its aim.
A precise form of radiation that shapes the beam to the tumor, sparing nearby healthy tissue.
snappy: Radiation therapy that sculpts beam intensity to the tumor's shape, sparing surrounding organs.
detail: IMRT uses computer-controlled beams of varying intensity to conform dose tightly to a tumor while sparing adjacent tissue. It's standard for head-and-neck, prostate, and many other cancers. You'll hear IMRT alongside proton therapy and SBRT in radiation-oncology discussion.

plain: How many people newly catch a disease in a given time. It measures how fast something is spreading, not how many already have it.
snappy: The rate of *new* cases of a disease in a population over a period — the flow, versus the standing pool that prevalence measures.
detail: This rate counts how many people develop a condition during a window — say, new flu cases per week. It captures risk and the speed of spread, which is why outbreak investigators and Disease Surveillance teams watch it. Distinguish it from prevalence, the total existing cases: a fast-killing or fast-curing disease can run high here but low there. You'll see these rates in every CDC field report.

snappy: The application a company files with the FDA to start testing a new drug in humans — the regulatory gate that opens Phase 1 trials.
detail: An IND submission includes preclinical data, manufacturing details (CMC), and the clinical-trial plan. The FDA has 30 days to object; if they don't, the trial proceeds. "Filing an IND" is a meaningful milestone that biotechs announce. You'll hear IND in early-stage pipeline discussions and at investor briefings on near-term clinical-development milestones.
plain: The paperwork a company files with the FDA to get permission to test a brand-new drug in people for the first time.

snappy: The specific disease or condition a drug is approved to treat — listed on the FDA-approved label.
detail: A drug's indication defines its commercial market and what doctors can prescribe legally on-label. Companies pursue "label expansion" by running new trials to add indications, often in adjacent cancer types or earlier lines of therapy. You'll hear indication in every commercial discussion, regulatory update, and in trial-design conversations about which patient populations to enroll.
plain: The exact disease a drug is officially approved to treat — what's printed on the label and what doctors can prescribe for.

snappy: An umbrella term for chronic conditions — Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis — where the immune system attacks the digestive tract, causing pain, bleeding, and severe diarrhea.
detail: IBD treatment ranges from steroids and 5-ASAs to biologics like Humira (adalimumab), Stelara (ustekinumab), and the IL-23 class led by Skyrizi (risankizumab) and Tremfya (guselkumab). Patients often cycle through multiple biologics as drugs lose effect over years. You'll hear IBD on AbbVie, J&J, and Takeda earnings calls as a multi-billion-dollar autoimmune market, and at Digestive Disease Week (DDW) when head-to-head trial readouts shake up prescribing patterns.
plain: Long-running conditions where the immune system attacks the gut — causing pain, bleeding, and constant, severe diarrhea.

snappy: The legal and ethical promise that patients in a clinical trial understand the risks, benefits, and alternatives — and agree freely, in writing, to participate.
detail: Informed consent is the cornerstone of human-subjects research, codified after the abuses of Tuskegee and Nuremberg. Patients receive a document — sometimes 30+ pages — covering everything from study procedures to potential side effects, and can withdraw at any time. You'll see informed consent surface in regulatory inspections, trial-misconduct lawsuits, and any commercial discussion of patient recruitment, since dense or rushed consent processes are a leading cause of FDA warning letters.
plain: The signed promise that trial participants understand the risks, the benefits, and the alternatives — and are joining freely.

snappy: A drug that blocks a protein from doing its job — most cancer drugs are inhibitors of one enzyme or receptor or another.
detail: Inhibitors come in many flavors: small-molecule kinase inhibitors (Gleevec, Tagrisso), antibody-based receptor blockers (Herceptin), enzyme inhibitors (PARP inhibitors). The common thread is shutting down a specific protein the cancer depends on. You'll hear "X inhibitor" used to label drug classes across every pharma pipeline and trial readout.
plain: A drug that jams a specific protein and stops it from doing its job — the workhorse design of most cancer medicines.
A patient who is admitted and stays overnight in the hospital, rather than going home the same day.
snappy: A patient *admitted to a hospital bed* — staying at least one night — as opposed to being treated and sent home the same day.
detail: Inpatient status begins with a formal admission and is the line that drives how care is paid for: hospitals bill an inpatient stay under a DRG, a fixed sum keyed to the diagnosis rather than the number of days. The length of stay and any readmission then become quality and cost yardsticks. Inpatient care covers everyone from a routine overnight to the sickest patients in the intensive care unit. You'll hear inpatient set against outpatient in every discussion of hospital utilization and billing.

snappy: The hormone your pancreas makes to move sugar out of your blood and into your cells — and the lifesaving drug people with diabetes use when their bodies can't.
detail: Insulin has been pharma since Banting's 1921 discovery, with modern forms ranging from short-acting Humalog (lispro) to ultra-long Tresiba (degludec). Pricing became a political flashpoint in the 2010s after list prices tripled, and the 2022 inflation Reduction Act capped Medicare insulin copays at $35. You'll hear insulin in every diabetes earnings call, in coverage debates, and at hearings on PBM and manufacturer pricing — it's the textbook example of US drug-pricing controversy.
plain: The hormone that moves sugar from your blood into your cells — and the daily lifesaver for people whose bodies can't make enough.
The hospital unit with the most equipment and staff, caring for the sickest patients whose lives are at risk.
snappy: The hospital unit for the *sickest patients* — continuous monitoring, ventilators, and intensive nursing for those whose lives hang in the balance.
detail: The intensive care unit concentrates the staff and technology to keep failing organs going: mechanical ventilation, blood-pressure support, dialysis, and round-the-clock vital signs. It's the most resource-intensive corner of acute care, and a long intensive care unit stay drives both the length of stay and the cost of an inpatient admission sharply up. Demand for its beds became a household worry during the pandemic. You'll hear intensive care unit capacity invoked whenever a health system is stretched to its limit.

snappy: A trial-analysis rule that counts every patient in the group they were originally assigned to, even if they dropped out or switched treatments midway.
detail: ITT analysis preserves randomization — the foundation of clinical-trial credibility — by refusing to cherry-pick the patients who actually completed treatment. The opposite, "per-protocol," can inflate apparent benefit by excluding non-compliers. Regulators almost always demand ITT as the primary analysis for confirmatory trials. You'll hear it on trial readouts at ASCO and in earnings calls when companies parse why a per-protocol number looked stronger than the headline ITT result.
plain: A rule that counts every trial patient in the group they were first assigned to, even if they dropped out or switched.
The ability of different health computer systems to share and actually use each other's data — so your records aren't trapped in one office.
snappy: Whether health IT systems can *exchange and use* each other's data — the long-sought goal that lets records follow the patient.
detail: The capacity of electronic health record systems and devices to exchange data and make it usable — not merely transmit it. It underpins health information exchange and is the reason standards like HL7 and FHIR exist. US rules now ban 'information blocking' to force it. Without it, data sits in silos; with it, clinical decision support and real-world evidence grow far richer.

snappy: Injected directly into a tumor — a delivery approach that concentrates drug where it's needed and minimizes whole-body side effects.
detail: Intratumoral delivery is used for some immunotherapies (oncolytic viruses like Imlygic), STING agonists, and TLR agonists, where the goal is local immune activation that then triggers a body-wide response. The approach has obvious limits — accessibility of the tumor — but is a major commercial bet for several biotechs. You'll hear intratumoral in immuno-oncology pipelines and at AACR/SITC.
plain: Injecting a drug straight into the tumor itself — concentrating the hit where it's needed and sparing the rest of the body.

snappy: The most common type of breast cancer — about 80% of cases — arising from cells in the milk ducts and breaking through into surrounding tissue.
detail: IDC is what most people mean by 'breast cancer.' It's classified by hormone-receptor status, HER2 status, and grade, with treatment determined by those features. Invasive lobular carcinoma is the second most common type. You'll hear IDC in pathology reports and breast-cancer trial enrollment criteria; commercial breast-cancer franchise discussions are essentially about IDC subtypes.
plain: The most common type of breast cancer — starting in the milk-duct lining and pushing out into the surrounding tissue.

snappy: An atom or molecule with an electrical charge because it has lost or gained electrons — sodium, calcium, and potassium ions are the ones biology cares about most.
detail: Cells use ion gradients across membranes to fire nerve signals, contract muscles, and trigger insulin release. Ion-channel drugs are a huge pharma category: calcium-channel blockers for blood pressure (amlodipine, diltiazem), sodium-channel blockers as anesthetics and antiarrhythmics, potassium-channel modulators in diabetes (sulfonylureas) and seizures.
plain: An atom carrying an electric charge — sodium, calcium, and potassium ions are the ones nerves and muscles run on.

snappy: The 2022 US law that for the first time lets Medicare negotiate prices on top-selling drugs — pharma's biggest pricing shock in decades.
detail: Signed in August 2022, the IRA's drug provisions cap insulin at $35 for Medicare patients, redesign Part D out-of-pocket costs, and authorize CMS to set 'maximum fair prices' on the highest-spend drugs, starting with 10 in 2026 and expanding annually. Pharma has fought the negotiation program in court on multiple constitutional grounds — so far unsuccessfully. You'll hear IRA in every earnings call discussing US pricing risk and in launch strategy debates over which indications to pursue.
plain: A 2022 US law letting Medicare haggle prices on top-selling drugs for the first time — the biggest pricing shock pharma has faced in decades.

snappy: The independent committee — usually based at a hospital or university — that reviews and approves clinical trials before they can enroll patients, focused on protecting participants.
detail: IRBs review every protocol, consent form, and amendment, ensuring risks are justified, vulnerable populations are protected, and informed consent meets standards. Commercial "central IRBs" handle multi-site trials. The FDA inspects IRBs as part of trial oversight, and IRB findings can pause or terminate studies. You'll see IRB approvals cited in every clinical-trial registration, in regulatory inspection news, and in academic-pharma partnership commentary about how site startup speed depends on IRB efficiency.
plain: The independent committee that vets a clinical trial before any patients can join — focused on keeping participants safe.

snappy: Molecules with the same chemical formula but different 3D shapes — and often dramatically different effects in the body.
detail: The classic cautionary tale is thalidomide: one isomer was a sedative, the other caused devastating birth defects, and the original drug was a 50-50 mix. Modern drug development almost always isolates a single 'enantiomer' (mirror-image isomer) to avoid this. Switching from a racemic mixture to a single enantiomer is a common life-cycle-extension play — Lexapro is the active enantiomer of Celexa, Nexium is the active enantiomer of Prilosec.
plain: Molecules built from the exact same atoms but arranged differently — same recipe, different shape, often wildly different effects.

snappy: Versions of the same element that differ only in how many neutrons they have — chemically identical, but some are radioactive.
detail: Pharma uses isotopes for two big things. Radiolabeled isotopes power diagnostic and therapeutic radiopharmaceuticals — PET tracers for imaging, and actinium-225 or lutetium-177 conjugates that deliver radiation directly to tumor cells (Pluvicto for prostate cancer is a recent blockbuster). Stable heavy isotopes (deuterium) are used in 'deuterated' drugs like Austedo, where swapping hydrogen for deuterium can slow metabolism and improve dosing.
plain: Versions of the same element with different weights — chemically identical, but some give off radiation that doctors can use.

full: Professional Society for Health Economics and Outcomes Research
plain: The professional society for the field that measures the value and cost-effectiveness of medical treatments.
snappy: The professional society for health economics and outcomes research (HEOR) — the discipline of valuing medical care.
detail: ISPOR sets methods and standards for HEOR — cost-effectiveness, quality-adjusted life years, and the evidence used in market-access and pricing decisions worldwide. You'll hear ISPOR alongside ICER in any value-assessment or reimbursement discussion.

snappy: Drug delivery directly into a vein — bypassing the digestive system entirely and giving you 100% bioavailability immediately.
detail: IV delivery is essential for biologics like antibodies (which would be destroyed in the gut), for emergency settings, and for chemotherapy where precise dosing matters. The cost is patient burden — clinic visits and infusion time — which is why companies push for subcutaneous or oral reformulations as products mature. You'll hear IV vs. SC compared in every biologic-lifecycle discussion.
plain: Putting a drug straight into a vein through a needle — bypassing the gut and getting the full dose into the blood instantly.
A signaling enzyme inside immune cells. Pills that block it calm inflammation in arthritis and other autoimmune diseases.
snappy: An intracellular kinase relaying inflammatory signals; oral 'JAK inhibitors' like Rinvoq treat autoimmune disease.
detail: JAK inhibitors — Rinvoq, Xeljanz — block the Janus-kinase pathway that immune cytokines use, offering an oral alternative to injected biologics for rheumatoid arthritis, atopic dermatitis, and inflammatory bowel disease. A boxed warning on cardiovascular and clotting risk shadows the class. You'll hear JAK debated at every immunology update.

snappy: A class of drugs that block JAK enzymes — quieting overactive immune signaling in conditions like rheumatoid arthritis and certain blood disorders.
detail: JAK inhibitors include Xeljanz (tofacitinib), Olumiant (baricitinib), Rinvoq (upadacitinib), and Jakafi (ruxolitinib). They're effective in RA, psoriatic arthritis, ulcerative colitis, and myelofibrosis, but carry safety warnings around cardiovascular events and infections. You'll hear JAK inhibitors in immunology pipeline discussions and in any commercial framing of oral biologic alternatives.
plain: A pill that quiets overactive immune signaling — used to calm conditions like rheumatoid arthritis and certain blood disorders.

snappy: A signaling pathway that runs from cell-surface receptors straight into the nucleus — central to immune responses, blood-cell production, and many cancers.
detail: JAK-STAT signaling translates external signals (cytokines, growth factors) into changes in gene expression. Disruption of the pathway underlies several diseases; modulation by JAK inhibitors is the basis for myelofibrosis treatment and several immunology drugs. You'll hear JAK-STAT in immunology and hematology research, and in any pipeline discussion of cytokine-targeted therapy.
plain: A relay system inside cells that carries outside signals straight to the gene controls in the nucleus.

snappy: A specific gene mutation that causes the bone marrow to make too many red blood cells — the defining genetic change in polycythemia vera.
detail: JAK2 V617F is found in nearly all polycythemia vera cases and most cases of essential thrombocythemia and primary myelofibrosis. The mutation is what makes Jakafi (ruxolitinib) effective in these myeloproliferative neoplasms. You'll hear JAK2 V617F in hematology contexts, MPN pipeline discussions, and in any commercial conversation about JAK-targeted therapy.
plain: A typo in a single gene that makes bone marrow churn out too many blood cells — the cause of a slow-burning blood disorder.
A diabetes pill that turned out to protect the heart and kidneys, making it a cornerstone treatment well beyond blood sugar.
snappy: An SGLT2 inhibitor that began as a diabetes pill and became a cornerstone heart-failure and kidney drug.
detail: Jardiance lowers blood sugar by spilling glucose into urine, but its outcome trials in heart failure and chronic kidney disease reshaped cardiology guidelines. A Lilly/Boehringer product. You'll hear Jardiance in every SGLT2 and cardiometabolic discussion at AHA.

snappy: A rare and aggressive childhood blood cancer driven by mutations in the RAS signaling pathway — and one of the few pediatric cancers with very limited treatment options.
detail: JMML usually develops before age 4, often associated with NF1, Noonan syndrome, or PTPN11 mutations. Bone-marrow transplant remains the only proven curative therapy, with relapse common. The rarity and aggressiveness make it a focus of pediatric rare-cancer drug development. You'll hear JMML in pediatric oncology research and rare-disease biotech pitches.
plain: A rare and aggressive blood cancer that strikes young children — with very few treatments beyond a bone-marrow transplant.
A healthcare giant whose drug arm makes major immunology and cancer treatments.
snappy: The healthcare conglomerate whose pharma arm spans immunology (Stelara, Tremfya) and oncology (Imbruvica).
detail: Johnson & Johnson's drug business (formerly Janssen) covers immunology blockbusters Stelara and Tremfya, the anti-TNF Remicade, and the oncology franchise Imbruvica. It spun off its consumer arm as Kenvue. You'll hear J&J across immunology and biosimilar discussion.

snappy: A clinical trial run at multiple sites simultaneously — usually because no single site can recruit enough patients quickly enough.
detail: Joint or multi-center trials are the norm for Phase 2 and Phase 3 studies, especially in rare diseases or specific cancers where any one center sees too few patients. They require coordinated protocols, central data management, and harmonized investigator training. You'll hear joint trial in operational discussions, in CRO contracts, and in any global registration program design.
plain: A study running at many hospitals at once — usually because no single hospital sees enough patients fast enough.
A 'guided missile' drug: a targeted antibody carrying a chemo payload straight into breast cancer cells while sparing healthy ones.
snappy: An antibody-drug conjugate — Herceptin wired to a chemo payload — that delivers poison straight into HER2-positive cancer cells.
detail: Kadcyla is an ADC linking trastuzumab to a cytotoxic drug, sparing healthy tissue. It treats HER2-positive breast cancer, often after Herceptin. You'll hear Kadcyla cited as a proof-of-concept ADC alongside its successor Enhertu.

snappy: A statistical method that draws a step-down curve showing the probability of patients surviving (or staying in remission) over time — the iconic graph in every oncology paper.
detail: Kaplan-Meier curves visualize time-to-event data, comparing treatment arms across months and years. The shape of the curves — and the gap between them — communicates trial results at a glance. You'll see Kaplan-Meier curves on every oncology trial readout slide, in every FDA review document, and in any earnings-call walkthrough of trial results.
plain: The staircase-shaped graph in cancer studies that shows what fraction of patients are still alive or doing well as months tick by.

snappy: A photo of all of someone's chromosomes laid out in order — a basic test that can spot major chromosomal changes driving disease.
detail: Karyotyping is a foundational technique for identifying chromosomal translocations (like the Philadelphia chromosome of CML), deletions, or extra copies. Modern molecular methods (FISH, NGS) have largely replaced it for fine-grained analysis, but karyotype remains useful for big-picture chromosomal changes. You'll hear karyotype in pediatric and hematologic disease workups.
plain: A snapshot of all someone's chromosomes lined up in order — a simple test that catches big genetic mix-ups driving disease.
A blockbuster cancer immunotherapy that releases a brake on the immune system, letting it attack tumors. Used across many cancers.
snappy: Merck's anti-PD-1 checkpoint inhibitor — for years the world's top-selling drug, approved across dozens of cancers.
detail: Keytruda blocks PD-1 to unleash T-cells against tumors. First in melanoma, it now spans lung, head-and-neck, MSI-H, and many other cancers — including a tissue-agnostic approval. You'll hear Keytruda headline every ASCO and Merck earnings call as the franchise facing a looming patent cliff.

snappy: A protein found inside dividing cells — pathologists measure how many tumor cells have it to estimate how fast a cancer is growing.
detail: Ki-67 staining gives a percentage; higher percentages mean more aggressive disease. The marker is widely used in breast cancer, lymphoma, and neuroendocrine tumors to guide treatment decisions and prognosis. You'll see Ki-67 in pathology reports, in trial enrollment criteria, and in any commercial discussion of patient stratification.
plain: A marker found inside dividing cells — pathologists count how many tumor cells carry it to gauge how fast a cancer is growing.

snappy: Renal cell carcinoma — the most common kidney cancer in adults, often discovered incidentally on imaging and increasingly treatable with immunotherapy combos.
detail: Clear cell RCC, the most common subtype, often carries VHL mutations driving the HIF pathway. Treatment combines anti-VEGF tyrosine kinase inhibitors (Inlyta, Lenvima, Cabometyx) with checkpoint inhibitors. You'll hear RCC at GU oncology meetings (ASCO GU), in immunotherapy combination pipelines, and in commercial discussions of the IO+TKI franchise.
plain: Cancer that grows in the kidneys, often spotted by chance on a scan and increasingly treated with drugs that wake up the immune system.

snappy: An enzyme that adds phosphate groups to other proteins — turning them on or off — and a workhorse target of cancer drug development.
detail: Kinases regulate cell growth, division, and signaling; mutated kinases drive many cancers. Kinase inhibitors are one of the largest classes of cancer drugs — Gleevec, Tagrisso, Imbruvica, Verzenio, Tafinlar are all kinase inhibitors. You'll hear kinase in any precision-oncology pipeline discussion and at every major oncology conference.
plain: An enzyme that flips other proteins on or off by sticking a tiny chemical tag on them — a favourite target for cancer drugs.

snappy: A cell-surface receptor that, when mutated, drives gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) and a handful of other cancers — and the target of imatinib's second great success story.
detail: KIT mutations are the defining feature of most GISTs and a subset of mast-cell diseases and AML. Gleevec was originally developed for CML but turned out to also dramatically treat KIT-driven GIST. Newer KIT inhibitors (Sutent, Stivarga, Qinlock, Ayvakit) handle resistance and additional KIT subtypes. You'll hear KIT in GIST contexts and rare-disease oncology pipelines.
plain: A switch on the outside of a cell that, when broken, makes the cell grow uncontrollably and cause rare stomach cancers.

snappy: The most commonly mutated cancer gene of all — and historically the most stubbornly undruggable, until KRAS G12C inhibitors finally cracked it in 2021.
detail: KRAS mutations occur in roughly 30% of all cancers, especially pancreatic (>90%), colorectal, and lung. After decades of failure, Lumakras (sotorasib) and Krazati (adagrasib) became the first FDA-approved drugs targeting KRAS G12C, opening the door to additional KRAS variants. You'll hear KRAS at every oncology conference and in commercial discussions of one of pharma's biggest emerging markets.
plain: The most commonly broken gene in cancer — and one scientists couldn't drug for forty years, until they finally cracked one version in 2021.
A cancer drug, rival to Lumakras, that targets a gene mutation once thought impossible to block with medicine.
snappy: A KRAS G12C inhibitor competing with Lumakras in lung and colorectal cancer.
detail: Krazati blocks the same KRAS G12C mutation as Lumakras, with data in NSCLC and colorectal cancer. You'll hear Krazati in the KRAS-class competitive picture at ASCO.

snappy: The mitochondrial chemical loop that finishes burning the products of glycolysis to extract most of the ATP from glucose and fat.
detail: Discovered by Hans Krebs in 1937, this cycle is universal across aerobic life. Several Krebs cycle intermediates are now recognized as signaling molecules with roles in cancer (succinate, fumarate, 2-hydroxyglutarate). The IDH mutations that drive certain leukemias and gliomas distort the Krebs cycle, and IDH inhibitors (Tibsovo, Idhifa) are an FDA-approved targeted-therapy class built on this insight.
plain: The loop of chemical reactions inside cells that finishes turning your food into usable energy.
The first 'living drug' approved — a patient's own immune cells, re-engineered to attack blood cancer in a single treatment.
snappy: The first approved CAR-T therapy — a one-time, CD19-directed living drug for leukemia and lymphoma.
detail: Kymriah was the first FDA-approved CAR-T (2017), re-engineering T-cells against CD19 for pediatric ALL and adult lymphoma. A Novartis product that opened the cell-therapy era. You'll hear Kymriah as the CAR-T pioneer at ASH.

snappy: The official document that tells doctors how to prescribe a drug — covering its approved indications, dosing, warnings, and known side effects.
detail: The drug label (officially "prescribing information") is what FDA approves alongside the drug. Every word is negotiated. "Label expansion" — adding indications via supplemental approvals — is a major commercial play. "Off-label" prescribing is legal for doctors but can't be promoted by manufacturers. You'll hear label in every commercial strategy discussion and at every regulatory affairs meeting.
plain: The official rulebook for a drug, telling doctors what it's approved for, how much to give, and what warnings to mind.
A medication for schizophrenia and bipolar depression, one of the newer 'atypical' antipsychotics.
snappy: An atypical antipsychotic for schizophrenia and bipolar depression.
detail: Latuda is a second-generation antipsychotic used in schizophrenia and bipolar depression, known for a relatively favorable metabolic profile. You'll hear Latuda in mental-health prescribing and, on the business side, as a major loss-of-exclusivity event.

snappy: The dose of a drug or substance that kills half the test animals in a toxicity study — historically the benchmark for how dangerous a chemical is.
detail: LD50 ("lethal dose 50%") comes from preclinical animal toxicology, providing a rough scale of acute toxicity before any drug ever reaches humans. Modern regulators have moved away from purely lethal endpoints toward more refined toxicity measures, but LD50 remains a familiar shorthand. You'll see LD50 cited in news reports comparing chemical hazards, in poison-control discussions, and in early preclinical readouts when companies disclose toxicology before filing IND applications.
plain: The dose of a substance that kills half the test animals in a safety study — a rough yardstick for how dangerous something is.
The 'bad cholesterol' that builds up in artery walls. Lowering it is the main goal of statins and newer heart drugs.
snappy: The 'bad cholesterol' particle that deposits in artery walls; lowering it is the central goal of statins and newer heart drugs.
detail: LDL carries cholesterol into artery walls, driving the plaque behind heart attacks and strokes. Statins, PCSK9 inhibitors like Repatha, and Leqvio all push it down. You'll hear LDL as the headline number at AHA and in any cardiovascular outcomes discussion.

plain: The number of days a patient spends admitted in the hospital, from admission to discharge.
snappy: *How many days* a patient occupies a hospital bed — the headline efficiency number for any inpatient admission.
detail: Length of stay counts the days from admission to discharge, and trimming it — safely — is a constant hospital goal, because under a DRG the payment is fixed no matter how long the bed is used. A stay stretched by complications or a delayed discharge eats into margin and ties up capacity; one cut too aggressively risks a readmission. The intensive care unit and surgical wards watch it most closely. You'll hear length of stay tracked in every hospital operations and utilization review.

plain: A pill that blocks several of a tumor's growth and blood-supply signals at once, often paired with an immunotherapy.
snappy: A multikinase inhibitor blocking VEGF receptors and more, used in thyroid, liver, and kidney cancer, often with Keytruda.
detail: Lenvima hits several kinases at once including VEGFR, and the Lenvima-plus-Keytruda combination is a notable chemo-free regimen in kidney and endometrial cancer. You'll hear Lenvima in those combination readouts at ASCO.

plain: A cholesterol drug given just twice a year that silences a gene to keep 'bad' cholesterol low — a new way to take heart medicine.
snappy: A twice-a-year siRNA injection that lowers cholesterol by silencing PCSK9 — a new way to dose chronic heart medicine.
detail: Leqvio uses RNA interference to switch off PCSK9 in the liver, cutting LDL with just two doses a year — a novel adherence model. A Novartis product. You'll hear Leqvio in PCSK9 and RNA-therapeutics discussion and in value-based contracting debates.

snappy: Cancer of the blood-forming cells in bone marrow — divided into acute or chronic, and lymphoid or myeloid, with very different behaviors and treatments.
detail: The four main leukemias — AML, ALL, CML, CLL — each have distinct genetics, treatment paths, and patient populations. ASH (December) is the central conference. The category has been at the leading edge of treatment innovation, from Gleevec to CAR-T to BCL-2 and BTK inhibitors. You'll hear leukemia constantly in oncology, often as the testing ground for the next mechanism.
plain: Cancer of the blood-making cells inside bone marrow, with several different types that behave and get treated very differently.

snappy: A rare inherited condition where people are born with a broken TP53 gene — leading to extraordinarily high lifetime risk of multiple cancers.
detail: Li-Fraumeni carriers face a near-certain lifetime risk of cancer, often diagnosed young, with sarcomas, breast cancer, brain tumors, and adrenocortical carcinoma being characteristic. Intensive screening (Toronto protocol) has improved outcomes. You'll hear Li-Fraumeni in genetic-counseling discussions and in any rare-cancer or pediatric oncology context where TP53 status matters.
plain: A rare inherited fault in a key protective gene that leaves carriers facing an extremely high chance of getting cancer during their lifetime.

snappy: A molecule that binds to a receptor — like a key fitting a lock — and triggers (or blocks) a biological response.
detail: Ligands include hormones, growth factors, and neurotransmitters in nature, and many drugs in medicine. Pharma drug development largely revolves around designing better artificial ligands for therapeutic receptors. You'll hear ligand in basic pharmacology, in receptor-targeted drug development, and in any pitch involving allosteric vs. orthosteric drug design.
plain: A molecule that fits into a receptor like a key into a lock and tells the cell what to do next.

snappy: Fats and fat-related molecules — cholesterol, triglycerides, phospholipids — that store energy, build cell membranes, and act as signaling molecules.
detail: Cardiovascular drugs aimed at lipids are one of pharma's all-time biggest categories: statins (Lipitor, Crestor) for cholesterol, fibrates and omega-3s for triglycerides, PCSK9 inhibitors (Repatha, Praluent) and the newer Inclisiran for hard-to-treat high cholesterol. Lipid nanoparticles are also the delivery vehicle that made mRNA vaccines possible at scale.
plain: Fats and fat-like molecules in the body — they store energy, form the wall around every cell, and carry messages between cells.

snappy: A blood test that detects fragments of tumor DNA — letting doctors track cancer or spot mutations without an invasive tissue biopsy.
detail: Liquid biopsies look for circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) shed by cancer cells. They're used to identify targetable mutations, monitor treatment response, and detect minimal residual disease (MRD) after treatment. Companies like Guardant Health, Natera, and Foundation Medicine have built large businesses here. You'll hear liquid biopsy in oncology trial monitoring and in commercial discussions of MRD-guided treatment decisions.
plain: A blood test that picks up tiny scraps of cancer DNA, letting doctors track a tumour without cutting anything out.

snappy: A larger initial dose given to quickly bring drug levels in the body up to where they need to be — followed by smaller maintenance doses.
detail: Loading doses are common in antibiotics, anticoagulants, and biologics with long half-lives, where waiting for steady-state through normal dosing would take days or weeks. The strategy gets the patient to therapeutic levels fast. You'll hear loading dose in clinical pharmacology and in dosing-schedule discussions where rapid onset matters.
plain: An extra-large first dose to get the drug working quickly, followed by smaller regular doses to keep it going.

snappy: Pharma shorthand for the moment generic competition arrives and a branded drug's protected profits end — the broader umbrella that includes patent cliffs and exclusivity expirations.
detail: LOE captures more than just patent expiration: it includes regulatory exclusivities (orphan, pediatric, biologic 12-year) and "first-to-file" generic 180-day windows. Companies model LOE 5-10 years out and stage launches, lifecycle management, and acquisitions accordingly. You'll hear LOE on every earnings call as the multi-year revenue forecast variable, and at JPMorgan when companies pitch how their pipeline replaces the LOE-exposed franchise — "LOE management" is a job title at most large-cap pharmas.
plain: The moment cheap copies of a brand-name drug are allowed to compete, and the original maker's big profits dry up.
A lung cancer drug that hits a mutation scientists spent 40 years calling 'undruggable' — until this and a rival broke through.
snappy: Amgen's drug against KRAS G12C — cracking a mutation long considered 'undruggable.'
detail: Lumakras was the first approved KRAS G12C inhibitor, a target that resisted drug development for decades, used in NSCLC. You'll hear Lumakras with Krazati in any discussion of finally drugging KRAS at ASCO.

snappy: The most common type of lung cancer — and the one most likely to carry targetable genetic mutations like EGFR, ALK, ROS1, and KRAS.
detail: Lung adenocarcinoma accounts for roughly 40% of lung cancers and has driven much of precision oncology. Standard-of-care now includes molecular testing for EGFR, ALK, ROS1, BRAF, MET, RET, NTRK, and KRAS G12C — each with approved targeted drugs. You'll hear lung adenocarcinoma at every oncology conference and in any commercial discussion of NSCLC franchise expansion.
plain: The most common type of lung cancer, and the one most likely to carry specific gene faults that targeted drugs can attack.
Cancer that starts in the lungs — the leading cause of cancer death, now split into types treated with very different targeted drugs.
snappy: The leading cause of cancer death; molecular subtyping (EGFR, ALK, KRAS, PD-L1) now steers treatment far beyond old chemo.
detail: Lung cancer is mostly non-small cell and small cell. NSCLC is now sub-divided by driver mutations — EGFR (Tagrisso), ALK (Xalkori), KRAS (Lumakras) — and PD-L1 for immunotherapy. You'll hear lung cancer headline every ASCO, the proving ground for precision oncology.

snappy: A chronic autoimmune disease where the immune system attacks the body's own tissue — joints, skin, kidneys, brain — causing flares that come and go unpredictably.
detail: Systemic lupus (SLE) affects roughly 200,000 Americans, mostly women. Treatment combines hydroxychloroquine, steroids, and biologics including Benlysta (belimumab) and the newer Saphnelo (anifrolumab) targeting type-1 interferon. Lupus nephritis — kidney involvement — is the most aggressive form and the focus of many trials. You'll hear lupus on AstraZeneca and GSK earnings calls as a high-profile autoimmune market, and at ACR when readouts on novel mechanisms (BAFF, type-1 IFN, BTK) reset expectations.
plain: A long-term illness where the immune system wrongly attacks the body's own tissue, flaring up and quieting down unpredictably.

snappy: Small bean-shaped immune outposts scattered throughout the body — and often the first place cancer spreads when it leaves the original tumor site.
detail: Lymph nodes filter foreign material and are where immune cells coordinate responses. In cancer, lymph node involvement (signaled by sentinel-node biopsy) is a key staging factor that determines treatment intensity. You'll hear lymph node in every cancer-staging discussion, in surgical oncology, and in early-stage trial design where nodal status defines the population.
plain: A small bean-shaped immune station scattered around the body, and often the first stop cancer makes when it spreads.

snappy: Cancer of the lymphatic system — the tissues and vessels that move immune cells around the body. Includes Hodgkin and the many non-Hodgkin lymphomas.
detail: Lymphomas range from indolent (follicular, MALT) to aggressive (DLBCL, mantle cell, Burkitt). The category has been the proving ground for many recent breakthroughs: rituximab, BTK inhibitors, BCL-2 inhibitors, CAR-T, bispecifics. You'll hear lymphoma at every ASH and at any pharma pipeline discussion of B-cell-targeted therapy.
plain: Cancer of the body's immune-cell highway system, with many varieties ranging from slow-growing to aggressive.

snappy: An inherited cancer syndrome caused by broken DNA-mismatch-repair genes — sharply raising lifetime risk of colorectal, endometrial, and several other cancers.
detail: Lynch syndrome (formerly hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer) affects roughly 1 in 300 people. Carriers benefit from enhanced screening colonoscopies and may consider risk-reducing surgery. Lynch tumors are MSI-high, making them strongly responsive to checkpoint inhibitors. You'll hear Lynch in genetic-counseling discussions, in colorectal-cancer screening protocols, and in immunotherapy biomarker conversations.
plain: An inherited fault in the cell's DNA-spellcheck system that sharply raises the chance of bowel and several other cancers.
The first drug to exploit a weakness in cancers with faulty DNA repair, like those caused by BRCA mutations.
snappy: The first PARP inhibitor — it exploits broken DNA repair in BRCA-mutant ovarian, breast, prostate, and pancreatic cancer.
detail: Lynparza blocks PARP, killing cancers (especially BRCA-mutant) that already can't repair DNA — the synthetic-lethality idea made real. An AstraZeneca/Merck product. You'll hear Lynparza as the founding PARP inhibitor in ovarian and breast cancer readouts.

snappy: Freeze-drying — a manufacturing process that removes water from a drug while preserving its structure, producing a stable powder for shipping and storage.
detail: Lyophilization extends the shelf life of biologics, vaccines, and unstable small-molecules that would otherwise degrade. The drug is reconstituted with sterile water before use. You'll hear lyophilization in manufacturing-process discussions, especially around biologics and emergency-stockpile drugs that need long-term storage stability.
plain: Freeze-drying a drug to remove the water, leaving a stable powder that ships and stores well until a nurse mixes it back up.

snappy: An essential amino acid with a positively charged side chain — important for collagen, calcium absorption, and immune function.
detail: Lysine residues on proteins are favorite spots for chemical modifications that regulate function: acetylation, methylation, ubiquitination. Cancer drugs targeting lysine modifications — HDAC inhibitors like vorinostat, EZH2 inhibitors like Tazverik — are an established class. Lysine is also a common conjugation site for antibody-drug conjugates, where the linker chemistry attaches to lysines on the antibody backbone.
plain: One of the building blocks of protein that your body can't make on its own — you have to get it from food.

snappy: A lab-made antibody designed to lock onto one specific target — and the basis for many of pharma's biggest blockbusters, all ending in '-mab.'
detail: Monoclonal antibodies bind specific proteins, marking them for immune destruction or blocking their function. Examples include Humira (adalimumab), Keytruda (pembrolizumab), Herceptin (trastuzumab), and dozens more. The naming convention (-mab) tells you the modality at a glance. You'll hear mAb in nearly every biologics discussion, at every immunology and oncology conference.
plain: A lab-made copy of an immune protein, designed to grab one specific target inside the body — most modern blockbuster drugs are these.

snappy: A lighter-touch treatment given after primary therapy works — to keep cancer in check and delay it coming back.
detail: Maintenance is common in lymphoma (rituximab, lenalidomide), ovarian cancer (PARP inhibitors), and lung cancer (targeted therapy continuation). The strategy aims for prolonged disease control with manageable side effects. You'll hear maintenance therapy in trial-design discussions of progression-free survival and in commercial framing of long-duration treatment.
plain: A gentler follow-on treatment given after the main one works, to keep the cancer from waking back up.

snappy: Persistent low mood, loss of interest, and physical symptoms like sleep and appetite changes — diagnosed when they last at least two weeks and disrupt daily life.
detail: MDD affects roughly 8% of US adults in any given year and is the leading cause of disability worldwide. First-line treatment is usually SSRIs or SNRIs paired with talk therapy, but newer options include Spravato (esketamine) for treatment-resistant cases and the rapid-acting Auvelity (dextromethorphan-bupropion). You'll hear MDD framed at JPMorgan as one of the largest underserved markets in pharma, and at investor days when companies pitch novel mechanisms beyond the serotonin pathway.
plain: A medical condition where low mood, no interest in things, and changes in sleep and appetite last weeks and disrupt daily life.
The dominant US insurance model where the insurer actively steers your care and costs, rather than just paying the bills.
