snappy: The dominant US model where an insurer actively steers cost and care through networks, prior authorization, and incentives — not just paying bills.
detail: Managed care organizations (HMOs, PPOs, Medicare Advantage) use provider networks, utilization management, and payment incentives to control spending. It replaced passive fee-for-service indemnity insurance. You'll hear managed care behind every formulary, prior authorization, and network-design decision.

snappy: An aggressive, hard-to-cure non-Hodgkin lymphoma defined by a specific gene translocation that switches on a key cell-cycle regulator.
detail: MCL accounts for ~5% of NHL cases, characterized by t(11;14) leading to cyclin D1 overexpression. Treatment includes intensive chemoimmunotherapy, BTK inhibitors (Imbruvica, Calquence, Brukinsa), and CAR-T (Tecartus). The disease is a frequent subject of next-generation B-cell-malignancy trials. You'll hear MCL at ASH and in BTK-inhibitor lifecycle discussions.
plain: An aggressive blood cancer caused by a specific gene swap that jams a cell's growth switch permanently on.

snappy: A protein that normally keeps the tumor-suppressor p53 in check — when MDM2 itself becomes overactive in cancer, it shuts down a critical brake on tumor growth.
detail: MDM2 amplification is common in well-differentiated and dedifferentiated liposarcomas; MDM2 inhibitors aim to release p53 and trigger cancer cell death. Several MDM2 inhibitors are in clinical development. You'll hear MDM2 in sarcoma research and in any pipeline discussion of p53-pathway-restoration therapies.
plain: A protein that normally holds the body's main cancer-stopper in check — when there's too much of it, the brake on tumours fails.

snappy: A pre-leukemic bone marrow disorder where blood cells don't form properly — often progresses to acute leukemia, especially in older adults.
detail: MDS is treated based on risk score: lower-risk with growth factors or lenalidomide, higher-risk with hypomethylating agents like Vidaza (azacitidine) or Dacogen (decitabine), often progressing to bone-marrow transplant. The IDH and TP53 mutation subsets have led to targeted approvals. You'll hear MDS at ASH, in MDS/AML transition discussions, and in pipeline conversations about hematology pre-leukemic disease.
plain: A bone-marrow disorder where blood cells form badly — often a stepping stone to full-blown leukemia, mostly in older people.

snappy: How a drug actually works at the molecular level — the specific protein it targets and the biological cascade it sets off.
detail: MOA defines drug class, predicts side effects, and shapes combination strategies. "Novel MOA" is a common biotech selling point in pipeline discussions, as it implies less competitive crowding and potential efficacy in patients who failed existing classes. You'll hear MOA in every pharmacology lecture, every drug-development pitch, and every commercial competitive-intelligence discussion.
plain: The story of how a drug actually works inside the body — which protein it grabs and what chain of events that sets off.
The joint federal-state program that covers low-income Americans — the largest single source of health coverage in the US.
snappy: The joint federal-state program covering low-income Americans — the largest single source of health coverage in the US.
detail: Medicaid is administered by states within federal rules and covers over 80 million people, including long-term care and a large share of births. Run with CMS oversight, its budgets and eligibility rules drive access for the poorest patients. You'll hear Medicaid in any coverage, safety-net, or 340B discussion.

plain: The share of your insurance premiums that, by law, must go to actual medical care rather than the insurer's profit and overhead.
snappy: The share of insurance premiums an insurer must spend on actual care rather than profit and overhead — capped by law.
detail: The Affordable Care Act requires insurers to spend at least 80-85% of premiums on medical care and quality (the medical loss ratio) or rebate the difference, limiting how much can go to administration and profit. You'll hear MLR in insurer-earnings and health-policy discussion.

plain: The US government health insurance program for people 65 and older — and the single most powerful payer in the market.
snappy: The US federal health insurance program for people 65 and older (and some younger people with disabilities) — and the market's most powerful payer.
detail: Medicare covers ~65 million Americans across Part A (hospital), Part B (outpatient), Part C (Medicare Advantage), and Part D (drugs). Run by CMS, its coverage and payment rules — now including drug-price negotiation — set the tone for the whole system. You'll hear Medicare in every US reimbursement and drug-pricing discussion.

plain: The private-insurer version of Medicare, where a company is paid a set amount to cover all of a member's care.
snappy: Privately run Medicare — insurers are paid a fixed amount to cover a member's care, the fast-growing alternative to traditional Medicare.
detail: Under Medicare Advantage (Part C), CMS pays a private insurer a capitated amount per enrollee to manage all their care, often with extra benefits and a network. It now covers more than half of Medicare beneficiaries. You'll hear Medicare Advantage in managed-care, risk-adjustment, and insurer-earnings discussion.

snappy: The federal program that pays for prescription drugs for seniors on Medicare — funded jointly by patient premiums, government dollars, and pharma rebates.
detail: Launched in 2006, Part D covers outpatient prescriptions through private plans contracted by CMS — plans negotiate with PBMs, set formularies, and structure tiers. The 2022 inflation Reduction Act gave Medicare new powers to negotiate prices on top-spend drugs starting 2026, a seismic shift pharma has been fighting in court. You'll hear Part D in every CFO commentary on pricing risk, and it dominates the policy track at JPMorgan.
plain: The US federal programme that helps seniors pay for the prescription drugs they pick up at the pharmacy.

snappy: The most common malignant brain tumor in children — usually arising from the cerebellum and increasingly classified by molecular subtype rather than appearance.
detail: Medulloblastoma is now divided into four molecular subgroups (WNT, SHH, Group 3, Group 4) with very different prognoses. Treatment combines surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy, with intensity adjusted by risk. You'll hear medulloblastoma in pediatric neuro-oncology discussions and in any rare-pediatric-cancer biotech pitch.
plain: The most common malignant brain cancer in children, growing at the back of the brain near the balance centre.

snappy: The special form of cell division that makes sperm and eggs — chromosomes get shuffled and the count is halved so kids inherit one set from each parent.
detail: Errors in meiosis are the source of most chromosomal disorders: Down syndrome (extra chromosome 21), Turner syndrome, Klinefelter syndrome. The 'crossing over' that happens in meiosis is the reason siblings look different — it shuffles parental DNA at random. Meiosis defects in egg quality with maternal age are a major driver of the success rates that IVF clinics quote.
plain: The special cell division that makes sperm and eggs, shuffling the genes so children inherit a fresh mix from each parent.

snappy: A class of drugs that block MEK enzymes in the MAPK signaling pathway — usually combined with BRAF inhibitors for stronger and more durable cancer control.
detail: MEK inhibitors include Mekinist (trametinib), Cotellic (cobimetinib), and Mektovi (binimetinib). They're standard partners for BRAF inhibitors in melanoma, where the combination beats single-agent BRAF and delays resistance. MEK inhibitors are also approved in NF1-related plexiform neurofibromas. You'll hear MEK inhibitors in melanoma trial readouts and rare-disease pediatric tumor discussions.
plain: A class of drugs that block a key relay station inside cancer cells, usually paired with another blocker for stronger effect.
A cancer pill given with Tafinlar that blocks the same growth pathway at a second point, making the pair work better together.
snappy: A MEK inhibitor given with Tafinlar to block the same cancer growth pathway at a second point.
detail: Mekinist blocks MEK, one step below BRAF in the same signaling pathway; pairing it with Tafinlar hits the pathway twice and slows resistance in melanoma and other BRAF-mutant cancers. You'll hear Mekinist as half of a textbook combination regimen.

snappy: An aggressive skin cancer arising from pigment-producing cells — historically deadly when advanced, transformed by checkpoint inhibitors and BRAF-targeted therapy.
detail: About 50% of melanomas carry BRAF mutations. Treatment options include immunotherapy (Keytruda, Opdivo, Yervoy combinations) and BRAF/MEK combos like Tafinlar+Mekinist. Five-year survival in metastatic melanoma rose from <10% pre-2011 to >50% today. You'll hear melanoma at every oncology conference and as the historical reference cancer for immuno-oncology success.
plain: An aggressive skin cancer that starts in the cells that give skin its colour — once a near-death sentence, now often treatable.
A US pharmaceutical giant, best known for the blockbuster cancer immunotherapy Keytruda.
snappy: The US pharma giant behind Keytruda — the cancer immunotherapy that became the world's top-selling drug.
detail: Merck (known as MSD outside North America) is anchored by Keytruda, plus vaccines like Gardasil. Keytruda's coming patent cliff is the company's defining strategic challenge. You'll hear Merck across every immuno-oncology and biopharma M&A discussion.

snappy: A rare cancer of the lining around the lungs and abdomen — almost always linked to past asbestos exposure, often with decades between exposure and diagnosis.
detail: Mesothelioma is uncommon but devastating, with median survival of about a year despite combination treatments including surgery, radiation, chemotherapy, and increasingly immunotherapy with Opdivo plus Yervoy. The disease has a long history in legal contexts due to asbestos liability. You'll hear mesothelioma at thoracic-oncology meetings and in legal/insurance contexts.
plain: A rare cancer in the lining around the lungs or belly, almost always caused by breathing in asbestos dust decades earlier.

snappy: A receptor on cells that signals for growth — when mutated or amplified, it drives a small but treatable subset of lung and other cancers.
detail: MET exon 14 skipping mutations and MET amplifications occur in 3-5% of lung cancers. Targeted drugs Tabrecta (capmatinib) and Tepmetko (tepotinib) are FDA-approved for MET exon 14-mutated NSCLC. You'll hear MET in lung-cancer molecular-testing discussions and in commercial pitches about niche-but-defensible NSCLC subtypes.
plain: A growth switch on the outside of cells that, when broken, drives a small but treatable slice of lung cancers.

snappy: All the chemical reactions in your body that turn food into energy and building blocks — and that also break down (or activate) the drugs you take.
detail: Drug metabolism is dominated by liver enzymes, especially the cytochrome P450 family — CYP3A4, CYP2D6, CYP2C19. Genetic variation in these enzymes makes some people 'fast metabolizers' and others 'slow metabolizers' of common drugs, which is why pharmacogenomic testing is becoming routine before prescribing certain antidepressants, anticoagulants, and cancer drugs. Drug-drug interactions are mostly stories about one drug inducing or inhibiting another's metabolism.
plain: All the chemistry going on inside your body to turn food into energy — and to break down the drugs you swallow.

snappy: What a drug becomes after your body breaks it down — sometimes inactive, sometimes the actual active form, sometimes the source of side effects.
detail: Some drugs are administered as inactive prodrugs that get converted to active metabolites in the liver (e.g., codeine to morphine). Others have toxic metabolites that explain side effects. Drug development pays close attention to metabolite profiles. You'll hear metabolite in pharmacology discussions, in DDI conversations, and at FDA reviews of drug-drug interaction risk.
plain: What's left of a drug after the body has chopped it up — sometimes harmless, sometimes the part that actually does the work.

snappy: The spread of cancer from where it started to other parts of the body — and the cause of most cancer deaths, since localized tumors are usually treatable.
detail: Metastasis involves cancer cells breaking away, traveling through blood or lymph, and establishing new tumors elsewhere. The biology is complex; preventing or treating metastasis is one of oncology's hardest problems. Most stage IV cancer trials are about metastatic-disease control. You'll hear metastasis in every oncology context — clinical, research, and commercial.
plain: When cancer escapes its starting spot and sets up new tumours elsewhere in the body — the cause of most cancer deaths.

snappy: A DNA-repair enzyme that fights chemotherapy — when its gene is silenced (methylated) in glioblastoma, the tumor responds much better to standard chemo.
detail: MGMT removes the DNA damage caused by temozolomide, the standard chemo for glioblastoma. Tumors with MGMT methylation can't repair this damage well, leading to better treatment response. MGMT methylation is the most established prognostic biomarker in GBM. You'll hear MGMT in neuro-oncology trial enrollment and stratification discussions.
plain: A repair tool inside cells that undoes chemotherapy damage — when it's switched off, brain tumours respond much better to chemo.

snappy: The trillions of bacteria, fungi, and viruses living in and on your body — increasingly recognized as a factor in how well drugs work, especially immunotherapy.
detail: Studies have linked specific gut bacteria to better or worse responses to checkpoint inhibitors. The field is in early days, with fecal microbiota transplants and engineered microbial therapeutics in clinical testing. You'll hear microbiome in immuno-oncology research, in biotech pipelines from companies like Vedanta and Seres, and in commercial conversations about response prediction.
plain: The trillions of bacteria and other tiny life forms living on and inside you, now known to affect how well some drugs work.

snappy: A pattern of widespread DNA repair errors — found in about 5% of cancers — that makes tumors visible to the immune system and unusually responsive to immunotherapy.
detail: MSI-H tumors arise from defective DNA mismatch repair, leading to high mutation loads that produce neoantigens. Keytruda became the first tumor-agnostic FDA approval based on MSI-H status in 2017, treating any solid tumor with this biomarker. You'll hear MSI-H in colorectal, endometrial, and tumor-agnostic oncology contexts.
plain: A pattern of DNA copy-errors in a tumour that makes it stand out to the immune system and respond well to immunotherapy.

snappy: A severe, often disabling headache — usually one-sided, throbbing, and accompanied by nausea, light-sensitivity, or visual auras — that can knock people out for hours or days.
detail: Acute migraine treatment ranges from triptans like sumatriptan to the newer gepants — Nurtec (rimegepant), Ubrelvy (ubrogepant). Prevention has been transformed by anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies (Aimovig/erenumab, Ajovy, Emgality) and oral CGRP-targeting drugs. You'll hear migraine pitched on AbbVie, Pfizer, and Lilly earnings calls as a high-growth specialty market, and at AHS when head-to-head data on CGRP drugs reshape prescribing — it's one of the most actively prescribed-by-neurologists categories.
plain: A severe, often disabling headache, usually on one side and throbbing, often with nausea and sensitivities to light or sound.

snappy: Tiny RNA molecules — about 22 letters long — that fine-tune which genes get expressed by silencing matching mRNAs.
detail: miRNAs were discovered in 1993 and won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Medicine. Each miRNA can regulate hundreds of genes, and abnormal miRNA patterns are a hallmark of cancer and many chronic diseases. miRNA-based diagnostics (looking at circulating miRNA in blood) are in development for early cancer detection, and several miRNA-targeting drugs have entered clinical trials.
plain: Tiny scraps of genetic code that act like dimmer switches, quietly turning down which proteins a cell makes.

snappy: The cell's power plants — small organelles that burn glucose and fat to produce ATP, the energy currency of every living thing.
detail: Mitochondria have their own small genome — a relic of their origin as ancient bacteria absorbed by larger cells billions of years ago — which means they can have their own mutations causing 'mitochondrial diseases' (a major focus in pediatric rare-disease drug development). Many cancer drugs target mitochondrial pathways, and mitochondrial damage from drugs like statins and certain antiretrovirals explains some of their best-known side effects.
plain: The tiny power plants inside every cell, burning sugar and fat to make the energy your body runs on.

snappy: How a cell divides into two identical daughter cells — the engine behind growth, healing, and (when it runs out of control) cancer.
detail: Mitosis copies the chromosomes and pulls them apart into two new nuclei. Many of the oldest chemotherapy drugs — vinblastine, paclitaxel (Taxol), the platinum agents — work by jamming mitosis in fast-dividing cells. The trade-off: they also hit normal fast-dividing cells in hair, gut, and bone marrow, which causes the classic chemo side effects.
plain: How a cell splits itself into two identical copies — the basic engine behind growth, healing, and uncontrolled cancer growth.
The biotech whose COVID-19 vaccine proved that mRNA — a new kind of medicine — works at global scale.
snappy: The mRNA biotech that, with its COVID-19 vaccine, validated a whole new class of medicine.
detail: Moderna went from clinical-stage to global scale on its mRNA COVID-19 vaccine, and is applying the same platform to RSV, flu, and cancer vaccines. You'll hear Moderna as the proof that mRNA is a durable drug platform, not a one-off.

snappy: Two or more atoms held together by chemical bonds — water, glucose, aspirin, DNA, antibodies all are molecules of varying sizes.
detail: Pharma divides drugs into 'small molecules' (generally under 900 daltons in molecular weight, like aspirin or atorvastatin — orally available, factory-synthesized) and 'large molecules' or biologics (antibodies, proteins, nucleic acids — usually injected, made in living cells). The economics of these two categories are completely different: small molecules go generic cheaply, biologics face complex biosimilar competition.
plain: Two or more atoms stuck together — everything from water to aspirin to DNA is made of molecules.

snappy: The single repeating subunit that gets chained together to form a polymer — amino acids are the monomers of proteins, nucleotides of DNA.
detail: When biotech engineers a new protein or RNA drug, they're choosing the order of the monomer building blocks. Synthetic monomer chemistry also matters in pharma: the monomers in PEG, PLGA, and lipid nanoparticles all have to be carefully purified and characterized for regulatory approval. Trace impurities at the monomer stage can cause downstream issues with drug stability or immunogenicity.
plain: A single building-block unit that chains together with copies of itself to form a bigger molecule, like beads on a string.
How much disease and ill-health there is in a group of people — sickness and disability, separate from how many die.
snappy: The burden of *illness* in a population — how much disease, disability, and ill-health there is, as distinct from mortality, which counts deaths.
detail: This captures sickness rather than death: cases, complications, disability, and reduced quality of life. Agencies pair it with mortality to size a disease's total toll — the CDC's flagship bulletin is literally the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. Chronic conditions with high prevalence drive most of it even when they rarely kill. You'll hear 'morbidity and mortality' as a fixed phrase at any health-policy briefing.

plain: How many people in a group die in a given time, often from a specific cause. The basic measure of how deadly something is.
snappy: The rate of *death* in a population — overall or from a specific cause — the grim companion to morbidity in every public-health tally.
detail: It measures deaths, usually per 100,000 people a year, all-cause or disease-specific. Epidemiologists read it alongside morbidity to judge how dangerous a condition is, while the case fatality rate narrows the lens to deaths among those who fall ill. Excess deaths above the expected baseline became a headline metric during the pandemic. The CDC and WHO publish death rates for every country.

plain: A diabetes and weight-loss injection that copies two gut hormones at once, with especially strong effects.
snappy: A dual GLP-1/GIP injection from Eli Lilly with especially strong blood-sugar and weight effects.
detail: Mounjaro hits two gut-hormone receptors (GLP-1 and GIP) for type 2 diabetes; the same molecule is sold as Zepbound for obesity. It made Eli Lilly the GLP-1 co-leader with Novo Nordisk. You'll hear Mounjaro in every incretin and obesity-market discussion.

plain: The tiny amount of cancer left after treatment — too small to see on scans but detectable with sensitive tests, hinting whether it may return.
snappy: The trace cancer remaining after therapy, found by ultra-sensitive tests; 'MRD-negative' is an increasingly accepted goal and trial endpoint.
detail: MRD detects one cancer cell among hundreds of thousands using flow cytometry or sequencing. MRD-negativity predicts longer remission in leukemia, multiple myeloma, and lymphoma, and regulators increasingly accept it as a surrogate endpoint to speed approvals. You'll hear MRD debated at ASH.

snappy: A scan that uses powerful magnets and radio waves — no radiation — to produce detailed images of soft tissue, especially brain, joints, and organs.
detail: MRI is essential to drug development in oncology (tumor measurement under RECIST), neurology (MS lesion counting, Alzheimer's brain volume), and musculoskeletal disease. The new anti-amyloid antibodies for Alzheimer's — Leqembi (lecanemab), Kisunla (donanemab) — require ongoing MRI monitoring for ARIA brain swelling. You'll see MRI cited in trial readouts and FDA approval announcements, and in commercial discussions of which centers can actually deliver new drugs that require advanced imaging access.
plain: A scan that uses powerful magnets, not radiation, to make detailed pictures of soft body parts like the brain or joints.

snappy: The working copy of a gene — a short-lived RNA message that ferries instructions from the DNA archive to the protein-making machinery.
detail: mRNA was the unsung hero of the COVID-19 response: Pfizer/BioNTech's Comirnaty and Moderna's Spikevax both deliver synthetic mRNA encoding the spike protein, which your cells briefly produce to train your immune system. The platform is now being applied to flu, RSV, cancer vaccines, and rare-disease protein replacement. Moderna and BioNTech own most of the IP and manufacturing know-how.
plain: A short-lived genetic message that carries a recipe from the DNA library out to the cell's protein factories.

snappy: A treatment that delivers a strand of genetic instructions to your cells, telling them to make a protein — used in COVID vaccines and now expanding to cancer.
detail: Messenger RNA was a niche idea until Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna's COVID vaccines validated the platform at global scale. The same technology now powers personalized cancer vaccines, including Moderna and Merck's mRNA-4157 paired with Keytruda (pembrolizumab) in melanoma. You'll hear mRNA pitched as a platform play at JPMorgan and on R&D days, and trial readouts in oncology and rare disease are increasingly studied as the next proof points beyond infectious disease.
plain: A treatment that hands your cells a temporary instruction sheet telling them to make a specific protein — the same trick behind COVID vaccines.
A tumor signature showing its DNA-proofreading is broken. These cancers often respond especially well to immunotherapy.
snappy: A biomarker of broken DNA mismatch repair; MSI-H tumors are unusually responsive to checkpoint inhibitors like Keytruda.
detail: MSI-H tumors accumulate mutations because DNA mismatch repair fails, making them visible to the immune system. Keytruda won the first-ever tissue-agnostic approval for MSI-H cancers anywhere in the body. You'll hear MSI-H in colorectal and endometrial cancer and immuno-oncology biomarker discussion.

snappy: A specialist field role inside pharma — typically a PhD or PharmD — who talks to leading doctors about the science behind a drug, separate from the sales reps.
detail: MSLs sit in medical affairs, not sales, and they're the people who present the science at academic centers, attend congresses like ASCO and AHA, and feed insights from key opinion leaders back to R&D. Strict rules separate them from commercial promotion. You'll hear about MSL teams ramping up in launch-readiness calls, in JPMorgan presentations on a company's medical capability, and in pharmaceutical compliance discussions about the line between scientific exchange and promotion.
plain: A scientist on a drug company's payroll whose job is to talk shop with top doctors — kept strictly separate from the sales team.

snappy: A blood cancer of plasma cells in the bone marrow — historically incurable, but now manageable for many years through repeated treatments.
detail: MM treatment has been transformed by IMiDs (Revlimid, Pomalyst), proteasome inhibitors (Velcade, Kyprolis), CD38 antibodies (Darzalex, Sarclisa), CAR-T (Carvykti, Abecma), and bispecifics (Tecvayli, Talvey). Survival has roughly doubled in 20 years. You'll hear MM at ASH and in any hematology pipeline discussion of B-cell-malignancy expansion.
plain: A blood cancer of immune cells in the bone marrow — once incurable, now manageable for many years through rounds of treatment.

snappy: An autoimmune disease where the immune system attacks the protective coating of nerves — disrupting signals between brain and body and causing symptoms that flare and remit.
detail: MS treatment is built around disease-modifying therapies that reduce relapses: high-efficacy infused drugs like Ocrevus (ocrelizumab) and Tysabri (natalizumab), oral options like Mavenclad (cladribine) and Tecfidera (dimethyl fumarate), and a growing class of S1P modulators. You'll hear MS at Roche, Biogen, and Novartis earnings calls as a fiercely competitive market, and at ECTRIMS and AAN when new readouts on remyelination or progressive MS shift competitive positioning.
plain: An illness where the immune system attacks the insulation around nerves, scrambling signals between brain and body in flares that come and go.

snappy: A change in the genetic code — sometimes harmless, sometimes the spark that turns a normal cell into a cancer cell.
detail: Cancer-driving mutations include single-letter changes (point mutations like KRAS G12C), insertions/deletions, fusions, and chromosomal rearrangements. Modern oncology revolves around identifying them, designing drugs against them, and tracking when they evolve to cause resistance. You'll hear mutation everywhere in oncology — in trial designs, FDA labels, and pathology reports.
plain: A change in the genetic code — sometimes harmless, sometimes the spark that turns an ordinary cell into a cancer cell.

snappy: A 'master regulator' gene that controls cell growth — overactive in many cancers but historically considered impossible to drug directly.
detail: MYC amplification or activation is one of the most common cancer changes — found in around 70% of human cancers. Direct MYC inhibitors have been an industry holy grail; current strategies focus on indirect approaches like targeting MYC partners or downstream pathways. You'll hear MYC in any biotech pitch claiming to have cracked an undruggable target.
plain: A master control gene for cell growth — overactive in most cancers, and famously something scientists have struggled to make a drug against.

snappy: A cousin of the MYC gene — when amplified in neuroblastoma, it's the single biggest predictor of aggressive disease and poor outcomes in children.
detail: MYCN amplification occurs in about 20% of neuroblastomas and defines a high-risk group requiring intensive treatment. The amplification has resisted direct targeting; alternative strategies include BET inhibitors and aurora kinase inhibitors in clinical trials. You'll hear MYCN in pediatric oncology, in neuroblastoma research, and in rare-cancer biotech pitches.
plain: A close cousin of a notorious cancer-driver gene — when there's too much of it in childhood nerve tumours, the disease turns aggressive.

snappy: A type of head and neck cancer that grows behind the nose — strongly tied to Epstein-Barr virus and disproportionately common in parts of Asia.
detail: NPC is heavily linked to EBV infection and is treated with radiation, often combined with platinum-based chemo and increasingly checkpoint inhibitors. The disease has a sharp geographic distribution — common in southern China and Southeast Asia, rare in the US. You'll hear NPC in head-and-neck oncology contexts and in any global oncology pipeline including Asian markets.
plain: A cancer that grows behind the nose, often linked to a common virus, and especially frequent in parts of Asia.

snappy: A nonprofit alliance of major US cancer centers that publishes the most-followed treatment guidelines in oncology — read by doctors, payers, and pharma.
detail: NCCN guidelines define what counts as standard-of-care for each cancer type and stage, updated continuously by expert panels. Insurers use NCCN to decide what they'll cover; pharma teams target NCCN listings to drive prescribing. You'll hear NCCN in any commercial discussion of clinical-guideline inclusion and in oncology medical-affairs strategy.
plain: A group of top US cancer hospitals that publishes the rule-book most doctors follow when deciding how to treat cancer.

snappy: The US government's main cancer-research agency — funding science, running trials, and publishing the plain-language definitions used across oncology.
detail: NCI is part of the NIH and the world's largest funder of cancer research. Its programs include the Cancer Moonshot, the SEER cancer registry, and the NCI Dictionary of Cancer Terms (a key glossary source). You'll hear NCI in academic oncology, clinical-trials infrastructure (NCI-MATCH), and federal cancer-policy discussions.
plain: The US government's main cancer-research agency — paying for studies, running trials, and writing the plain-language definitions doctors lean on.

snappy: The big package a company submits to the FDA asking for approval to sell a new drug — typically thousands of pages of clinical, manufacturing, and safety data.
detail: NDAs are filed for small-molecule drugs (BLAs are filed for biologics). Once accepted, the FDA has 10 months for standard review or 6 for priority review under PDUFA. NDA filing acceptance is itself a stock-moving event. You'll hear NDA in any biotech regulatory milestone announcement and in earnings calls projecting approval timelines.
plain: The huge paperwork bundle a company hands the FDA when asking permission to sell a new drug.

snappy: Uncontrolled cell death — usually caused by injury, infection, or lack of blood supply — that triggers inflammation and tissue damage.
detail: Unlike apoptosis (clean, programmed cell death), necrosis is messy and inflammatory. In tumors, central necrosis often appears as growth outpaces blood supply. Pathologists describe necrosis grade in tumor reports as part of aggressiveness assessment. You'll hear necrosis in pathology, in tumor imaging discussions, and in clinical trial response assessment.
plain: Messy, accidental cell death caused by injury or starvation, which leaves debris that inflames nearby tissue.
When a test comes back negative, how likely it is you really don't have the disease — usually very high for rare conditions.
snappy: If your test reads *negative*, the chance you're truly disease-free — usually high when the disease is rare, reassuring after a clear result.
detail: The probability that a negative result is a true negative. Like the positive predictive value it depends on disease prevalence, but in the opposite direction: when a disease is rare a negative result is almost always right, so the negative predictive value runs high. It rises with a test's sensitivity. You'll hear negative predictive value cited when clinicians ask how confidently a negative test rules a condition out.

snappy: Treatment given before the main therapy — usually before surgery — to shrink a tumor or test how well a drug works while there's still tumor to measure.
detail: Neoadjuvant therapy is widely used in breast, rectal, lung, and bladder cancer, often delivering chemotherapy, hormone therapy, or immunotherapy before surgery. The pathologic complete response rate (pCR) at surgery is a powerful early efficacy signal. You'll hear neoadjuvant constantly at oncology conferences and in any drug pitch claiming early-disease impact.
plain: Treatment given before the main one, usually before surgery, to shrink a tumor or see if a drug is working.

snappy: The medical word for a 'new growth' in the body — a tumor that may be benign or cancerous, but in either case represents abnormal cell proliferation.
detail: Not all neoplasms are cancer; benign neoplasms (lipomas, fibroids) can grow but don't invade or spread. Malignant neoplasms are cancers. The term shows up in pathology reports and ICD codes. You'll hear neoplasm in formal medical writing, in tumor classification, and in cancer registry data.
plain: The medical word for any abnormal new growth in the body, whether harmless or cancerous.

snappy: A diverse family of cancers arising from hormone-producing cells — slow-growing in many cases, but capable of secreting hormones that cause distinctive symptoms.
detail: NETs include carcinoids, pancreatic NETs, and pheochromocytomas. Treatment depends on grade and location: surgery, somatostatin analogs (Octreotide, Sandostatin), peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (Lutathera), and targeted drugs (Afinitor, Sutent). You'll hear NET at GI and endocrine oncology meetings and in radioligand-therapy commercial discussions.
plain: A family of cancers that grow from hormone-making cells, often slowly, sometimes flooding the body with hormones that cause odd symptoms.

snappy: A childhood cancer that arises from immature nerve tissue — typically diagnosed before age 5 and ranging from spontaneously regressing to highly aggressive.
detail: Neuroblastoma is the most common cancer in infants. High-risk disease (often MYCN-amplified) requires intensive multimodal treatment including surgery, chemo, radiation, stem-cell transplant, and the GD2-targeting antibody Unituxin (dinutuximab). You'll hear neuroblastoma in pediatric oncology, in CAR-T expansion attempts, and in any rare-pediatric-cancer drug-development pitch.
plain: A childhood cancer that starts in immature nerve tissue, usually showing up before age five and ranging from mild to very dangerous.

snappy: Nerve damage that can cause numbness, tingling, or pain — a common side effect of certain chemotherapy drugs and a key dose-limiting toxicity.
detail: Chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN) is associated with platinum drugs, taxanes, vincristine, and bortezomib. It can be permanent and significantly affects quality of life. Newer ADCs like Enhertu also carry neuropathy risk. You'll hear neuropathy in trial safety profiles, in patient experience discussions, and in any commercial framing of tolerability advantages.
plain: Nerve damage that causes numbness, tingling, or pain, and is a common, sometimes lasting side effect of certain chemo drugs.

snappy: A chemical messenger that nerve cells use to talk to each other across the tiny gap between them.
detail: Serotonin, dopamine, norepinephrine, GABA, glutamate, acetylcholine — these are the workhorses, and most CNS drugs work by tweaking their levels or receptor activity. SSRIs raise serotonin, antipsychotics block dopamine, benzodiazepines amplify GABA, ketamine and esketamine block glutamate's NMDA receptor. The neurotransmitter framework explains why pharmacology in psychiatry, neurology, and pain medicine all rests on a relatively small number of molecular systems.
plain: A chemical messenger that nerve cells use to pass signals to each other across the tiny gap between them.

snappy: A low count of neutrophils — a key infection-fighting white blood cell — usually caused by chemotherapy and the main reason cancer patients risk dangerous infections.
detail: Severe neutropenia (febrile neutropenia) is a medical emergency. Growth factors like Neulasta (pegfilgrastim) help reduce risk. Most chemotherapy regimens monitor and adjust dose around neutrophil counts. You'll hear neutropenia in oncology safety discussions, in supportive-care drug development, and in any commercial framing of safer chemo regimens.
plain: A shortage of the white blood cells that fight infection, usually caused by chemo, leaving patients open to dangerous bugs.

snappy: A high-throughput technology that reads millions of stretches of DNA at once — making it cheap and fast to find the mutations driving a person's cancer.
detail: NGS underpins modern precision oncology. Comprehensive genomic profiling tests (Foundation Medicine, Tempus, Caris) sequence hundreds of cancer-related genes from tumor tissue or blood. You'll hear NGS in oncology pathology, in companion-diagnostic discussions, and in any commercial pitch around biomarker-driven drug selection.
plain: A technology that reads millions of pieces of DNA at once, making it cheap and fast to spot the mutations driving a cancer.

snappy: The big umbrella covering all the lymphomas that aren't Hodgkin lymphoma — a wildly diverse group ranging from indolent to dramatically aggressive.
detail: NHL includes DLBCL, follicular lymphoma, mantle cell lymphoma, marginal zone lymphoma, and many rarer subtypes. Treatment depends entirely on subtype and stage; B-cell-targeted drugs (rituximab, BTK inhibitors, BCL-2 inhibitors, CAR-T, bispecifics) dominate. You'll hear NHL constantly at ASH and in any pharma pipeline discussion of B-cell malignancies.
plain: The huge umbrella covering every lymphoma that isn't Hodgkin lymphoma — wildly varied, from slow-burning to fast and deadly.
The US government's medical-research agency — the world's largest public funder of health science.
snappy: The US government's biomedical research agency — the world's largest public funder of medical science.
detail: The NIH funds and conducts the basic and clinical research underpinning much of modern medicine, through institutes like the NCI (cancer) and NIMH (mental health). You'll hear NIH as the source of foundational science that companies later turn into drugs.

snappy: The umbrella name for dozens of distinct cancers of the lymphatic system — collectively the seventh-most-common cancer in the US.
detail: NHL is split mainly into B-cell and T-cell lymphomas, with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) and follicular lymphoma being the most common. Treatment runs from rituximab-based chemo combos to BTK inhibitors (Imbruvica, Calquence, Brukinsa), CAR-T therapies (Yescarta, Breyanzi, Kymriah), bispecifics (Lunsumio, Epkinly), and ADCs (Polivy). Different NHL subtypes have completely different drug regimens — a generic 'lymphoma' headline rarely tells you what's actually moving.
plain: An umbrella label for dozens of different cancers of the body's immune-cell network, collectively one of the most common cancers in the US.

snappy: A trial designed to prove a new drug is at least as good as the existing standard — not necessarily better, just close enough not to be worse.
detail: Non-inferiority is the design pharma reaches for when the new drug offers something other than raw efficacy — better tolerability, simpler dosing, lower cost. The trial sets a "margin" — typically how much worse the new drug could be while still being acceptable — and tries to show the difference falls inside it. You'll see this design in cardiovascular trials of new anticoagulants and infectious-disease readouts where the bar is matching, not beating, the standard.
plain: A study designed to prove a new drug is roughly as good as the existing one — not better, just close enough to be acceptable.
The most common type of lung cancer — the one whose treatment is now picked by testing the tumor's specific mutations.
snappy: The most common lung cancer (~85%); the precision-oncology proving ground where driver mutations and PD-L1 dictate therapy.
detail: NSCLC includes adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma. Treatment is chosen by biomarker: EGFR, ALK, ROS1, KRAS mutations get matched targeted drugs, while PD-L1 guides checkpoint inhibitors like Keytruda. You'll hear NSCLC subtyped in detail at every ASCO lung session.

snappy: The most common form of lung cancer (about 85% of cases) — split into adenocarcinoma, squamous, and large-cell subtypes.
detail: NSCLC is where most precision oncology drama plays out: targetable mutations like EGFR, ALK, ROS1, KRAS G12C, and MET each have approved targeted therapies, and PD-1/PD-L1 immunotherapy (Keytruda, Opdivo) is now standard in many lines. Companies routinely segment NSCLC trials by mutation status — a Keytruda earnings discussion will sound completely different from a Tagrisso one even though they're both NSCLC drugs.
plain: The most common kind of lung cancer, accounting for about 85% of cases and now full of precision-medicine options.

snappy: A signaling pathway that decides cell fate during development — when mutated, it can drive certain leukemias and several solid tumors.
detail: NOTCH1 is mutated in about 60% of T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemias (T-ALL) and is implicated in some breast cancers and triple-negative subtypes. Direct NOTCH inhibitors (gamma-secretase inhibitors) have been challenging to develop due to GI toxicity. You'll hear NOTCH in pediatric leukemia research and in early-stage targeted-therapy pipelines.
plain: A signaling system that helps decide what type of cell each one becomes; broken versions can drive certain leukemias and other cancers.
A disease that doctors must legally report to health officials whenever they diagnose it, so authorities can track and respond to it.
snappy: A condition doctors and labs are *legally required to report* to health authorities — the raw feed for disease surveillance.
detail: Must by law be reported to public-health authorities on diagnosis — measles, tuberculosis, certain STIs, novel pathogens. The mandatory flow feeds disease surveillance and lets agencies launch contact tracing or quarantine fast. Each US state sets its own list; the CDC aggregates nationally while the WHO runs international reporting for events of global concern. It is the legal backbone of outbreak detection.

plain: A Swiss pharmaceutical giant behind the landmark cancer pill Gleevec and the first CAR-T cell therapy.
snappy: The Swiss pharma giant behind Gleevec, the CAR-T pioneer Kymriah, and the RNA cholesterol drug Leqvio.
detail: Novartis spans targeted oncology (Gleevec, Tafinlar, Mekinist), the first CAR-T Kymriah, and cardiovascular RNA therapy Leqvio, having spun off its generics arm Sandoz. You'll hear Novartis in cell-therapy and RNA-therapeutics discussion.

plain: The Danish company behind Ozempic and Wegovy that pioneered the GLP-1 weight-loss wave.
snappy: The Danish company that pioneered the GLP-1 weight-loss wave with Ozempic and Wegovy.
detail: Novo Nordisk, long the insulin and diabetes leader, became one of Europe's most valuable companies on semaglutide — Ozempic for diabetes and Wegovy for obesity. You'll hear Novo Nordisk in every obesity-market, supply, and pricing discussion.

snappy: The major form of lung cancer — about 85% of cases — and the part of oncology that has been most transformed by precision medicine and immunotherapy.
detail: NSCLC includes adenocarcinoma, squamous cell, and large-cell types. Treatment is dominated by molecular testing (EGFR, ALK, ROS1, BRAF, MET, RET, NTRK, KRAS G12C) plus immunotherapy with Keytruda or Opdivo for non-targetable cases. You'll hear NSCLC at every oncology conference and in nearly every pharma oncology pipeline discussion.
plain: The most common kind of lung cancer, about 85% of cases, and the area transformed most by precision drugs and immunotherapy.

snappy: A family of genes whose rare fusions can drive cancers across many different tissues — and which are fully treatable with two FDA-approved targeted drugs.
detail: NTRK fusions occur in less than 1% of common cancers but in nearly all of certain rare cancers (infantile fibrosarcoma, secretory breast carcinoma). Vitrakvi (larotrectinib) and Rozlytrek (entrectinib) are tumor-agnostic FDA approvals — they treat any NTRK-positive cancer regardless of organ. You'll hear NTRK in tumor-agnostic-approval discussions and as a model for biomarker-driven drug development.
plain: A family of genes whose rare misfirings can spark cancers in many different organs and are treatable with two FDA-approved drugs.

snappy: The single chemical letter that makes up DNA and RNA — chain millions of them together and you get a genome.
detail: Each nucleotide has three parts: a sugar, a phosphate, and one of four bases (A, T, G, C in DNA; A, U, G, C in RNA). When pharma talks about 'oligonucleotide' drugs — antisense therapies, siRNAs, mRNA vaccines — these are short stretches of synthetic nucleotides designed to silence, replace, or instruct genes. The chemistry of modifying nucleotides for stability is one of the unsung breakthroughs behind modern RNA medicine.
plain: One of the chemical 'letters' that spells out DNA and RNA — string millions together and you get a genome.

snappy: The cell's command center — the membrane-bound compartment that houses the chromosomes and where DNA is read and copied.
detail: The nucleus is the defining feature of eukaryotic cells (animals, plants, fungi) and what separates them from bacteria. Many drugs target processes that happen in the nucleus: chemotherapies that damage DNA, hormone therapies whose receptors travel into the nucleus to switch genes on or off, and emerging gene-editing tools like CRISPR that have to physically enter the nucleus to reach their target.
plain: A cell's command center — the walled-off compartment that holds the chromosomes and where DNA is read and copied.
How many people need the treatment for one extra person to be helped — a value of 20 means treating twenty to help one.
snappy: How many patients must take a drug for *one* to benefit — the absolute risk reduction flipped into a single, clinic-ready number.
detail: The reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction: a 5% absolute risk reduction gives a number needed to treat of 20. Lower is better. It turns abstract statistics into a tangible sense of how much effort a benefit takes, cutting through an inflated relative risk. Its dark mirror is the number needed to harm. You'll hear number needed to treat when clinicians and HEOR teams judge whether a marginal benefit is worth it.

plain: A nurse with advanced training who can diagnose illness, order tests, and prescribe medicine, often like a doctor.
snappy: An *advanced-practice nurse* who can diagnose, treat, and prescribe — often running a primary care practice much like a physician.
detail: A nurse practitioner is a registered nurse with graduate training and an expanded scope: in many US states they assess, diagnose, order tests, and prescribe independently. Alongside the physician assistant, they're central to filling the primary care gap, especially in rural and underserved areas where physicians are scarce, and increasingly staff specialty care and emergency department teams too. How much independence they get — full versus restricted practice — varies by state and is a running policy fight. You'll hear nurse practitioner discussed in every debate about the clinician workforce and access to care.

snappy: A chronic disease defined by excess body fat that raises the risk of dozens of conditions — heart disease, diabetes, cancer — affecting roughly 42% of US adults.
detail: Obesity treatment was a backwater of niche pills until GLP-1 agonists — Wegovy (semaglutide), Zepbound (tirzepatide) — delivered 15-22% weight loss in trials and reshaped the entire pharma landscape. Older drugs like phentermine and Contrave (naltrexone-bupropion) remain but look modest by comparison. You'll hear obesity framed at JPMorgan as the largest emerging therapeutic market in pharma history, and on every Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly earnings call as the dominant growth story.
plain: A long-term condition of carrying too much body fat that raises the risk of many diseases and affects roughly 42% of US adults.

snappy: A second-generation antibody against the CD20 protein on B-cells — designed to be more potent than rituximab against certain lymphomas and CLL.
detail: Gazyva is approved with chemo for CLL, follicular lymphoma, and DLBCL. It's a glycoengineered antibody intended to recruit immune cells more effectively than its predecessor. You'll hear obinutuzumab in CD20 lifecycle-management discussions, especially as rituximab biosimilars erode the original franchise.
plain: A newer lab-made antibody that targets a marker on certain immune cells, designed to be more powerful than its predecessor against some lymphomas.
A way to compare the chances of an outcome between two groups using odds rather than plain percentages — common in look-back studies.
snappy: The *odds* of an outcome in one group divided by the odds in another — the natural output of a case-control study and logistic models.
detail: Compares odds rather than probabilities; a case-control study reports it because such studies can't measure incidence directly. When an outcome is rare it approximates the relative risk, but for common outcomes it overstates the effect — a frequent source of headline confusion. It's quoted with a confidence interval to show precision. You'll hear odds ratio throughout epidemiology and genome-wide association results.

snappy: Prescribing a drug for a condition or population the FDA hasn't formally approved it for — legal for doctors but heavily restricted for manufacturers to promote.
detail: Off-label prescribing is common in oncology, especially when guidelines outpace formal approvals. Pharma can't market off-label uses, but doctors and payers may rely on NCCN guidelines for decisions. You'll hear off-label in commercial-strategy discussions, FDA enforcement (Department of Justice settlements over off-label promotion are major events), and reimbursement debates.
plain: When a doctor prescribes an approved drug for a condition the FDA hasn't formally signed off on — legal for them, restricted for drugmakers to promote.

snappy: The first PARP inhibitor approved by the FDA — pioneered the strategy of attacking cancers whose DNA-repair machinery is already broken.
detail: Lynparza is approved for BRCA-mutated ovarian, breast, prostate, and pancreatic cancers, exploiting synthetic lethality (the broken DNA repair plus PARP inhibition is too much for the cancer cell). It launched the PARP inhibitor class. You'll hear olaparib in any PARP-inhibitor commercial discussion, in BRCA-testing strategies, and in maintenance-therapy economics.
plain: The first drug of its class — it attacks cancers whose DNA-repair tools are already broken, hitting them so hard they can't survive.

snappy: Cancer that has spread, but only to a small number of sites — a state where aggressive local treatment of every spot may produce long-term disease control.
detail: Oligometastatic disease (typically 1-5 metastases) is being increasingly treated with stereotactic radiosurgery or targeted surgery alongside systemic therapy, sometimes producing years of disease-free survival. The concept has reshaped how doctors think about advanced cancer. You'll hear oligometastatic at radiation-oncology meetings and in commercial discussions of localized-treatment platforms.
plain: Cancer that has spread, but only to a few spots, where treating each one aggressively may give patients years of disease-free time.

snappy: A gene that, when activated or amplified abnormally, drives cells toward cancer — the opposite of a tumor-suppressor gene.
detail: Classic oncogenes include MYC, RAS family, HER2, and many kinases. They're often the targets of precision-oncology drugs because activation creates dependency: cancers driven by an oncogene need it to survive, making them vulnerable to inhibitors. You'll hear oncogene in basic cancer biology and in any drug-discovery pitch around 'oncogene-addicted' tumors.
plain: A gene that, when stuck switched on, pushes cells toward becoming cancer — the flip side of a tumor suppressor.

snappy: A doctor specializing in cancer treatment — usually subdivided into medical, surgical, radiation, and pediatric oncology, each handling a different piece of care.
detail: Medical oncologists prescribe chemo, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy; surgical oncologists remove tumors; radiation oncologists deliver radiation. Tumor boards bring all three together to make treatment decisions. You'll hear oncologist in patient-experience discussions, in commercial sales-targeting conversations, and in any clinical-trial-investigator context.
plain: A doctor who specializes in cancer treatment, usually focused on one slice such as medicine, surgery, radiation, or children's care.

snappy: The medical specialty dedicated to diagnosing and treating cancer — one of the largest, fastest-growing, and most innovation-heavy areas of medicine.
detail: Oncology is divided into many subspecialties: medical, surgical, radiation, pediatric, hematologic, gynecologic, and so on. The field has been the leading edge of pharma innovation for two decades and accounts for the largest share of new drug approvals. You'll hear oncology referenced as the dominant therapeutic area in nearly every pharma strategy discussion.
plain: The branch of medicine devoted to diagnosing and treating cancer — one of the largest and fastest-moving areas of pharma.
The first approved drug to work by silencing a faulty gene — treating a rare inherited disease that damages nerves and the heart.
snappy: The first-ever approved RNA-interference drug — it silences a faulty gene to treat hereditary amyloidosis.
detail: Onpattro was the landmark 2018 approval that made RNA interference (siRNA) a real drug class, silencing transthyretin to treat hereditary ATTR amyloidosis nerve damage. An Alnylam product. You'll hear Onpattro as the proof-of-concept in any RNA-therapeutics discussion.

plain: A cancer immunotherapy that takes a brake off the immune system, often given with a partner drug to hit tumors harder.
snappy: Bristol Myers Squibb's anti-PD-1 checkpoint inhibitor, often paired with Yervoy across melanoma, lung, and kidney cancer.
detail: Opdivo blocks PD-1 like Keytruda and is frequently combined with the CTLA-4 inhibitor Yervoy for deeper responses. It anchors BMS's immuno-oncology franchise. You'll hear Opdivo in melanoma, NSCLC, and kidney cancer readouts at ASCO.

snappy: A clinical trial where everyone — patients, doctors, sponsors — knows who's getting what treatment, in contrast to blinded trials.
detail: Open-label trials are common in early-phase oncology and rare diseases where placebo isn't ethical or practical. The lack of blinding can introduce bias, especially for patient-reported outcomes, so open-label results often need confirmation. You'll hear open-label in trial-design discussions and in any FDA review where bias-mitigation is debated.
plain: A trial where everyone — patients, doctors, sponsors — knows who's getting which treatment, with nothing hidden behind a placebo or code.

snappy: A drug for a rare disease — defined in the US as fewer than 200,000 patients — that gets FDA incentives like extended exclusivity and tax credits to make development worthwhile.
detail: Orphan Drug Designation grants 7 years of market exclusivity, 25% tax credits on clinical trial costs, and waiver of FDA application fees. The Orphan Drug Act of 1983 transformed rare-disease drug development. You'll hear orphan drug in rare-disease biotech pitches, in pricing debates (orphan drugs often cost more), and in regulatory affairs strategy.
plain: A drug for a rare disease, given special incentives like extra exclusivity and tax breaks to make it worth developing.

snappy: The percentage of patients in a trial whose tumors shrink by a defined amount after treatment — a fast, early measure of whether a drug is doing anything.
detail: ORR is a common endpoint for accelerated approval, especially in single-arm Phase 2 trials of targeted therapies. It's faster to measure than survival, but doesn't tell you about durability or whether patients live longer. You'll hear ORR in every oncology trial readout and in regulatory discussions about confirmatory-trial requirements.
plain: The share of patients in a trial whose tumors shrink by a set amount — a quick early read on whether a drug is doing anything.

snappy: The gold-standard cancer trial outcome: how long patients actually live from the start of treatment — the metric the FDA most wants to see improved.
detail: OS is the unambiguous endpoint — patients are either alive or not — but it takes years to mature, especially in cancers with long-term outcomes like indolent lymphomas. Trials use surrogate endpoints (PFS, ORR) to support earlier approvals, with OS as the confirmatory measure. You'll hear OS in every oncology trial readout and at FDA advisory committees evaluating accelerated approvals.
plain: The gold-standard measure in cancer trials: how long patients actually live from when treatment starts.

snappy: A third-generation EGFR inhibitor that became the standard first-line treatment for EGFR-mutant lung cancer — and AstraZeneca's biggest oncology product.
detail: Tagrisso targets the T790M resistance mutation that defeated earlier EGFR drugs and is now used in front-line and adjuvant EGFR-mutant NSCLC. With sales over $5B annually, it's a cornerstone of AstraZeneca's oncology franchise. You'll hear Tagrisso at lung-cancer trial readouts, AstraZeneca earnings calls, and any commercial discussion of EGFR lifecycle management.
plain: A third-generation pill that became the standard first treatment for a common mutation-driven lung cancer.

snappy: A condition where bones become thin and fragile — most common in postmenopausal women — quietly raising the risk of fractures from minor falls or even sneezes.
detail: Osteoporosis treatment has moved from older bisphosphonates (Fosamax/alendronate, Reclast/zoledronic acid) to monoclonal antibodies that block bone breakdown — Prolia (denosumab), Evenity (romosozumab) — and the bone-builder Forteo (teriparatide). DEXA scans diagnose and track the disease. You'll hear osteoporosis on Amgen earnings calls (Prolia is one of its top franchises) and in commercial discussions of how Medicare coverage and women's-health primary-care patterns shape who actually gets diagnosed and treated.
plain: A condition where bones quietly turn thin and fragile, often in older women, raising the risk of breaks from even small falls.

snappy: The most common primary bone cancer — typically affecting teenagers in growing bones — and a disease where treatment hasn't meaningfully changed in decades.
detail: Osteosarcoma treatment has been combination chemotherapy plus limb-sparing surgery since the 1980s, with cure rates of about 70% in localized disease and far lower in metastatic disease. The lack of progress has made it a focus of pediatric and rare-cancer drug development. You'll hear osteosarcoma at pediatric oncology meetings and in rare-disease biotech pitches.
plain: The most common bone cancer, mostly hitting teenagers, where treatment has barely changed in decades.

snappy: Drugs you can buy without a prescription — pulled off the shelf based on FDA monographs that decide which ingredients are safe for self-care.
detail: OTC drugs cover everything from ibuprofen to nicotine patches to the recently approved Opill — the first non-prescription daily birth control pill in the US. The FDA can switch a drug from prescription to OTC after evidence shows consumers can use it safely without a doctor, a process called "Rx-to-OTC switch." You'll hear it in commercial discussions when companies pitch OTC switches as a second life for aging brands losing exclusivity.
plain: Medicines you can buy off the shelf without a prescription, based on FDA lists of ingredients judged safe for self-care.
The yearly limit on what you can be made to pay; once you reach it, insurance covers the rest of your covered care.
snappy: The yearly cap on what you can be forced to pay; once you hit it, insurance covers 100% of covered care.
detail: The out-of-pocket maximum limits a patient's total annual cost-sharing — deductible plus copays plus coinsurance — after which the plan pays everything for covered services. It's the backstop that makes catastrophic illness survivable financially. You'll hear it in benefit-design and affordability discussion.

plain: A sudden jump in cases of a disease in one place or group. The earliest, most local stage before it can grow into an epidemic.
snappy: A *sudden, localized* cluster of cases above the norm — the smallest fire, which contact tracing can contain before it grows into an epidemic.
detail: A sharp, often local rise in cases above normal — a foodborne cluster, a measles flare in an under-vaccinated school. Caught early, contact tracing and quarantine can snuff it out before it becomes an epidemic. These events trigger disease surveillance and, for notifiable diseases, mandatory reporting to the CDC. The line between a large one and an epidemic is mostly a matter of scale.

plain: Care you get without staying overnight — you come in, get treated, and leave the same day.
snappy: Care delivered *without an overnight stay* — you arrive, get treated, and go home the same day.
detail: Outpatient care spans the doctor's visit, the lab draw, the day surgery, and the infusion clinic — anything that doesn't convert you to inpatient status. Much of it happens in ambulatory care settings, and the long shift of procedures from hospital wards to outpatient sites is one of the biggest cost stories in modern medicine. Payers and value-based care models push hard to keep care outpatient when it's safe. You'll hear outpatient paired with inpatient whenever site-of-care and reimbursement are weighed.

snappy: A frequently fatal gynecologic cancer that often spreads silently before being detected — and a disease where PARP inhibitors have been transformative.
detail: Most ovarian cancers are epithelial; high-grade serous (often BRCA- or HRD-driven) is the dominant subtype. Treatment is surgery plus platinum-based chemo, with PARP inhibitors (Lynparza, Zejula, Rubraca) as standard maintenance. You'll hear ovarian cancer at gynecologic oncology meetings and in any commercial discussion of PARP-inhibitor-driven franchise economics.
plain: A women's cancer that often spreads quietly before being caught, where a newer class of drugs has dramatically improved outcomes.
A diabetes injection that mimics a gut hormone to lower blood sugar and curb appetite — famous for causing weight loss.
snappy: The GLP-1 injection for type 2 diabetes that became a cultural phenomenon for its weight-loss effect.
detail: Ozempic mimics the GLP-1 gut hormone to lower blood sugar and curb appetite; off-label weight use drove global shortages. Novo Nordisk markets the same molecule as Wegovy for obesity. You'll hear Ozempic dominate every Novo earnings call and diabetes discussion.

plain: A number estimating how likely a result is just luck — the smaller it is, the less likely the finding came from chance alone.
snappy: The probability your result is a *fluke* — the chance of an effect this big if the drug truly did nothing; below 0.05 is the customary line.
detail: It's the probability of data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis — no real effect — held. The arbitrary 0.05 threshold defines statistical significance and accepts a 5% type I error rate, but a small p-value says nothing about effect size, so pair it with the confidence interval. Misuse and 'p-hacking' fueled the replication crisis. You'll hear p-value dissected wherever randomized controlled trial results and their credibility are weighed.

snappy: The 'guardian of the genome' — a tumor suppressor that triggers cell death when DNA damage is too severe. Disabled in more than half of all cancers.
detail: TP53 mutations are the most common genetic change in cancer, found in around 50% of solid tumors. When p53 fails, damaged cells survive and accumulate further mutations. Restoring p53 function or exploiting p53-deficient biology has been a long-running drug-development goal. You'll hear p53 in any cancer-mechanism discussion and in pipeline pitches around p53-pathway therapies.
plain: The 'guardian of the genome' — a built-in alarm that kills cells with badly damaged DNA, switched off in more than half of all cancers.

snappy: A chemotherapy drug originally derived from the Pacific yew tree — works by jamming cancer cells in a mid-division state until they self-destruct.
detail: Paclitaxel and the related docetaxel are mainstays of breast, ovarian, lung, and pancreatic cancer treatment. The mechanism — stabilizing microtubules — is distinctive among chemo drugs. Generic and nanoparticle-bound (Abraxane) formulations are widely used. You'll hear paclitaxel in oncology trial designs as a comparator and in any chemo backbone discussion.
plain: A chemo drug originally pulled from yew tree bark that jams cancer cells mid-division until they self-destruct.

snappy: A DNA-repair gene that works alongside BRCA1 and BRCA2 — when mutated, it raises breast and pancreatic cancer risk and predicts PARP-inhibitor response.
detail: PALB2 mutations are less common than BRCA but functionally similar, and PALB2-mutant tumors often respond to PARP inhibitors. Genetic testing panels routinely include PALB2 alongside BRCA. You'll hear PALB2 in hereditary-cancer counseling and in commercial discussions of expanded biomarker eligibility for PARP-inhibitor labels.
plain: A DNA-repair gene that works hand-in-hand with the famous breast-cancer genes; when broken, it raises breast and pancreatic cancer risk.

snappy: Care focused on relieving symptoms and maximizing quality of life rather than curing disease — important at any cancer stage, not just end of life.
detail: Palliative care includes pain management, symptom control, and psychosocial support. It's increasingly delivered alongside curative treatment, not as an alternative to it. Studies show early palliative care can extend survival in some cancers. You'll hear palliative in supportive-oncology discussions, in commercial pitches around symptom-management drugs, and in healthcare policy debates.
plain: Care focused on easing symptoms and improving quality of life, useful at any stage of serious illness — not just at the end.

snappy: One of the deadliest common cancers — usually diagnosed late, with median survival under a year despite recent advances in chemotherapy combinations.
detail: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) carries KRAS mutations in over 90% of cases, traditionally considered undruggable. Standard treatment is FOLFIRINOX or gemcitabine-based chemo, with KRAS G12C inhibitors and CAR-T trials emerging. You'll hear pancreatic cancer at GI oncology meetings, in 'underserved-indication' biotech pitches, and in any KRAS-targeted-therapy commercial discussion.
plain: One of the deadliest common cancers, usually caught late, with most patients surviving less than a year despite better chemo options.
An epidemic that has spread across many countries or the whole world at the same time, like COVID-19.
snappy: An *epidemic gone global* — a disease spreading across many countries or continents at once, as COVID-19 and influenza have done.
detail: An epidemic that has crossed international borders on a large scale, hitting whole regions of the world at once; the WHO formally declares them. These events strain disease surveillance, vaccine supply, and herd immunity all at the same time, and their toll is counted in excess mortality. After a pathogen settles into steady circulation, the crisis phase can fade toward an endemic equilibrium rather than vanishing.

snappy: A progressive movement disorder caused by the loss of dopamine-producing brain cells — leading to tremor, stiffness, and slowness, and often affecting mood and thinking later.
detail: Parkinson's treatment has been dominated for 50 years by levodopa, which replaces missing dopamine but loses effectiveness over time. Newer extended-release and inhaled formulations — Inbrija (inhaled levodopa), Crexont — and adjuncts like MAO-B inhibitors fill gaps. Disease-modifying therapy remains the holy grail. You'll hear Parkinson's at every neurology investor day where companies pitch alpha-synuclein and GBA-targeted programs, and at MDS Congress when surgical approaches like deep brain stimulation get reframed by new device generations.
plain: A slow-creeping brain disorder where dopamine-making cells die off, leading to tremors, stiffness, and slowed movement.
A DNA-repair enzyme. Block it in tumors that already struggle to fix DNA — like BRCA cancers — and they collapse.
snappy: A DNA-repair enzyme; blocking it kills tumors that have lost another repair route — the *synthetic lethality* behind BRCA-targeted drugs.
detail: PARP inhibitors — Lynparza, Zejula — exploit synthetic lethality: cancers with BRCA mutations already can't repair DNA one way, so blocking PARP's backup route is fatal to them while sparing normal cells. You'll hear PARP in ovarian and breast cancer readouts at ASCO and in HRD-biomarker discussion.

snappy: A class of drugs that block a key DNA-repair enzyme — devastating to tumors that already have broken DNA-repair machinery (especially BRCA-mutated cancers).
detail: PARP inhibitors (Lynparza, Zejula, Rubraca, Talzenna) work via 'synthetic lethality' — combining PARP inhibition with existing BRCA mutations is too much for cancer cells to survive. Approved across ovarian, breast, prostate, and pancreatic cancer with BRCA or HRD biomarkers. You'll hear PARP inhibitors at every breast/ovarian/prostate cancer trial readout.
plain: A class of drugs that block a key DNA-repair enzyme, devastating to tumors whose repair tools are already broken.

snappy: The point in a drug's lifecycle when its patent protection runs out — and generic or biosimilar competitors flood in, often vaporizing 80-90% of revenue within a year.
detail: Lipitor's 2011 expiration is the textbook example: $13B in peak revenue collapsed to under $2B within two years. Pharma calendars are organized around patent cliffs, driving M&A and pipeline urgency. The 2030s loom as one of the steepest cliffs in industry history with Keytruda (pembrolizumab), Eliquis (apixaban), and dozens of biologics losing exclusivity. You'll hear "patent cliff" on every earnings call as the existential question CFOs spend their careers preparing for, and at JPMorgan when M&A speculation hits.
plain: The moment a drug's patent runs out and cheap copies flood in, often wiping out most of its sales within a year.

snappy: When surgery after pre-treatment shows no remaining live cancer in the removed tissue — the cleanest signal that a drug is working.
detail: pCR rates are increasingly used as accelerated-approval endpoints in early-stage breast cancer, where they correlate (imperfectly) with long-term survival benefit. Drugs that meaningfully boost pCR can advance to FDA approval years before survival data matures. You'll hear pCR in neoadjuvant breast-cancer trials and in commercial pitches around early-disease drug positioning.
plain: When surgery after pre-treatment finds no living cancer cells left in the removed tissue — the cleanest sign a drug truly worked.
A secure website or app where you can see your test results, message your doctor, and book appointments.
snappy: The *patient-facing window* into the electronic health record — view results, message clinicians, book visits, refill prescriptions.
detail: The secure online front end to a provider's electronic health record, letting people read notes and labs, message care teams, and schedule visits. US rules now guarantee patients fast electronic access to their data, often via FHIR-based apps. Uptake varies with digital literacy. You'll hear patient portal in patient-engagement and interoperability discussion.

snappy: The middleman between drugmakers, insurers, and pharmacies — they negotiate prices, decide what's covered, and ultimately shape what you pay at the counter.
detail: The big three — CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, and OptumRx — manage formularies for most US insurance plans, extracting rebates from pharma in exchange for preferred placement. They've been a frequent target of Congressional hearings and FTC scrutiny over how rebates flow. You'll hear PBM constantly in pharma earnings calls when companies discuss pricing pressure, and at JPMorgan when launch teams game out access strategy.
plain: A middleman between drugmakers, insurers, and pharmacies that negotiates prices, decides coverage, and shapes what you pay at the counter.
A protein that keeps 'bad' cholesterol high. Block it and LDL plummets — a newer option when statins aren't enough.
snappy: A liver protein that degrades the receptors clearing 'bad' cholesterol; block it and LDL falls sharply — the target of Repatha and Leqvio.
detail: PCSK9 inhibitors lower LDL by preserving the receptors that clear it. Repatha and Praluent are antibodies; Leqvio is a twice-yearly siRNA. You'll hear PCSK9 at AHA in any discussion of residual cardiovascular risk and the cost-effectiveness debates ICER has weighed in on.

plain: A brake on immune cells that tumors learn to press so the body leaves them alone. Drugs that release it can fight cancer.
snappy: A receptor on T-cells that acts as an off-switch — tumors exploit it to hide, and *checkpoint inhibitors* exist to flip it back on.
detail: PD-1 sits on T-cells; when it binds PD-L1 on another cell, the T-cell stands down. Many tumors display PD-L1 to switch off the immune response. Anti-PD-1 drugs like Keytruda and Opdivo block that handshake, freeing T-cells to attack. You'll hear PD-1 in every immuno-oncology readout at ASCO and in pipeline talk of combination therapy.

snappy: The immune checkpoint that cancer most often hijacks to hide — and the target of the biggest immunotherapy success story in oncology.
detail: PD-1 sits on T-cells; PD-L1 sits on cancer cells. When they bind, T-cells are switched off. Drugs blocking either side — Keytruda, Opdivo, Tecentriq, Imfinzi, Bavencio — have transformed melanoma, lung, kidney, bladder, head-and-neck, and many other cancers. You'll hear PD-1/PD-L1 at every immuno-oncology discussion and in essentially every solid-tumor commercial conversation.
plain: The immune system's 'off-switch' that cancer most often hijacks to hide — and the target of the biggest immunotherapy successes.
The molecule tumors wave to switch off attacking immune cells — and a marker doctors test to predict who responds to certain cancer drugs.
snappy: The 'don't attack me' flag tumors wave to engage PD-1 and shut down T-cells — and a biomarker that guides checkpoint-inhibitor use.
detail: PD-L1 is the ligand that binds PD-1. Tumors expressing a lot of it evade immune attack, so pathologists score PD-L1 levels to predict response to Keytruda, Tecentriq, and Imfinzi. You'll hear PD-L1 status quoted in every NSCLC trial and as a companion-diagnostic talking point at ASCO.

snappy: The deal where drug companies pay the FDA to review their applications on a clock — and Congress renews it every five years.
detail: PDUFA sets the FDA's review timeline — typically 10 months for standard drugs, 6 months for priority ones — and is funded by industry fees rather than taxpayers. Investors and journalists watch the "PDUFA date" the way they watch earnings: it's the day the FDA must rule on whether a drug gets approved.
plain: The deal where drug companies pay the FDA to review their applications on a clock, renewed by Congress every five years.

snappy: Merck's checkpoint inhibitor — the best-selling cancer drug in the world, and the first ever approved based on a biomarker rather than a tumor type.
detail: Keytruda blocks PD-1, with approvals across more than 20 cancer types. The 2017 MSI-H tumor-agnostic approval was a regulatory landmark. With sales above $25B annually, Keytruda dominates immuno-oncology economics. You'll hear Keytruda at every oncology conference, in any combination-therapy pipeline pitch, and in patent-cliff discussions about Merck's late-2020s exposure.
plain: Merck's checkpoint-blocking cancer drug — the best-selling drug in the world and the first approved based on a tumor's genetics, not its location.

snappy: A short chain of amino acids — basically a tiny protein, usually under 50 amino acids long.
detail: Peptide drugs sit between small molecules and full-size protein biologics: easier to manufacture than antibodies, more selective than small molecules. Insulin (51 amino acids) is the original peptide drug; modern blockbusters include the GLP-1 agonists Ozempic/Wegovy (semaglutide) and Mounjaro/Zepbound (tirzepatide), all peptides delivered by weekly injection. Oral peptide formulations (Rybelsus) are an active development frontier.
plain: A short chain of amino acids — basically a tiny protein, usually under fifty links long.

snappy: A drug made of a short chain of amino acids — bigger than a small molecule, smaller than a full antibody — designed to hit targets neither extreme can reach.
detail: Peptide drugs sit between traditional pills and biologics, and the GLP-1 class — Ozempic (semaglutide), Mounjaro (tirzepatide), Wegovy — has made them the most-watched drug category in pharma. Other approved peptides include Sandostatin (octreotide) for hormone-secreting tumors and oral GLP-1s now reaching late-stage trials. You'll hear "peptide" everywhere now in earnings calls about obesity and diabetes pipelines, and at JPMorgan when companies pitch their position in the GLP-1 race.
plain: A drug made of a short chain of amino acids — bigger than a pill, smaller than a full antibody — hitting targets neither can reach.
A targeted breast cancer drug given alongside Herceptin to shut down the same growth signal more completely.
snappy: Roche's second anti-HER2 antibody, given with Herceptin to block HER2 signaling more completely in breast cancer.
detail: Perjeta binds a different part of HER2 than Herceptin; the pair plus chemo is a standard for HER2-positive breast cancer. You'll hear Perjeta in breast cancer regimens and HER2-franchise lifecycle discussion at ASCO.
