snappy: Treatment chosen based on the specific genetic and molecular features of each patient's disease — instead of a one-size-fits-all approach.
detail: Precision medicine in oncology means testing tumors for specific mutations and matching patients to drugs targeting those mutations. The approach has been transformative in lung cancer, melanoma, and several blood cancers. You'll hear personalized medicine in any trial-design discussion involving biomarker selection, in companion-diagnostic strategy, and in any commercial pitch about niche-but-defensible markets.
plain: Picking treatment based on the specific genetic features of each patient's disease instead of giving everyone the same thing.
A pharmaceutical giant, widely known for co-developing the first major COVID-19 vaccine.
snappy: The pharma giant that co-developed the first widely used COVID-19 vaccine with BioNTech.
detail: Pfizer's portfolio spans the blood thinner Eliquis (with BMS), oncology (Xalkori, Sutent), and the COVID vaccine and antiviral that briefly made it the largest drugmaker by revenue. You'll hear Pfizer in vaccine, M&A, and post-COVID-cliff discussion.

snappy: The time from treatment start until the disease gets worse — a faster-to-measure efficacy endpoint than overall survival, widely used in oncology trials.
detail: PFS captures both stable disease and tumor shrinkage, ending when imaging or symptoms show clear progression. It's the most common primary endpoint in metastatic-cancer trials and supports many accelerated approvals. You'll hear PFS in every oncology trial readout, in FDA review discussions, and in commercial pitches around treatment durability.
plain: The stretch of time from starting treatment until the disease clearly gets worse — a faster signal than waiting for survival data.

snappy: A 0-14 scale for how acidic or basic something is — 7 is neutral, lower is more acidic, higher is more basic.
detail: Different parts of the body sit at different pH: blood at 7.35-7.45, stomach at 1.5-3.5, urine 4.5-8. Drug absorption depends heavily on pH because it changes whether a molecule is charged or neutral. Tumor microenvironments tend to be slightly acidic, which has been exploited in some 'pH-sensitive' antibody and nanoparticle designs that release their payload only in the tumor.
plain: A 0-to-14 score for how acidic or alkaline something is, where 7 is neutral, lower is sour, higher is soapy.
What your body does to a drug — how it absorbs, spreads, breaks down, and clears it. Half of every dosing decision.
snappy: What the body does to a drug — how it's absorbed, distributed, broken down, and cleared; the 'PK' half of every dosing decision.
detail: Pharmacokinetics tracks a drug's journey via measures like Cmax, Tmax, half-life, volume of distribution, and AUC. It pairs with pharmacodynamics (what the drug does to the body) to set dose and schedule. You'll hear 'PK/PD' in every early-phase trial and FDA review.

snappy: The ongoing job of watching for safety problems after a drug is on the market — collecting reports, spotting patterns, and acting before a small signal becomes a crisis.
detail: Pharmacovigilance — "PV" in industry shorthand — combines spontaneous adverse-event reports (FDA's FAERS, EMA's EudraVigilance), claims data, and active surveillance to catch risks trials missed. PV findings can trigger label changes, Black Box Warnings, or full withdrawals — Vioxx (rofecoxib) is the textbook example. You'll see PV teams cited in every FDA safety communication, and in earnings calls when a competitor's safety signal becomes a market opportunity.
plain: The detective work of watching for safety problems after a drug is on the market, so small warning signs get caught early.
The middlemen who run drug coverage for insurers — negotiating discounts and deciding which medicines you can get and at what cost.
snappy: The middlemen who run drug benefits for insurers — negotiating rebates, building formularies, and steering which drugs you can get and what they cost.
detail: PBMs sit between drugmakers, insurers, and pharmacies, negotiating rebates in exchange for formulary placement and processing prescription claims. The big three control most of the market, and their opaque economics draw constant scrutiny. You'll hear pharmacy benefit manager in every drug-pricing and gross-to-net discussion.

snappy: The first-in-human stage of drug development — small, focused on safety and dosing rather than whether the drug actually works.
detail: Phase 1 trials typically enroll 20-100 healthy volunteers (or patients with the target disease in oncology) and last several months. Endpoints are pharmacokinetics (how the body handles the drug), pharmacodynamics (what the drug does to the body), and the maximum tolerated dose. A clean Phase 1 readout is necessary but far from sufficient — most drugs that pass Phase 1 still fail later. Biotech earnings discussions of 'Phase 1 data' usually focus on safety signals and any early efficacy hints in oncology dose-escalation cohorts.
plain: The very first time a new drug is given to people, in small numbers, mainly to check it is safe and find the right dose.

snappy: Mid-stage trials in patients with the target disease — focused on whether the drug actually works at the doses chosen in Phase 1.
detail: Phase 2 typically enrolls 100-500 patients across several months to a couple of years. This is the 'go/no-go' decision point for most programs — if Phase 2 efficacy doesn't impress, Phase 3 investment is hard to justify. Successful Phase 2 readouts often drive significant biotech stock moves; failures kill programs. The Phase 2-to-Phase 3 attrition rate is the single highest in drug development.
plain: The middle round of human testing, given to people who actually have the disease, to see if the drug really helps them.

snappy: Large, expensive late-stage trials that produce the data the FDA actually wants to see — usually thousands of patients across many sites.
detail: Phase 3 is where most drug development money is spent. Trials run 1-4 years, cost hundreds of millions, and are designed to prove the drug works better than (or at least as well as) the existing standard of care. Top-line Phase 3 readouts are major catalysts for both biotech stocks and pharma franchises. Phase 3 failure can wipe billions off market caps overnight (see 2024's gantenerumab Alzheimer's failure for Roche).
plain: The big, expensive final test of a new drug across thousands of patients, designed to prove it works well enough to be approved.

snappy: The post-approval studies a drugmaker runs after the FDA has greenlit the medicine — to track real-world safety, expand uses, and meet conditions of accelerated approvals.
detail: Phase 4 covers everything from FDA-mandated post-marketing requirements (PMRs) to investigator-initiated studies pharma supports for label expansion. Failed Phase 4 confirmatory trials can pull accelerated-approval drugs off the market, as the Aduhelm (aducanumab) saga showed. You'll hear Phase 4 in FDA approval announcements that come with conditions, in pharmacovigilance discussions of post-market signals, and on earnings calls when companies announce label expansions from real-world evidence and observational studies.
plain: The follow-up studies a company runs after a drug is approved, to keep an eye on how it performs in the real world.

snappy: The standard sequence of human drug testing — Phase 1 finds the safe dose, Phase 2 tests effectiveness, Phase 3 confirms benefit in large populations.
detail: Phase 1 enrolls small groups (often healthy volunteers, or patients in oncology) for safety. Phase 2 tests efficacy in target populations. Phase 3 is the pivotal large randomized trial that supports FDA approval. Phase 4 happens post-approval. You'll hear phase numbers everywhere in pharma — they tell you the stakes and the data quality at a glance.
plain: The three steps a new drug walks through in people: first check safety, then check it works, then prove it works at scale.

snappy: A specific chromosomal swap that creates the BCR-ABL fusion gene — found in chronic myeloid leukemia and a subset of acute lymphoblastic leukemia.
detail: The Philadelphia chromosome (translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22) was the first genetic abnormality consistently linked to a specific cancer. Its product, BCR-ABL, is the target of imatinib and successor TKIs. Ph+ ALL has worse prognosis than Ph-negative ALL but is now treatable with TKI-chemo combinations. You'll hear Philadelphia chromosome in CML and ALL discussions and as a historical landmark in cancer genetics.
plain: A swapped piece between two chromosomes that creates a faulty gene driving certain blood cancers, and the first cancer cause ever pinned down.
A licensed health professional trained to diagnose, treat, and prescribe, working together with doctors.
snappy: A *licensed clinician* trained on the medical model who diagnoses, treats, and prescribes — practicing in partnership with physicians across every specialty.
detail: A physician assistant completes a graduate medical-model program and is licensed to examine, diagnose, order tests, and prescribe, traditionally under a physician's collaboration. Like the nurse practitioner, the physician assistant helps close the primary care shortfall and flexibly fills gaps across specialty care, the emergency department, and surgery. The profession is debating a rebrand to 'physician associate,' a sign of its growing independence. You'll hear physician assistant alongside nurse practitioner whenever the future of the clinical workforce is discussed.

snappy: A central signaling pathway that pushes cells to grow and survive — frequently mutated in cancer, and a perennial drug-development target with mixed results.
detail: PIK3CA mutations occur in around 40% of breast cancers and many other tumors. Approved PI3K inhibitors include Piqray (alpelisib) for breast cancer and several drugs for B-cell lymphomas, though several drugs in this class have been withdrawn due to safety. You'll hear PI3K in breast cancer trial readouts, in pathway-targeted commercial pitches, and in safety-signal discussions.
plain: A signal switch inside cells that tells them to grow and stay alive, often jammed on in cancers and a popular drug target.

snappy: Pharmacokinetics is what your body does to the drug; pharmacodynamics is what the drug does to your body — together they predict how a treatment will behave.
detail: PK/PD modeling supports dose selection, drug-drug interaction predictions, and special-population dosing (renal impairment, pediatric). It's central to every drug-development program from Phase 1 onward. You'll hear PK/PD in any clinical pharmacology discussion, in FDA review divisions of clinical pharmacology, and in dose-optimization debates.
plain: Two sides of how a drug behaves: what the body does to the drug, and what the drug does to the body.

snappy: An inactive substance — usually a sugar pill or saline injection — given to a control group in trials to isolate the real effect of the drug being tested.
detail: Placebos can produce real measurable improvements (the placebo effect), so trials use them to establish whether a drug's benefit is from the drug itself. Placebo controls aren't ethical when standard-of-care exists for serious conditions, so trials often compare to active comparators instead. You'll hear placebo in every randomized controlled trial discussion.
plain: A fake pill or shot with no active ingredient, given to one group in a trial so researchers can prove the real drug actually works.

snappy: A class of chemotherapy drugs (cisplatin, carboplatin, oxaliplatin) that kill cancer cells by binding to and damaging their DNA.
detail: Platinum-based chemo is a backbone for lung, ovarian, bladder, head-and-neck, and germ-cell cancers. Side effects include kidney damage, nerve damage, and hearing loss, which limit dosing. Platinum-resistance is a major treatment problem. You'll hear platinum in any chemo-comparator trial design and in commercial discussions of post-platinum treatment lines.
plain: A group of older chemotherapy drugs that kill cancer cells by tangling up and damaging their DNA so they can no longer divide.

snappy: A long molecule made by linking many small repeating units (monomers) together — proteins, DNA, starch, plastics are all polymers.
detail: In pharma, synthetic polymers underpin drug delivery: PLGA microspheres for sustained-release injectables (long-acting antipsychotics, GLP-1s in development), polyethylene glycol (PEGylation) attached to proteins to extend their circulation time, and polymer-based hydrogels for ocular implants. The lipid 'polymers' in mRNA vaccines' lipid nanoparticles are arguably one of the most consequential pharma polymer applications of the past decade.
plain: A very long molecule made by stringing many tiny identical building blocks together, like beads on a necklace.
When a test comes back positive, how likely it is you actually have the disease — which depends heavily on how common it is.
snappy: If your test reads *positive*, the chance you truly have the disease — and, unlike specificity, it sinks when the condition is rare.
detail: The probability that a positive result is a true positive. Unlike sensitivity and specificity, it swings with disease prevalence: in a rare disease even an excellent test produces many false positives, dragging the positive predictive value down — the core argument against mass screening for uncommon conditions. Its mirror is the negative predictive value. You'll hear positive predictive value whenever a screening program's real-world usefulness, not just its lab accuracy, is debated.

plain: A more flexible, pricier insurance plan: see specialists without referrals and go outside the network for a higher cost.
snappy: A managed-care plan that costs more but offers flexibility — see specialists without referrals and go out-of-network for a higher share of the cost.
detail: A PPO lets members see any provider, paying less for in-network 'preferred' ones, with no gatekeeper referrals. The trade-off versus an HMO is higher premiums for more freedom. You'll hear PPO in any plan-design or benefits discussion.

snappy: All the laboratory and animal testing a drug must complete before it can be given to humans — typically years of work and millions of dollars.
detail: Preclinical research includes target validation, in vitro screening, animal efficacy and toxicology, ADME profiling, and CMC development. Most drug candidates fail at this stage. You'll hear preclinical in early-stage biotech pipeline discussions, at investor briefings on near-term IND filings, and in academic licensing conversations.
plain: All the lab dishes and animal testing a drug must survive before regulators will let it anywhere near a human.

snappy: A daily pill or injection that lowers a person's risk of getting HIV by roughly 99% when taken as directed — a public-health breakthrough hiding in plain sight.
detail: PrEP is delivered as oral Truvada (emtricitabine-tenofovir) and Descovy, plus the long-acting injectable Apretude (cabotegravir) given every two months. Apretude addresses adherence, the biggest weak point of daily pills. Yet uptake remains far below need, especially in Southern US states most affected by HIV. You'll hear PrEP at Gilead and ViiV earnings calls, in CDC End the HIV Epidemic updates, and in policy debates about Medicaid and 340B coverage that determine whether PrEP actually reaches at-risk populations.
plain: A pill or shot taken by HIV-negative people to cut their chance of catching the virus by around 99 percent.
Out of everyone in a group, the portion who have a disease right now — counting both new and long-standing cases.
snappy: The share of a population that *has* a condition at a given moment — the standing pool, counting old and new cases alike, unlike incidence.
detail: A snapshot: what fraction of people live with diabetes today, regardless of when they were diagnosed. It reflects both how often a disease arises — its incidence — and how long people live with it, so chronic conditions show high figures. The number drives budgeting and public-health planning, and pairs with morbidity to size total burden. Reporters quote it when they say '1 in 10 adults has...'; the CDC publishes it for major chronic diseases.

plain: The regular doctor you see first for most health problems, who treats common issues and sends you to specialists when needed.
snappy: Your *first point of contact* with the health system — the generalist who treats everyday problems, coordinates care, and follows you over the years.
detail: Primary care is the front door to medicine: a family doctor, internist, or pediatrician who manages common conditions like hypertension and type 2 diabetes, catches new ones early, and writes the referral when you need specialty care. Under managed care it often serves as the gatekeeper to specialists, and it anchors chronic care management for people carrying several conditions at once. Its quiet strength is continuity — one clinician who knows your whole story. You'll hear primary care invoked in every debate about access, cost, and the shortage of generalist clinicians.

snappy: The single, pre-declared measurement a clinical trial is built to answer — the outcome the whole study is powered to detect, win or lose.
detail: Companies pick a primary endpoint before the trial starts: overall survival, progression-free survival, A1C reduction, blood-pressure drop. Hitting it is the difference between a positive readout and a failed one — and statistical adjustments make it harder to claim wins on backup measures if the primary misses. You'll hear "hit the primary" celebrated on the day of trial readouts, and "missed the primary" wipe billions off market caps within minutes.
plain: The single main question a clinical trial is set up to answer, decided in advance, and what the whole study lives or dies on.

snappy: The original cancer site where the disease started — distinct from metastases, which are where the cancer has since spread.
detail: The primary tumor's tissue type usually defines the cancer (e.g., a breast tumor that has spread to the lungs is still called breast cancer). Treatment is generally based on primary-tumor type, though tumor-agnostic biomarker-driven drugs (NTRK, MSI-H) are growing in importance. You'll hear primary tumor in pathology, in cancer staging, and in commercial market-segmentation discussions.
plain: The very first place a cancer started growing, before any of it spread elsewhere in the body.

snappy: The paperwork hurdle where your doctor has to convince your insurer that a specific drug is medically necessary before they'll cover it.
detail: Prior auth — "PA" in industry shorthand — is the most common utilization-management tool insurers use to gate expensive drugs, often requiring documentation of failed alternatives or specific diagnostic criteria. Physicians complain it consumes hours of staff time per case and delays care. You'll see it cited as a launch barrier on pharma earnings calls, and it's a frequent target in policy reform conversations from both parties in Congress.
plain: The paperwork battle where a doctor must convince an insurance company that a specific drug is needed before they will pay for it.
A docking point for the hormone progesterone, read alongside the estrogen receptor to classify and guide breast-cancer treatment.
snappy: The protein progesterone binds; PR status is read with the estrogen receptor and HER2 to subtype breast cancer and predict endocrine-therapy response.
detail: Progesterone-receptor status appears with the estrogen receptor and HER2 on every breast cancer pathology report; PR-positive tumors generally respond better to endocrine therapy. You'll hear ER/PR/HER2 quoted in one breath in any breast cancer tumor board or ASCO discussion.

snappy: The most common cancer in men — often slow-growing and detected through PSA screening — with a wide spectrum from watch-and-wait to aggressive lethal disease.
detail: Treatment depends on stage and risk: active surveillance for low-risk disease, surgery or radiation for localized disease, hormone therapy and increasingly androgen-receptor inhibitors (Xtandi, Erleada, Nubeqa) plus PARP inhibitors and PSMA-targeted radioligand therapy for advanced cases. You'll hear prostate cancer at GU oncology meetings and in commercial discussions of androgen-axis franchises.
plain: The most common cancer in men, often slow-moving and found through a blood test, but sometimes aggressive and life-threatening.

snappy: A new class of drug molecules that grab a disease-causing protein and a cellular waste-disposal protein at the same time — forcing the cell to destroy the bad one.
detail: PROTACs are 'event-driven' rather than 'occupancy-driven' — they don't need to fully block a protein, just trigger its degradation. Companies like Arvinas, Kymera, and C4 Therapeutics are pioneering the class. You'll hear PROTAC in next-generation small-molecule pipeline discussions and in any pitch about previously undruggable targets.
plain: A clever new drug design that drags a disease-causing protein over to the cell's trash crew, which then chews it up.
Any health data that can be tied to you — like your diagnoses or test results — that the law says must be kept private.
snappy: *Individually identifiable* health data — the category HIPAA protects, from diagnoses to billing records to the very fact of a visit.
detail: Any health data linked to an identifiable person — names, diagnoses, test results, even appointment dates. HIPAA governs its use; stripping identifiers ('de-identification') frees data for research and real-world evidence. Mishandling it — often from unsecured electronic health record systems — drives most healthcare data-breach penalties. You'll hear PHI in privacy, security, and data-sharing discussion across every digital health vendor.

snappy: The molecular workhorses of the cell — long chains of amino acids that fold into precise shapes to do almost every job in the body.
detail: There are tens of thousands of distinct proteins in the human body: enzymes that catalyze reactions, antibodies that fight infection, hemoglobin that carries oxygen, collagen that holds tissues together, the receptors and channels on cell surfaces. Most modern drugs work by binding a specific protein to switch its activity on or off. Biologics — including all monoclonal antibodies, insulin, and clotting factors — are themselves proteins, manufactured in bioreactors.
plain: The tiny molecular machines that do most of the work in your body, built from chains of amino acid building blocks folded into shapes.

snappy: The detailed playbook for a clinical trial — covering eligibility, dosing, schedule, endpoints, safety monitoring, and statistical analysis. The trial's contract with regulators.
detail: Protocols are negotiated with FDA and IRBs before enrollment begins. Amendments require formal approval. Operationally, the protocol is what every site, investigator, and CRO follows. You'll hear protocol in any clinical-operations role, in regulatory-submissions, and in trial-design discussions where protocol design affects feasibility and cost.
plain: The detailed rulebook for a clinical trial that spells out exactly who joins, what they take, when, and how results are measured.

snappy: A chronic autoimmune skin disease where overactive immune signals make skin cells multiply too fast — leaving thick, scaly red patches that can crack and bleed.
detail: Psoriasis treatment has moved from topical creams to a procession of biologics — TNF inhibitors, IL-17 blockers like Cosentyx (secukinumab) and Taltz (ixekizumab), and IL-23 blockers like Skyrizi (risankizumab) — each cycle delivering higher skin-clearance rates. Up to 30% of patients also develop psoriatic arthritis. You'll hear psoriasis on AbbVie, Novartis, and Lilly earnings calls as one of the most competitive biologic markets, and at AAD when new clearance data resets the standard of care.
plain: A long-term skin condition where the immune system goes haywire and makes skin cells pile up into thick, scaly red patches.

snappy: A tumor-suppressor gene that brakes the PI3K growth pathway — when lost or inactivated, cells grow unchecked. Common in many cancers including prostate and brain.
detail: PTEN loss occurs in roughly half of advanced prostate cancers and a meaningful fraction of glioblastoma, endometrial cancer, and others. PTEN-deficient tumors are vulnerable to PI3K inhibitors and AKT inhibitors. You'll hear PTEN in precision-oncology trial-enrollment criteria and in pathway-targeted-therapy pipelines.
plain: A natural brake gene that holds back cell growth, and when it breaks, cells multiply without restraint and tumors take hold.

snappy: The testing every batch of drug must pass before being released — making sure the actual product meets every spec for purity, strength, and consistency.
detail: QC is part of GMP, run by manufacturing-facility teams. Failures lead to lot rejections, lost revenue, and sometimes drug shortages. You'll hear QC in manufacturing operations, in supply-chain discussions, and at FDA inspections where QC documentation is key audit material.
plain: The lab tests every batch of a drug must pass before leaving the factory, to make sure it is pure, strong, and consistent.

snappy: How a treatment affects a patient's day-to-day wellbeing — increasingly measured in trials, not just survival or tumor shrinkage.
detail: QoL endpoints are captured through patient-reported outcomes (PROs) covering pain, fatigue, function, and psychological wellbeing. They're particularly important for chronic-disease and palliative-setting trials. You'll hear QoL in trial-design discussions, in FDA labels (where some claims are added), and in HTA reviews where payers care about more than just efficacy.
plain: A measure of how much a treatment helps or harms a patient's everyday wellbeing, beyond simply living longer.

snappy: A measure of heart rhythm — when prolonged, it warns that a drug could trigger a dangerous arrhythmia. A standard safety check in drug development.
detail: Many drugs (some kinase inhibitors, antibiotics, antipsychotics) prolong the QTc and require ECG monitoring. The FDA reviews QTc data closely; significant prolongation can lead to label restrictions or rejection. You'll hear QTc in cardiac-safety discussions, in early-clinical trial design, and in any drug-development pitch involving QT-active classes.
plain: A heart-rhythm measurement on an electrocardiogram that flags when a drug might be making the heartbeat dangerously off-beat.

snappy: A breast-conserving surgery that removes about a quarter of the breast — used to take out a tumor along with a generous margin of surrounding tissue.
detail: Quadrantectomy is more extensive than a lumpectomy but less than a mastectomy, with comparable survival outcomes when combined with radiation in appropriate patients. It's most often discussed in early-stage breast cancer treatment planning. You'll hear quadrantectomy in surgical-oncology and breast-cancer treatment discussions.
plain: A breast surgery that removes about a quarter of the breast around a tumor, leaving most of the breast intact.

snappy: A laboratory technique that measures exactly how much of a specific DNA or RNA sequence is in a sample — used to detect mutations and monitor disease.
detail: qPCR is foundational in molecular diagnostics — used for COVID testing, BCR-ABL monitoring in CML, and minimal residual disease detection. Faster and cheaper than NGS for known targets, less comprehensive. You'll hear qPCR in molecular-diagnostics labs, in MRD-monitoring strategies, and in any commercial pitch around fast turnaround molecular testing.
plain: A lab method that copies a specific stretch of DNA over and over so you can measure exactly how much was there to start with.
Keeping people who might have caught a contagious disease away from others for a while, in case they become sick and spread it.
snappy: *Separating and restricting* people who may have been exposed to a contagious disease — distinct from isolating those already confirmed sick.
detail: Keeps apart people who were exposed to a contagious disease but aren't yet known to be infected, during the incubation period; isolation, by contrast, separates the confirmed sick. The word traces to the 40-day ('quaranta') ship holds of plague-era Venice. Paired with contact tracing, it helps choke off an outbreak. Authorities hold legal quarantine powers for notifiable diseases, balanced against civil liberties.

snappy: Non-dividing cells — cancer's hideout — that survive most chemotherapy drugs because chemo targets actively dividing cells.
detail: Quiescent (G0) cancer stem cells are thought to be a key reason cancers come back after seemingly successful treatment. Strategies to kill quiescent cells (or force them out of dormancy) are an active research area. You'll hear quiescent in cancer-stem-cell biology and in any drug-discovery pitch around dormancy-targeting therapies.
plain: Cells that are alive but parked, not dividing, which lets them dodge many chemotherapy drugs that only attack dividing cells.

snappy: Using high-energy beams (X-rays, protons, electrons) to damage cancer cell DNA and trigger their death — usually delivered over weeks of daily treatments.
detail: RT is used in roughly half of all cancer patients, either curatively (early-stage disease) or palliatively (symptom relief). Modern techniques (IMRT, SBRT, proton therapy) allow precise targeting that spares healthy tissue. You'll hear RT at radiation-oncology meetings (ASTRO), in combined-modality treatment discussions, and in commercial debates over proton-therapy economics.
plain: Using carefully aimed high-energy beams to scramble the DNA inside cancer cells so they cannot survive or multiply.

snappy: A family of signaling proteins (including BRAF and CRAF) that pass growth signals down the MAPK pathway — frequently mutated in melanoma and other cancers.
detail: BRAF is the most clinically important RAF, with V600E mutations in around 50% of melanomas, and approved drugs Tafinlar (dabrafenib), Zelboraf (vemurafenib), and Braftovi (encorafenib). Pan-RAF inhibitors targeting multiple family members are in development. You'll hear RAF in melanoma and colorectal cancer pipelines and in pathway-resistance discussions.
plain: A family of relay proteins inside cells that pass growth signals along, and when one gets stuck on, cancers like melanoma can take off.
A study that splits people randomly into a treatment group and a comparison group, so you can trust the difference came from the treatment.
snappy: The *gold standard* of clinical evidence — patients assigned at random to treatment or control, so the groups differ only by chance, not bias.
detail: Random assignment breaks the link between who gets which treatment and their prognosis, defeating confounding by design — which is why it outranks the cohort study and case-control study in evidence. Add blinding and a placebo and you isolate a drug's true effect. It is the backbone of the phase 3 trial and the FDA approval that follows. You'll hear randomized controlled trial cited as the bar every new therapy must clear.

snappy: The RAS family of genes (KRAS, NRAS, HRAS) — among the most-mutated drivers of human cancer, controlling cell growth signaling at the cellular membrane.
detail: RAS mutations occur in roughly 30% of all cancers, with KRAS the most clinically relevant in pancreatic, colorectal, and lung. After decades of being undruggable, KRAS G12C inhibitors (Lumakras, Krazati) opened the field; pan-KRAS and KRAS G12D inhibitors are in clinical testing. You'll hear RAS in any precision-oncology discussion of newly targetable drivers.
plain: A family of genes that act like a starter button for cell growth, jammed in the on position in about a third of all cancers.

snappy: A tumor-suppressor protein that controls when cells divide — loss of Rb function unleashes the cell cycle and is foundational to many cancers.
detail: RB1 mutations cause retinoblastoma in children; loss of Rb function is also widespread in lung, breast, prostate, and other adult cancers. Rb is the gatekeeper that CDK4/6 inhibitors work through — those drugs only help when Rb is intact. You'll hear Rb in cell-cycle pathway discussions and in CDK4/6-inhibitor trial design.
plain: A natural brake protein that decides when cells are allowed to divide; lose it, and the brakes come off, helping many cancers grow.
Going back into the hospital soon after leaving — usually counted within 30 days, and watched as a sign of care quality.
snappy: A patient *back in the hospital* soon after discharge — often within 30 days, and often a sign something slipped.
detail: A readmission is an unplanned return to inpatient care shortly after a discharge, conventionally measured at 30 days. It's a marquee quality metric: under value-based care, Medicare penalizes hospitals with high readmission rates, betting that better discharge planning and primary care follow-up could have prevented the bounce-back. Not every readmission is avoidable, which keeps the measure contentious. You'll hear readmission rates quoted whenever hospital quality and the DRG payment model are debated.

plain: Health data gathered during everyday care — from records, claims, and devices — rather than from a formal clinical trial.
snappy: The *raw data of everyday care* — electronic health records, claims, registries, wearables — that, once analyzed, becomes real-world evidence.
detail: Health information collected outside controlled trials: electronic health record entries, claims data, disease registries, and wearable streams. Analyzed, it becomes the real-world evidence the FDA increasingly accepts for label expansions and safety monitoring. Its messiness — missing fields, confounding — is the central challenge. You'll hear RWD across HEOR, regulatory, and digital health discussion.

snappy: Data on how drugs perform in routine clinical practice — drawn from electronic health records, insurance claims, and patient registries — rather than controlled trials.
detail: RWE is increasingly accepted by FDA for label expansions, post-marketing safety, and rare-disease evidence generation. Companies like Flatiron, Aetion, and Komodo Health build platforms around it. You'll hear RWE in commercial conversations about market access, in payer negotiations, and in regulatory submissions for hard-to-trial populations.
plain: Information about how drugs actually perform out in everyday life, pulled from medical records and insurance data, not tidy trials.

snappy: A discount drugmakers pay back to insurers and PBMs after the fact — in exchange for putting their drug on the formulary.
detail: Rebates are negotiated privately between manufacturers and PBMs, with the size often tied to formulary placement and market share. They're the engine behind US drug pricing's gross-to-net gap and a major target of policy reform — the Trump and Biden administrations both proposed rebate-reform rules. You'll hear pharma CFOs reference "rebate pressure" as the biggest variable in net pricing, and analysts model rebate trajectories at JPMorgan and on launch calls.
plain: A behind-the-scenes refund a drugmaker pays back to insurers later, in return for getting their drug onto the approved list.

snappy: A protein on cell surfaces or inside cells that receives biological signals — and the most common type of drug target in pharma.
detail: Receptors include G-protein-coupled receptors (the largest drug-target family), nuclear hormone receptors, kinase receptors, and many others. Drugs work as agonists (activate) or antagonists (block) at receptors. You'll hear receptor in basic pharmacology, in target-discovery pipelines, and in any drug-mechanism discussion.
plain: A protein on or inside a cell that catches incoming signals, like a docking station, and most drugs work by latching onto one.

snappy: When cancer comes back after treatment — either at the original site or somewhere new — the central problem oncology is trying to solve.
detail: Recurrence can be local (same site), regional (nearby lymph nodes), or distant (metastatic). The risk depends on stage at diagnosis, biology, and treatment received. Adjuvant and maintenance therapies aim to lower recurrence risk. You'll hear recurrence in every oncology survivorship discussion, in trial endpoints (disease-free survival), and in commercial pitches around early-stage drug positioning.
plain: When a cancer that seemed to be gone comes back, either at the original spot or somewhere new in the body.
When your regular doctor sends you to a specialist, often required before the specialist's visit is covered.
snappy: A primary care doctor's *formal hand-off* to a specialist — the ticket you often need before specialty care will see you.
detail: A referral is the request that moves a patient from primary care to specialty care, carrying the clinical reason and records with it. Under managed care it doubles as a cost-control valve: an insurer may require a referral, and sometimes a prior authorization, before it will cover the specialist visit. A smooth referral keeps care coordinated; a lost one is a classic crack patients fall through. You'll hear referral patterns analyzed in any look at access, network design, and care fragmentation.

snappy: Disease that fails to respond to treatment — different from relapsed disease, which initially responded and then came back.
detail: Refractory cancers are typically the toughest to treat, often having molecular features that confer resistance from the start. Trials in 'relapsed/refractory' (R/R) settings are common pathways for novel mechanisms to gain initial approval before moving earlier in treatment lines. You'll hear refractory in CAR-T trial enrollment, in salvage-therapy discussions, and in drug-development sequence framing.
plain: A disease that simply refuses to respond to a treatment from the start, unlike a relapsed one that worked first and then stopped.
A research-focused biotech whose antibody technology produced the blockbuster eczema drug Dupixent.
snappy: A science-driven biotech whose antibody platform produced Dupixent and the eye drug Eylea.
detail: Regeneron's antibody-discovery technology yielded the IL-4/13 blocker Dupixent (with Sanofi) and the retinal drug Eylea, plus an oncology pipeline. You'll hear Regeneron in immunology and antibody-engineering discussion.

snappy: Everything related to the FDA, EMA, and other agencies that decide whether and how a drug can be sold — and the function within pharma that manages those interactions.
detail: Regulatory affairs covers IND filings, NDA/BLA submissions, label negotiations, and post-marketing commitments. Strong regulatory strategy can shave months off approval timelines. You'll hear regulatory in any drug-development discussion, in earnings calls about expected approvals, and in M&A diligence around assets close to approval decisions.
plain: The world of government agencies, like the FDA, that decide whether a drug can be sold and exactly what its label can say.
How many times more likely something is in one group than another — a doubling of risk is a relative risk of two.
snappy: How many *times* more likely an outcome is in one group versus another — intuitive, but it can exaggerate a tiny absolute difference.
detail: Divides the outcome rate in a treated or exposed group by the rate in the comparison group; 1 means no difference. The cohort study and randomized controlled trial measure it directly. A scary 'doubling' can hide a trivial absolute risk reduction when the baseline is tiny, so read it beside the number needed to treat. You'll hear relative risk in every results write-up and guideline debate.

plain: An infused drug that was the first to treat inflammatory bowel disease by blocking an inflammatory signal.
snappy: An anti-TNF antibody that pioneered biologic treatment of inflammatory bowel disease.
detail: Remicade is an infused anti-TNF that transformed Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis along with rheumatoid arthritis. A Johnson & Johnson product, now facing biosimilars. You'll hear Remicade as the founding IBD biologic in gastroenterology discussion.

snappy: A state where cancer signs and symptoms are reduced or absent — partial when some disease remains, complete when no detectable disease is left.
detail: Complete remission doesn't always mean cure — microscopic disease can persist. Minimal residual disease (MRD) testing can detect what eyes and scans miss, increasingly guiding treatment decisions. You'll hear remission in hematology-oncology, in CAR-T efficacy discussions, and in commercial pitches around durable response.
plain: A welcome stretch where cancer signs shrink or vanish, though some hidden disease may still be lurking out of sight.
Using connected devices at home — like blood-pressure cuffs or glucose monitors — to send your health data to your care team between visits.
snappy: Home *connected devices* streaming a patient's vitals to clinicians between visits — a pillar of telehealth for chronic-disease care.
detail: It uses connected devices — blood-pressure cuffs, glucose meters, pulse oximeters, wearables — to capture health data at home and route it to clinicians. It extends telehealth into continuous care, helping manage chronic conditions and catch deterioration early. Medicare now reimburses it with dedicated codes. You'll hear RPM alongside wearable sensors and digital biomarkers in connected-health discussion.

snappy: A safety program the FDA can require for drugs whose benefits only outweigh the risks if specific guardrails — like patient registries or pharmacist training — stay in place.
detail: REMS programs vary in intensity: a simple medication guide for one drug, a full restricted-distribution system requiring physician certification for another. Examples include Clozaril (clozapine) for schizophrenia, which requires regular blood monitoring, and isotretinoin for acne, which requires the iPLEDGE registry to prevent fetal exposure. You'll see REMS discussed in FDA approval announcements and in commercial planning, since strict programs can substantially limit how easily a drug gets prescribed.
plain: A special FDA safety plan attached to risky drugs, requiring extra steps like monitoring or registries before patients can get them.
An injection that drives down 'bad' cholesterol by blocking a key protein, for people statins can't help enough.
snappy: An antibody that lowers LDL cholesterol by blocking PCSK9, used when statins aren't enough.
detail: Repatha is a PCSK9-blocking antibody that drives LDL to very low levels and cut cardiovascular events in outcome trials. An Amgen product whose price ICER scrutinized. You'll hear Repatha with Praluent and Leqvio in any PCSK9 discussion.

snappy: When a previously effective treatment stops working — typically because cancer cells evolved new mutations to escape the drug's mechanism.
detail: Resistance is the central challenge of targeted-therapy oncology. Mechanisms include new mutations (T790M in EGFR), pathway redundancy (MEK inhibition activating other pathways), and tumor heterogeneity. Combination strategies and next-generation drugs aim to delay or overcome resistance. You'll hear resistance in every targeted-therapy pipeline discussion.
plain: When a treatment that used to work stops working, usually because the disease has evolved a clever way around the drug.

snappy: A receptor that, when mutated or fused with other genes, drives certain thyroid and lung cancers — and that has approved targeted therapies.
detail: RET fusions occur in 1-2% of NSCLC and a fraction of papillary thyroid cancers; RET point mutations cause familial medullary thyroid cancer. Retevmo (selpercatinib) and Gavreto (pralsetinib) are highly active selective RET inhibitors. You'll hear RET in lung-cancer molecular-testing discussions and in commercial pitches around niche-but-defensible NSCLC subtypes.
plain: A docking-station protein on cells that, when broken or fused to another gene, drives certain thyroid and lung cancers.

snappy: A rare childhood eye cancer — almost always diagnosed before age 5 — caused by mutations in the RB1 tumor-suppressor gene.
detail: Retinoblastoma is rare (300-400 US cases annually) but historically devastating. Modern treatment (chemotherapy, focal therapies, occasionally enucleation) has cure rates above 95% in developed countries. The disease was the first to demonstrate the 'two-hit' tumor-suppressor model. You'll hear retinoblastoma in pediatric ophthalmology contexts and in cancer-genetics teaching.
plain: A rare eye cancer that almost always shows up in very young children, caused by losing both copies of a key brake gene.

snappy: An autoimmune disease where the immune system attacks the lining of joints — causing pain, swelling, and over time the kind of damage that deforms hands and feet.
detail: RA treatment has evolved from old-school methotrexate to TNF inhibitors like Humira (adalimumab), JAK inhibitors like Rinvoq (upadacitinib), and IL-6 blockers like Actemra (tocilizumab). Patients are typically managed by rheumatologists who escalate therapy as the disease progresses. You'll hear RA mentioned at every immunology investor day as the foundational autoimmune market, and on AbbVie and Lilly earnings calls when JAK inhibitors come up — they carry FDA Black Box Warnings for cardiovascular and cancer risk.
plain: A disease where the immune system mistakenly attacks the lining of joints, causing pain, swelling, and eventual damage to hands and feet.

snappy: The molecular machine that builds proteins by reading mRNA and stringing together amino acids in the right order.
detail: Each cell has millions of ribosomes, all working in parallel. They're made mostly of rRNA with some scaffold proteins. Several major antibiotic classes — macrolides, tetracyclines, aminoglycosides, oxazolidinones — work by gumming up bacterial ribosomes while leaving human ribosomes alone. New oncology research targets the human ribosome as a vulnerability in fast-growing cancers.
plain: The tiny molecular factory inside every cell that reads genetic instructions and builds proteins one amino acid at a time.
A pill — instead of an injection — that calms many autoimmune diseases by blocking an inflammation-signaling enzyme.
snappy: An oral JAK inhibitor across rheumatoid arthritis, atopic dermatitis, and inflammatory bowel disease — AbbVie's other post-Humira pillar.
detail: Rinvoq blocks JAK enzymes, offering a pill alternative to injected biologics across many immune diseases, though the JAK class carries a boxed warning. With Skyrizi it anchors AbbVie's growth. You'll hear Rinvoq in every immunology pipeline update.

snappy: The molecular messenger that carries genetic instructions from DNA to make proteins — and the basis for a new wave of vaccines and therapies.
detail: RNA-targeted therapies include antisense oligonucleotides (Spinraza, Kynamro), siRNA (Onpattro, Givlaari, Leqvio), and mRNA technologies that powered COVID-19 vaccines. Companies like Alnylam, Ionis, Moderna, and BioNTech built businesses here. You'll hear RNA in vaccine pipelines, rare-disease drug development, and any biotech pitch around nucleic-acid platforms.
plain: A messenger molecule that copies instructions from DNA and carries them to the parts of the cell that build proteins.

snappy: A natural cellular silencer that pharma has hijacked to switch off harmful genes — turning down the volume on disease at the source rather than blocking it downstream.
detail: RNAi drugs like Onpattro (patisiran) for hereditary amyloidosis and Leqvio (inclisiran) for high cholesterol use small RNA molecules to degrade specific mRNAs before they're translated into proteins. Alnylam pioneered the platform after the 2006 Nobel-winning discovery, and the field has expanded into liver, kidney, and CNS targets. You'll hear RNAi pitched as a platform alongside mRNA and gene therapy at JPMorgan, and earnings calls increasingly track the silencing-drug pipeline.
plain: A natural off-switch cells use to silence specific genes, which drugmakers now borrow to dial down disease-causing proteins.
A Swiss healthcare giant — owner of Genentech — that pioneered cancer antibody drugs and leads in medical testing.
snappy: The Swiss group that owns Genentech — a pioneer of cancer antibodies and the leader in diagnostics.
detail: Roche, through Genentech, pioneered antibody oncology (Herceptin, Avastin, Perjeta, Tecentriq, Rozlytrek) and pairs drugs with its world-leading diagnostics arm. You'll hear Roche in companion-diagnostic, biosimilar, and oncology discussion.

snappy: A receptor tyrosine kinase whose rare gene fusions drive a small subset of lung and other cancers — and that's strongly targetable with FDA-approved drugs.
detail: ROS1 fusions occur in 1-2% of NSCLC and are also seen in glioma, cholangiocarcinoma, and other cancers. Approved ROS1 inhibitors include Xalkori (crizotinib), Rozlytrek (entrectinib), Lorbrena (lorlatinib), and Augtyro (repotrectinib). You'll hear ROS1 in lung-cancer molecular-testing and in commercial discussions of next-generation TKIs.
plain: A docking-station protein that, in rare cases, fuses with other genes and drives a small slice of lung and other cancers.
A drug for rare cancers defined by a specific gene fusion — given based on the tumor's DNA, not where in the body it started.
snappy: A tissue-agnostic drug for the rare cancers driven by an NTRK gene fusion, wherever in the body they arise.
detail: Rozlytrek targets NTRK fusions (and ROS1), part of the shift to treating cancers by mutation rather than organ. You'll hear Rozlytrek with Vitrakvi in any discussion of NTRK fusions and tissue-agnostic approvals.

snappy: The structural and catalytic RNA that makes up the bulk of the ribosome — the protein-synthesis machine itself.
detail: Despite the name 'protein synthesis,' it's actually rRNA — not protein — that catalyzes the chemical bond-forming step inside ribosomes. Bacterial rRNA differs enough from human rRNA that drugs can selectively poison bacterial ribosomes without harming us; that's the basis for entire antibiotic classes. Sequencing rRNA (especially the 16S gene in bacteria) is the foundation of modern microbiome research.
plain: The structural RNA that makes up most of a ribosome, the cell's protein-building machine, and actually does the chemistry inside it.
A French pharmaceutical giant whose biggest drug, the eczema and asthma medicine Dupixent, is shared with Regeneron.
snappy: The French pharma giant whose biggest product, Dupixent, it shares with Regeneron.
detail: Sanofi's growth centers on the IL-4/13 blocker Dupixent (with Regeneron), alongside a major vaccines business. You'll hear Sanofi in immunology and vaccine discussion.

snappy: A diverse family of cancers arising from connective tissues — bone, muscle, fat, cartilage — collectively rare but covering more than 70 distinct subtypes.
detail: Sarcomas are uncommon (around 1% of adult cancers, more in children) but dramatic in their variety. Treatment is highly subtype-specific: GIST responds to imatinib, leiomyosarcoma to doxorubicin-based chemo, Ewing sarcoma to intensive multi-agent regimens. You'll hear sarcoma at specialized cancer centers and in any commercial pitch around tumor-agnostic biomarker-driven approvals.
plain: A broad family of cancers that start in connective tissues like bone, muscle, or fat, rather than in glands or skin.
Short for squamous cell carcinoma — a cancer of the flat surface cells that line the skin, lungs, and head and neck.
snappy: The common abbreviation for squamous cell carcinoma — a cancer of the flat surface cells lining skin, lung, head and neck, and other organs.
detail: SCC arises from squamous epithelium and is a major subtype of skin, lung, and head-and-neck cancer. You'll hear 'SCC' shorthand in pathology reports and at ASCO; the full picture lives under squamous cell carcinoma.

snappy: A serious mental illness causing hallucinations, delusions, and disorganized thinking — typically emerging in young adulthood and lifelong, but manageable with the right treatment.
detail: Treatment relies on antipsychotics — older ones like haloperidol and newer atypicals like Abilify (aripiprazole), Latuda (lurasidone), and Cobenfy (xanomeline-trospium), the first non-dopamine antipsychotic approved by the FDA in decades. Long-acting injectable forms help patients who struggle with daily pills. You'll hear schizophrenia framed at JPMorgan as one of the most stagnant therapeutic areas before Cobenfy's 2024 approval reset expectations, and on launch calls discussing the long-acting injectable market.
plain: A serious brain illness that distorts thinking and perception, often bringing hallucinations and delusions, usually first appearing in young adults.

snappy: A particularly aggressive form of lung cancer that grows fast, spreads quickly, and is almost always linked to a long smoking history.
detail: SCLC accounts for around 15% of lung cancers and historically had grim prognosis with limited treatment evolution. Recent additions of checkpoint inhibitors (Tecentriq, Imfinzi) plus chemo and the DLL3-targeting bispecific Imdelltra (tarlatamab) have brought new hope. You'll hear SCLC at thoracic-oncology meetings and in commercial discussions of immunotherapy and bispecific-antibody expansion.
plain: A fast-growing and aggressive form of lung cancer, almost always tied to a long history of smoking, that spreads quickly through the body.
Testing people who feel fine to catch a disease early, like mammograms or colonoscopies, when it's easier to treat.
snappy: Testing *apparently healthy* people to catch disease early — mammograms, colonoscopies, newborn blood spots — before symptoms appear.
detail: Looking for disease in people without symptoms, to catch it when treatment works best — cancer (mammography, colonoscopy, Pap), newborn metabolic panels, blood-pressure checks. A good program weighs a test's sensitivity and specificity against the harms of false alarms and overdiagnosis. Population programs can lower mortality, but only where early action helps, by shifting detected incidence toward earlier stages — and are most worthwhile where prevalence is high enough to justify mass testing. Coverage rules often hinge on task-force recommendations.

snappy: The treatment given when first-line therapy fails or stops working — usually less effective than first-line, with smaller patient populations and tougher commercial economics.
detail: Second-line treatments are critical safety nets but typically face declining response rates and shorter survival. Drugs often launch in second-line indications and migrate to first-line over time. You'll hear second-line in oncology trial-enrollment criteria, FDA labels (often initial approval), and commercial framing of treatment-line strategy.
plain: The treatment doctors turn to when the first one stops working, usually with smaller chances of success than the original.

snappy: The most common type of testicular cancer — historically deadly, now one of the most curable cancers thanks to platinum-based chemotherapy.
detail: Seminomas are highly sensitive to radiation and chemotherapy, with cure rates above 95% even at advanced stages. The success story made testicular cancer a model for what targeted treatment can achieve. You'll hear seminoma in GU oncology contexts and as a historical reference for cancer treatment progress.
plain: The most common kind of testicular cancer, and one of medicine's biggest success stories, with cure rates above 95 percent.

snappy: A permanent state where cells stop dividing — a built-in protection against cancer that, paradoxically, can also accumulate aging-related damage.
detail: Cellular senescence prevents damaged cells from becoming cancerous, but senescent cells secrete inflammatory factors that may contribute to aging and chronic disease. 'Senolytic' drugs that clear senescent cells are an emerging therapeutic category. You'll hear senescence in cancer biology, in aging research, and in early-stage biotech pitches.
plain: A retirement state for cells — they stop dividing as a guard against cancer, but the stuck cells can leak signals that age the body.
How good a test is at catching people who really have a disease — a very sensitive test rarely misses a true case.
snappy: A test's ability to *catch true cases* — high sensitivity means few sick people are missed, so a negative result is reassuring.
detail: The share of people with a disease whom a test correctly flags — its true-positive rate. A highly sensitive test produces few false negatives, so a clear result helps rule disease out, prized in screening. It trades off against specificity: dialing one up often drags the other down. Combined with disease prevalence, it shapes the negative predictive value. You'll hear sensitivity quoted for every diagnostic and screening tool.

plain: A kidney protein that reabsorbs sugar. Block it and you pass excess glucose in urine — a diabetes drug that also protects the heart.
snappy: A kidney glucose-reabsorption pump; blocking it spills sugar into urine — the mechanism behind Jardiance, now a heart-failure mainstay.
detail: SGLT2 inhibitors — Jardiance, Farxiga — were developed for type 2 diabetes but proved to cut heart-failure and kidney-disease events, reshaping cardiology guidelines. You'll hear SGLT2 at AHA and on every cardiometabolic earnings call as one of the decade's most important mechanisms.

snappy: A class of pills that lowers blood sugar by making the kidneys flush excess glucose into the urine — and unexpectedly turned out to also protect the heart.
detail: Originally approved for type 2 diabetes, SGLT2 inhibitors — Jardiance (empagliflozin), Farxiga (dapagliflozin), Invokana (canagliflozin) — proved in landmark trials to reduce cardiovascular death and hospitalization in heart failure patients regardless of diabetes status, and to slow chronic kidney disease. The class has become standard of care across cardiology and nephrology. You'll hear SGLT2s on every cardio earnings call and at AHA when guideline updates expand their use.
plain: A pill for diabetes that lowers blood sugar by making the kidneys flush extra sugar out into urine, and quietly protects the heart too.

snappy: An inherited blood disorder where a single mutation causes red cells to deform into a rigid sickle shape, blocking blood vessels and causing crippling pain crises.
detail: Sickle cell affects millions globally, mostly people of African ancestry. After decades of underinvestment, 2023 brought two competing gene therapies: Vertex/CRISPR Therapeutics' Casgevy (the first CRISPR-edited drug ever approved) and bluebird bio's Lyfgenia. Both run ~$2.2-3.1M with intensive transplant-style preparation. Adavosertib (Oxbryta) was withdrawn 2024 over mortality data — a setback for the small-molecule approach.
plain: An inherited disease where a tiny genetic typo bends red blood cells into rigid crescents that clog vessels and cause searing pain attacks.

snappy: Any unintended effect of a drug beyond its main therapeutic action — ranges from mild (nausea, dry mouth) to dangerous (organ damage, death).
detail: Every drug has side effects and the entire drug-approval framework is fundamentally a benefit-vs-risk calculation. Common terms you'll hear: 'adverse event' (the formal regulatory term), 'tolerability' (the patient experience), 'black box warning' (the most serious labeling requirement), and 'discontinuation rate' (how often patients quit due to side effects). Many drug-launch failures trace to side-effect profiles being too punishing relative to the benefit — see 2022's Aduhelm and many other examples.
plain: Anything a drug does that you didn't want it to — from mild nausea to serious organ damage — running alongside its intended job.

snappy: Short pieces of RNA that silence specific genes — the basis of a new class of drugs for previously hard-to-treat genetic diseases.
detail: siRNA therapies (Onpattro, Givlaari, Leqvio, Amvuttra) selectively reduce production of disease-causing proteins. The technology is central to Alnylam's pipeline and increasingly to broader RNA medicine. You'll hear siRNA in rare-disease drug development, in cardiovascular pipelines (PCSK9, lipoprotein(a)), and in any biotech pitch around the RNAi platform.
plain: Tiny snippets of genetic code used as drugs that switch off a single faulty gene, telling cells to stop making the protein causing trouble.
A newer psoriasis and gut-disease drug that blocks a specific inflammatory signal, picked to replace the blockbuster Humira.
snappy: An IL-23 blocker for psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease — AbbVie's designated successor to Humira.
detail: Skyrizi targets IL-23 with infrequent dosing and strong skin-clearance results in psoriasis, expanding into Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis. With Rinvoq it's AbbVie's post-Humira growth engine. You'll hear Skyrizi in every AbbVie immunology update.

snappy: A traditional chemical drug — small enough to be made into a pill, swallowed, and absorbed. Most cancer drugs and almost everything in your medicine cabinet.
detail: Small molecules contrast with biologics (large protein drugs that need injection). They're typically cheaper to make, easier to administer, and can cross cell membranes to hit intracellular targets. Most kinase inhibitors and degraders are small molecules. You'll hear small molecule in modality-comparison discussions and in commercial competitive-intelligence.
plain: An old-school chemical drug small enough to swallow as a pill — most of what's in your medicine cabinet falls into this category.

snappy: The aggressive 15% of lung cancers — fast-growing, strongly tied to smoking, and historically chemo-only.
detail: SCLC's natural history is grim: it spreads early and chemo response is usually short-lived. Recent additions are atezolizumab (Tecentriq) and durvalumab (Imfinzi) added to chemo, plus the DLL3-targeting bispecific tarlatamab (Imdelltra) approved 2024 — the first novel mechanism in this space in decades. SCLC commentary on biotech earnings calls focuses heavily on novel targets because the unmet need is so high.
plain: The aggressive flavour of lung cancer, tightly tied to smoking, that grows fast and has long resisted anything beyond chemotherapy.

snappy: The currently accepted best treatment for a condition — what doctors prescribe by default and what new drugs have to beat to get approved.
detail: SOC is defined by clinical guidelines (NCCN, ESMO, ASCO) and changes as new evidence emerges. Trials usually compare the new drug to SOC; superiority over SOC is what gets a drug approved and onto commercial guidelines. You'll hear SOC in every trial-design discussion, in competitive-positioning conversations, and in payer access debates.
plain: The treatment doctors normally give for a condition — the benchmark a new drug has to outperform before regulators will approve it.
The everyday conditions — money, housing, schooling, food, neighborhood — that affect your health more than doctors and medicine do.
snappy: The *non-medical* conditions — income, housing, education, food, neighborhood — that shape health long before any clinic visit does.
detail: The circumstances people are born, live, and work in: economic standing, education, food security, housing, and access to care. They explain much of the gap in morbidity and mortality between populations — often more than medical care itself. Payers and value-based care programs increasingly screen for them, since fixing housing or nutrition can cut costly hospital use. You'll hear the term at every health-equity discussion.

plain: Software that does a medical job on its own — like an app that detects a heart problem — and is regulated as a medical device.
snappy: *Software that is itself the medical device* — diagnosing or treating without hardware — and is regulated by the FDA as such.
detail: It performs a medical function on its own — an algorithm flagging strokes on a CT scan, an app detecting arrhythmia — rather than running a physical instrument. The FDA regulates it, with evolving pathways for AI models that keep learning. It overlaps with digital therapeutics (DTx). You'll hear SaMD wherever health AI, regulatory clearance, and clinical decision support are discussed.

snappy: A genetic change that happens in a body cell during life — not inherited from parents, and only present in the descendants of that one cell.
detail: Most cancer-driving mutations are somatic — they accumulate in cells over a lifetime due to DNA damage. The distinction from germline (inherited) mutations matters for genetic counseling, family-screening recommendations, and reproductive decisions. You'll hear somatic in tumor-sequencing discussions and in any counseling around hereditary vs. sporadic cancer.
plain: A genetic typo that happens inside a single body cell during life, passed only to its descendants — not inherited, not passed to children.
The pill that made hepatitis C curable — a real triumph whose very high price set off years of drug-cost debate.
snappy: The hepatitis C pill that turned a chronic liver infection into a curable disease — and ignited the drug-pricing wars.
detail: Sovaldi cures most hepatitis C with a short oral course, a genuine medical triumph. Its ~$1,000-per-pill launch price made it the flashpoint of US drug-pricing politics. A Gilead product. You'll hear Sovaldi as the case study in innovation-versus-affordability.

plain: Care from a doctor who focuses on one area of medicine, like the heart or cancer, usually seen after a referral.
snappy: Care from a *narrow expert* — a cardiologist, oncologist, or neurologist — usually reached through a referral rather than walking in off the street.
detail: Specialty care picks up where primary care hands off: a clinician trained deep in one organ system or disease who manages the complex or unusual. Reaching it typically needs a referral, and under managed care a prior authorization as well. Specialists deliver much of the high-cost, high-acuity medicine — the cancer regimens, the heart failure devices — which makes them a focus of both clinical advance and spending control. You'll hear specialty care contrasted with primary care whenever access, wait times, or the cost of fragmented care comes up.

plain: A pharmacy set up to handle complex, very expensive drugs — like biologics and cancer treatments — that need special care and support.
snappy: A pharmacy built to handle complex, high-cost drugs — biologics, cancer and rare-disease therapies — that need special handling and support.
detail: Specialty pharmacies dispense expensive, often injectable or refrigerated drugs requiring patient education, adherence support, and prior authorization. They're where most of pharma's revenue growth flows and a focus of PBM consolidation. You'll hear specialty pharmacy in any biologics or market-access discussion.

plain: How good a test is at correctly clearing people who don't have a disease — a very specific test rarely raises a false alarm.
snappy: A test's ability to *clear the truly healthy* — high specificity means few false alarms, so a positive result is more believable.
detail: The share of disease-free people a test correctly clears — its true-negative rate. High specificity means few false positives, so a positive result is more trustworthy and confirmatory testing leans on it. It trades against sensitivity. With disease prevalence it sets the positive predictive value — which is why even a specific test throws many false alarms when a disease is rare. You'll hear specificity beside sensitivity in any diagnostic's performance claims.

snappy: A common type of cancer arising from flat 'squamous' cells found in skin, lung, head and neck, cervix, and esophagus — covering several quite distinct diseases.
detail: Cutaneous SCC is among the most common skin cancers; lung SCC and head-and-neck SCC are tied to smoking and HPV; esophageal SCC has a different geographic and risk profile. Treatment differs dramatically by site. You'll hear SCC in pathology reports across many cancer specialties.
plain: A cancer of the flat, scale-like cells that line the skin, lungs, throat and other surfaces — actually a family of quite different diseases.

snappy: The most-prescribed class of antidepressants — they raise serotonin levels in the brain by blocking the molecular vacuum that would normally pull it back into nerve cells.
detail: Prozac (fluoxetine), Zoloft (sertraline), and Lexapro (escitalopram) are the household-name SSRIs, used in depression, anxiety, OCD, and PTSD. They work over weeks rather than instantly, and carry the FDA's Black Box Warning for suicide risk in young patients. You'll hear SSRIs in earnings calls when generics-vs-brand pricing comes up, and in policy debates around mental-health access — they're one of the most prescribed drug classes in the US.
plain: The most-prescribed family of antidepressants — they boost mood by stopping brain cells from sucking the chemical serotonin back out of circulation.

snappy: The body of testing that proves a drug stays safe and potent through its claimed shelf life — under storage temperatures, light exposure, and packaging conditions.
detail: Stability programs run for years and follow ICH guidelines, with samples pulled at intervals and tested for potency, impurities, and degradation products. The data set the expiration date printed on every package and dictate cold-chain requirements. You'll see stability cited in FDA inspection reports, in formulation patents, and in earnings-call discussions when temperature excursions force product recalls or extend launches in markets without reliable cold storage.
plain: The testing that proves a drug still works and stays safe through its shelf life under real storage conditions like heat, light, and packaging.

snappy: How far cancer has spread — usually 1 (localized) to 4 (metastatic) — and the single most important factor in choosing treatment and predicting outcomes.
detail: Staging is done through imaging, biopsy, and surgery using systems like TNM. Stage migration (better detection moving more patients to earlier stages) confounds long-term outcome comparisons. You'll hear stage in every oncology context — clinical decisions, trial enrollment, commercial market segmentation.
plain: A number from 1 to 4 saying how far cancer has spread — the biggest clue to what treatment is needed and how things may go.

snappy: The treatment that's currently considered best practice for a given condition — the benchmark new drugs need to beat (or match with better tolerability).
detail: Standard of care evolves over time and varies by region — what's SOC in the US may not be elsewhere due to drug approval timing or pricing. Trial designs choose SOC as the comparator arm whenever ethically possible (placebo-controlled trials in serious diseases are increasingly rare). 'Front-line' or '1L' SOC is a particularly contested space because that's where most patients start — reorganizing the SOC of a major indication is one of the highest-value things a new drug can do.
plain: The treatment currently considered best practice for a condition — the bar a new drug must clear, or at least match with fewer side effects.

snappy: The class of cholesterol-lowering pills nearly every American over 50 has been offered — they block the liver enzyme that builds cholesterol from scratch.
detail: Statins — Lipitor (atorvastatin), Crestor (rosuvastatin), simvastatin — are among the most-prescribed drugs in history, proven to cut heart attacks and strokes by roughly 25% in at-risk patients. All major statins are now generic and cost pennies a pill. You'll hear statins on cardio earnings calls as the durable backdrop newer cholesterol drugs (PCSK9 inhibitors, RNAi like Leqvio) have to beat on either potency or convenience, and in formulary discussions as the textbook generic baseline.
plain: The cholesterol-lowering pills millions take every day — they block the liver from building cholesterol and cut heart attack risk substantially.
A study's ability to spot a real effect when there is one — too small a study can miss a true benefit just by being underpowered.
snappy: A study's *ability to detect a real effect* if one exists — too little, and a genuine benefit hides in the noise as a false negative.
detail: The probability of avoiding a type II error — of catching an effect that is truly present. By convention trials target 80–90% statistical power, which drives the sample-size calculation: rarer outcomes and smaller effects demand more patients. An underpowered study risks a falsely negative result and wasted patients. You'll hear statistical power argued over at the design stage of any randomized controlled trial.

plain: A drug for psoriasis and gut disease that blocks two related inflammatory signals at once.
snappy: An IL-12/23 blocker for psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease, a major Johnson & Johnson product now meeting biosimilars.
detail: Stelara blocks the shared subunit of IL-12 and IL-23, treating psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, Crohn's disease, and ulcerative colitis. You'll hear Stelara as a biosimilar target and the predecessor to selective IL-23 drugs like Skyrizi and Tremfya.

snappy: An undifferentiated cell that can both renew itself and develop into specialized cell types — the source of every tissue in the body.
detail: Hematopoietic stem-cell transplants (bone marrow transplants) are decades-old and used for blood cancers and severe immune disorders. Embryonic and induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) underpin newer regenerative therapies in development for Parkinson's, diabetes (Vertex's VX-880 and zimislecel), and macular degeneration. The field has long been dogged by hype-vs-evidence tension; most actual approvals to date are in transplant rather than the 'grow-a-new-organ' future scenarios.
plain: A blank-slate cell that can both copy itself and grow into any specialised tissue — the body's raw material for skin, blood, bone, everything.

snappy: Replacing damaged blood-forming cells with healthy ones — either the patient's own (autologous) or a donor's (allogeneic) — to enable high-dose chemotherapy or treat blood cancers directly.
detail: Allogeneic SCT can be curative in leukemias and lymphomas but carries graft-versus-host disease risk. Autologous SCT is safer but more limited in efficacy. CAR-T therapies have replaced SCT in some settings. You'll hear SCT in hematology contexts, in cell-therapy commercial discussions, and in transplant-center economics.
plain: Swapping out damaged blood-making cells in the bone marrow for healthy ones, either the patient's own or from a matched donor.

snappy: An insurance rule that makes you try a cheaper drug first — and only pay for the expensive one if the cheap one fails.
detail: Also called "fail-first," step therapy is a cost-control tool insurers and PBMs use to steer patients toward generics or preferred brands before approving newer, pricier options. Patients and physicians often appeal it as a barrier to care, especially in autoimmune diseases where biologics like Humira (adalimumab) sit behind a step. You'll hear it on earnings calls when pharma talks about "access barriers," and in policy debates about restrictive utilization management.
plain: An insurance rule that forces you to try a cheaper drug first, and only covers the pricier one if the cheaper option fails.
Sorting study participants into groups by an important trait — like disease stage — before assigning treatment, so the groups stay comparable.
snappy: Splitting *enrollment into subgroups* — by stage, biomarker, or risk — then randomizing within each, so key factors stay balanced across the groups.
detail: Dividing participants by prognostic factors — disease stage, a biomarker, prior therapy — and randomizing within each layer guarantees those factors split evenly, stopping them from confounding the result. It also lets pre-planned subgroup analysis proceed honestly, and is set by the enrollment criteria. You'll hear stratification in trial-design and biomarker discussion, where a positive subgroup can rescue or sink a whole program.

snappy: A medical emergency where blood flow to part of the brain is cut off — by a clot or a bleed — causing brain cells to die within minutes.
detail: Strokes are split into ischemic (clot, ~85%) and hemorrhagic (bleed) — treatment hinges on which one and how fast. Ischemic strokes get tPA (alteplase) or mechanical thrombectomy if caught within hours. Stroke prevention drives huge anticoagulant markets — Eliquis (apixaban) for atrial fibrillation, statins for atherosclerosis. You'll hear stroke at every BMS-Pfizer earnings call linked to Eliquis, in cardiovascular trial readouts at AHA and ESC, and in policy commentary about the unequal US burden across geography and race.
plain: A brain emergency where blood flow gets blocked or a vessel bursts, killing brain cells within minutes — every second of delay means more damage.

snappy: Drug delivery into the fatty layer just under the skin — usually through an at-home injection, instead of an IV at the clinic.
detail: SubQ formulations (Darzalex Faspro, Phesgo, Tecentriq Hybreza) are major lifecycle plays for biologics, reducing patient burden, infusion-suite costs, and time on infusion. The reformulation can also extend patent protection. You'll hear SubQ in every biologic lifecycle-management discussion.
plain: An injection given just under the skin into a fatty layer — usually self-administered at home instead of an IV at the clinic.

snappy: A measurable outcome that's expected to predict real clinical benefit — a faster proxy that can support drug approval before long-term outcomes are known.
detail: Common oncology surrogates: progression-free survival, overall response rate, pathologic complete response. The FDA increasingly demands that surrogates be validated to predict survival or quality of life. You'll hear surrogate endpoints in regulatory discussions, in accelerated-approval debates, and at any FDA AdCom evaluating a non-OS-based approval.
plain: A quicker measurement, like tumour shrinkage, used as a stand-in for the real goal of living longer — letting drugs get approved faster.
An early 'multi-target' pill for kidney cancer that blocks several of a tumor's growth and blood-supply signals at once.
snappy: An early multikinase inhibitor for kidney cancer and GIST, blocking VEGF receptors among other targets.
detail: Sutent blocks multiple kinases to cut tumor blood supply and growth, long a standard in advanced kidney cancer and in GIST after Gleevec. You'll hear Sutent as a first-generation multikinase reference in any kidney cancer discussion.

snappy: A drug-discovery strategy where a treatment is harmless to normal cells but lethal to cancer cells that already carry a specific defect — a one-two punch the cancer can't absorb.
detail: PARP inhibitors in BRCA-mutated cancers are the textbook synthetic lethality success: BRCA loss + PARP inhibition = cancer cell death; either alone is survivable. The concept underlies many emerging precision-oncology programs. You'll hear synthetic lethality in DNA-damage-response biotech pipelines and in any commercial pitch around biomarker-driven selectivity.
